en: Vālmīki: Rāmāyaṇa, 4. Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 4.001.001a Having gone to that lotus pond, which was teeming with lotuses, water-lilies, and fish...
4.001.001c Accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, Rāma lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
4.001.002a Upon merely seeing her, his senses trembled with passion;
having fallen under the power of desire, he spoke this to the son of Sumitrā.
"O Saumitri, behold the beautiful forest of Pampā,
where the trees, resembling mountains, shine as if they were peaks. But as for me, tormented by grief, my anxieties truly afflict me."
Due to the sorrow of Bharata and the abduction of Vaidehī,
this dark-green and yellow meadow appears even more radiant,
as if covered with the variegated flower-blossoms of the trees like decorative carpets.
"O Saumitri, this breeze is pleasant; it is a season abounding in passion.
This fragrant month is perfumed, and the trees are laden with blossoms and fruit. Behold, O Saumitri, the forms of the forests adorned with flowers."
They released showers of flowers like the rain from water-bearing clouds;
and upon the lovely grassy slopes, various forest trees,
shaken by the force of the wind, strewed the earth with blossoms.

A breeze, cool as sandalwood and pleasant to the touch, blows through the forests fragrant with honey, where bees hum in harmony; it moves across delightful mountain plateaus adorned with beautiful, flowering trees.
The mountains, with their closely joined peaks, shine forth with great trees;
and look at these *karṇikāra* trees on all sides, their tops in full bloom,
appearing like men clad in yellow garments covered with gold.
"O Saumitri, this spring, resounding with the songs of various birds,
inflames my grief as I am separated from Sītā.
For the god of love torments me, who am already overwhelmed by sorrow."
"Exultant and calling out, the cuckoo challenges me; and this joyful gallinule, crying out by the lovely forest waterfall,
will cause me grief as I am possessed by love, O Lakṣmaṇa."
O Saumitri, these birds of sweet song, mingled with their mates and rejoicing in their own flocks, are as delighted as the *bhṛṅgarāja* birds;
yet that lady with eyes like a young deer’s has overcome me with the force of her anxiety and grief.
O Saumitri, this cruel breeze from the Caitra forest causes me great anguish. On the mountain ridges, the peacocks surrounded by their peahens increase my passion as I am already overwhelmed by love.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this crested peahen is dancing beside her dancing mate;
afflicted by love on these mountain slopes,
she surely has not been carried off by a rākṣasa from the forest where the peacock dwells."
"But for me, living without him is utterly unbearable during this month of flowers.
Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at these blossoms; they have become fruitless for me, even though the forests are so rich with their burden of flowers at the end of winter."
4.001.021a The birds, filled with joy, utter sweet notes in their flocks;
4.001.021c as if calling out to one another, they provoke my passion for love. 4.001.022a Surely Sītā too, being under the power of others, must be grieving just as I do.
"My beloved is dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, and she speaks softly; this flower-bearing breeze, cool to the touch yet bringing frost,
resembles a fire to me as I think of that lovely woman."
Then, without her, that bird, the crow perched upon the tree, cried out;
he was shouting with great joy.
Indeed, this bird there was the messenger for Vaidehī.
"The bird will surely lead me to the presence of the large-eyed lady.
Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the chorus in the forest that increases my longing,
as the birds warble among the trees with blossoming tops."
"O Saumitri, look! Amidst the variegated forest groves of Pampā, the lotuses shine upon the water like the rising sun.
This lake, with its clear waters, is filled with lotuses and blue water-lilies."

The Pampā lake, filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and abounding in fragrant lotuses, is ever frequented by ruddy geese; its forested slopes are variegated, and it is graced by herds of wild elephants seeking water.
"Indeed, O Lakṣmaṇa, my sight longs to behold the petals of the lotus-buds,
for they resemble the two eye-sockets of Sītā.
Emerging from between the trees, it is mingled with the filaments of the lotuses."
The enchanting breeze blows like the sigh of Sītā. O Saumitri, behold upon the southern mountain slope of Pampā that most beautiful flowering branch of a *karṇikāra* tree.
This king of mountains is further adorned with mineral ores;
struck by the force of the wind, it produces a variegated dust.
O son of Sumitrā, the mountain plateaus are covered everywhere with trees in full bloom.
With their leaves fallen yet beautiful on all sides, these *kuṃśuka* trees are like lamps;
and these trees growing on the banks of the Pampā stand closely together, fragrant with honey,
along with groves of *mālatī* and *mallikā* jasmine and blossoming *karavīra* flowers.
4.001.036a Ketakī flowers, sinduvāra, and vāsantī trees in full bloom;
4.001.036c mādhavī vines rich with fragrance, and kunda shrubs on all sides;
4.001.037a ciribilva, madhūka, vañjula, and likewise bakula trees.
Campaka trees, tilakas, and nāga trees were in full bloom;
nīpas, varaṇas, and kharjūras were beautifully flowering;
as were aṅkolas, kuraṇṭas, cūrṇakas, and pāribhadrakas.
Mango trees, *pāṭala*s, and blossoming *kovidāra*s, as well as *mucukunda*s and *arjuna*s, are seen upon the mountain ridges; likewise,
*ketaka*, *uddālaka*, *śirīṣa*, *śiṃśapā*, and *dhava* trees.
There were *śālmali* trees, *kiṃśuka* trees, and red *kurabaka* trees; likewise *tiniśa*, *naktamāla*, sandalwood, and *syandana* trees—
various kinds [of trees] with various flowers upon those mountain ridges.
"O Saumitri, the ground has been strewn with [flowers] that have acquired a yellowish-red luster.
O Saumitri, behold the blossoming of the trees at the end of winter;
for in this month of flowers, the trees have burst into bloom as if from mutual emulation."
"Behold, O Saumitri, this river of cool waters, filled with ten thousand lotuses,
frequented by *cakravāka* birds and inhabited by *kāraṇḍava* ducks; it is crowded with water-fowl and cranes, and frequented by boars and deer."
The Pampā lake shines all the more with the warbling birds;
these various joyful birds seem to inflame my desire as I remember my beloved Śyāmā, who has a moon-like face and eyes like lotuses.
On the variegated mountain ridges, he saw deer accompanied by does; but me, deprived of Vaidehī, whose eyes are like those of a young fawn—
he, thus lamenting there, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
He beheld the auspicious Pampā, flowing with delightful waters and beautiful;
gazing upon it, the high-souled one suddenly surveyed the entire forest, along with its waterfalls and caves.
With an agitated mind, he set out together with Lakṣmaṇa, reflecting and overcome by sorrow;
those two then proceeded together toward Ṛṣyamūka.
Seeing that place frequented by Sugrīva and the monkeys,
the monkeys became terrified upon beholding those two of great splendor, Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa.
But seeing those two high-souled brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, heroes bearing excellent weapons, Sugrīva became apprehensive;
with an anxious heart, he gazed in all directions.
The bull among monkeys did not halt in any single place;
looking about for those two of great strength, he could not fix his mind on any spot.
As the monkey was seized by supreme fear, his heart sank.
Having reflected and deliberated upon the relative gravity of the situation,
that righteous Sugrīva became deeply anxious along with all his followers.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, spoke to his ministers.

4.002.005c Seeing those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke, greatly agitated: 4.002.006a "These two have surely been dispatched by Vālin to this impenetrable forest; 4.002.006c wearing garments of bark as a disguise, they have come here wandering about."
Then the ministers of Sugrīva, having seen those two supreme archers,
went from that mountain slope to another excellent peak. Having quickly approached the leader of the host, those leaders of the hosts [spoke].
The monkeys stood surrounding the best of monkeys;
moving from mountain to mountain by a single path,
they leaped along, shaking the peaks of the mountains with their speed.
Then all those mighty monkeys, leaping about,
broke down the flowering trees situated on that difficult terrain;
those best of monkeys leaped everywhere across that great mountain.
Then, terrifying the deer, wildcats, and tigers, they proceeded.
Thereupon, the ministers of Sugrīva, who were dwelling upon that lord of mountains,
all approached the chief of monkeys and stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Then Hanumān, skilled in speech, addressed these words to Sugrīva, who was terrified by fear and apprehensive of Vālin’s transgression:
"O bull among monkeys, since you have fled with a troubled mind..."

"I do not see that cruel Vālin here, of fierce appearance, from whom, O gentle one, you have fear of your elder brother who committed evil deeds. That wicked-souled Vālin is not here; therefore, I see no cause for your fear."
"O monkey, it is clearly evident that you are but a branch-dweller,
for because of your fickle mind, you do not steady yourself in thought. Though endowed with intelligence and discernment, you act upon everything merely by outward gestures."
"For a king who has not attained wisdom does not indeed govern all living beings.
Then Sugrīva, having heard all those auspicious words of Hanumān,
spoke even more auspicious words to Hanumān.
"Whose fear would not arise upon seeing these two, who have long arms and large eyes, and who carry arrows, bows, and swords— resembling the sons of the gods?
I suspect these two excellent men have been dispatched by Vālin."
Kings have many friends, yet trust in them is not appropriate here; for enemies move about in disguise among men,
and being themselves untrustworthy, they strike at those who trust them during moments of vulnerability.
"In their undertakings, the wise King Vālī and kings of great vision appear as if they were destroyers of others; they must be understood thus by ordinary men.
Therefore, O monkey, having gone there, you too must recognize them as such, for you are indeed an ordinary man."
By means of various suspicious gestures and by conversing with them,
observe their disposition to see if they are joyful at heart;
inspire confidence in them again and again with words of praise and through your physical expressions.
"Standing right before me, O bull among monkeys, ask these two archers the purpose of their entry into this forest; O monkey,
find out whether they are pure-souled."
"Whether by their speech or by their physical forms, the wickedness of these two shall be recognized.
Having been thus instructed by the king of monkeys, the son of the Wind-god set his mind on going to where Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were.
Saying "So be it," Hanumān, the high-souled one, honored the words of that monkey who was both greatly terrified and difficult to approach, and then departed.
Having understood the words of the high-souled Sugrīva regarding where the exceedingly powerful Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were,
Hanumān leapt from Mount Ṛśyamūka to where the two descendants of Raghu were.
Having gone there, the powerful Hanumān, the best of monkeys and one whose valor is truth, approached those two with gentle words;
having abandoned his own form, the monkey appeared in the guise of a mendicant.
He spoke to those two heroes and praised them appropriately, saying:
"O ascetics of rigid vows, resembling royal sages and gods,
how have you two of excellent complexion come to this region?"
Terrifying herds of deer and other forest-dwelling creatures,
the two powerful ones gazed all around at the trees growing on the banks of the Pampā,
beautifying this river of auspicious waters.
"Who are you two, so courageous and golden-hued, yet clad in garments of bark? You heroes, with the gaze of lions and the exceeding strength and prowess of lions,
hold in your massive arms bows resembling the rainbow of Indra."
"Fortunate, endowed with beauty, possessing the gait of the most excellent bulls,
with arms like the trunks of elephants, radiant and foremost among men—
by your splendor, this lord of mountains has been illuminated."

"How have these two heroes, worthy of sovereignty, resembling immortals, with eyes like lotus petals and wearing circles of matted hair, come to this land? These two heroes, so similar to one another, appear as if they have descended from the world of the gods."
The two heroes, broad-chested, human yet possessing the forms of gods, arrived upon the earth as if by chance— the sun and the moon—
lion-shouldered, endowed with great strength, like two bulls in rut.
4.003.012c Long and well-rounded, these arms are like supreme iron clubs;
4.003.012e worthy of being adorned with every ornament, why are they not decorated?
4.003.013a I consider both of you capable of protecting this earth.
[He beheld] the entire earth, including its oceans and forests, adorned with the Vindhya and Meru mountains.
And these two wonderful bows, smooth and decorated with variegated inlays,
shine like Indra’s gold-adorned thunderbolts.
The beautiful quivers were filled with sharp arrows—
terrible, life-ending shafts that blazed like serpents.
They were of great size and breadth, adorned with refined gold.
"These two swords shine like two snakes that have cast off their skins.
Why do you not speak to me as I address you thus?
"There is a certain leader of monkey troops named Sugrīva, whose soul is devoted to righteousness."
"Defeated by his brother, the hero wanders the world in misery. I have arrived here, sent by that high-souled Sugrīva;
I am a monkey named Hanumān, belonging to the king of the foremost monkeys."
"The righteous Sugrīva desires friendship with you both.
Know me to be his minister, a monkey and the son of the Wind,
disguised in the form of a mendicant out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Sugrīva."
"From Ṛśyamūka, I have arrived here on this desire-granting, shape-shifting [monkey] who travels at will.
Having spoken thus to those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa— who were themselves skilled in speech— Hanumān,
who was himself an expert in words, said nothing further.
Having heard these words of his, the glorious Rāma, with a joyful countenance, spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa who was standing by his side:
"This is the minister of the high-souled Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys."
"He has come into my presence while I was longing for him alone.
O Saumitri, he addressed that monkey, the minister of Sugrīva,
who was skilled in speech, a subduer of enemies, with sweet words full of affection.
Then Hanumān, having heard those sweet words, "I have accomplished my task," was delighted and went mentally to Sugrīva. He thought,
"The acquisition of the kingdom for that high-souled Sugrīva is now assured."
"Since he who was to be served has arrived and this task has been accomplished,
Hanumān, the bull among monkeys, was then exceedingly joyful;
skilled in speech, he addressed these words to Rāma."

"For what purpose have you come to this formidable forest, adorned with the groves of Pampā— a difficult place filled with various beasts of prey and wild animals— accompanied by your younger brother?
Having heard those words of his, Lakṣmaṇa, urged by Rāma, [replied].
He described the high-souled Rāma, the son of Daśaratha:
"There was a king named Daśaratha, radiant and devoted to dharma;
this is his eldest son, known among people by the name Rāma."

He is a refuge for all beings and one who has fulfilled his father’s instructions; this hero is the most virtuous among the sons of Daśaratha. Having been deprived of his kingdom, he has come here with me to dwell in the forest.
Accompanied by his wife Sītā, the self-controlled one of great splendor was followed by her,
like the sun at the end of the day followed by its radiance;
I am his younger brother, who has entered into servitude because of my qualities.
To him who was grateful and possessed of great knowledge, whose name was Lakṣmaṇa, who deserved happiness and was worthy of the highest honor, whose soul was devoted to the welfare of all beings,
yet who was now deprived of sovereignty and dwelling in the forest.
4.004.011 Her wife was abducted by a *rākṣasa* who could assume any form at will while she was alone;
yet that *rākṣasa* by whom her wife was taken is not known.
4.004.012 He is named Danu, the son of Śrī, who fell into the state of a *rākṣasa* due to a curse.
4.004.012c By him, Sugrīva, the capable lord of the monkeys, has been described.
4.004.013a That one of great heroism will recognize the abductor of your wife.
4.004.013c Having spoken thus, Danu, shining brightly, departed happily for heaven.
4.004.014a All this has been told to you exactly as it happened, since you asked.
4.004.014c Indeed, both I and Rāma have gone to Sugrīva for refuge.
4.004.015a And he, having bestowed wealth and attained unsurpassed glory, [remains here].
4.004.015c Having formerly been the Lord of the World, he now desires Sugrīva as his protector.
4.004.016a Since Rāma is overcome by grief, afflicted by sorrow, and has come for refuge,
Sugrīva ought to show favor along with the leaders of his troops.
To Saumitri, who was speaking thus piteously with falling tears,
Hanumān, skilled in speech, replied with these words:
"Those endowed with such wisdom, who have conquered anger and subdued their senses..."
"By good fortune, they have come into his sight; they must be seen by the lord of monkeys.
For he has been deprived of his kingdom, has incurred the enmity of Vālin, has had his wife taken away, and, having been severely wronged by his brother, dwells in the forest in terror."
"That son of the Sun, Sugrīva, together with us, will provide assistance to you both in the search for Sītā. Having spoken thus in smooth and sweet tones, Hanumān—
4.004.021c He said to Rāghava, "Let us go to Sugrīva.
4.004.022a To Hanumān, who was speaking thus, the righteous Lakṣmaṇa,
having honored him according to custom, spoke this to Rāghava.
The monkey, the son of the Wind-god, speaks joyfully:
"He too has arrived with his purpose accomplished; you, O Rāghava, have achieved what was to be done.
With a bright complexion on your face, you speak clearly and with evident delight."
4.004.024c The hero Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, will not speak a falsehood.
4.004.025a Then that highly wise Hanumān, son of the Wind-god,
4.004.025c took those two heroic Raghavas and went to the king of the monkeys.
But that hero among monkeys, the son of the Wind, possessed of vast fame and great prowess, set out for the excellent mountain, as delighted as one who had accomplished his purpose.
Then that Śubhamati, together with Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
and Hanumān having gone from Ṛśyamūka to that Malaya mountain,
informed the heroic king of the monkeys of the two Rāghavas.
"This Rāma has arrived, O wise one, possessed of firm prowess;
this Rāma, whose valor is truth, is here with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, Rāma is the son of Daśaratha."

He is firmly established in dharma and is an observer of his father’s commands. While that high-souled one was dwelling in the forest, restrained in his vows, his wife was abducted by a rākṣasa; he has now come to you for refuge.
By him the sacrificial fire was fully gratified through the performance of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
likewise, cows were bestowed as sacrificial fees by the hundreds of thousands. By him the earth was protected through asceticism and truthful speech.
"For the sake of that woman, this son of his, Rāma, has come to you for refuge.
You should accept these two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who desire your friendship, and honor them both, for they are most worthy of worship."
Having heard the words of Hanumān, Sugrīva, his mind filled with joy,
cast off his terrible fear of Rāghava and was freed from his distress.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, assumed a human form.
Becoming most handsome to behold, he spoke with affection to Rāghava: "You are disciplined in dharma, valiant, and beloved by all;
the son of Vāyu has truly described your virtues to me."
"O Lord, this is an honor for me alone, and it is my supreme gain,
that you desire friendship with me, a monkey. If this alliance pleases you, here is my arm extended."
"Let hand be taken by hand; let a firm covenant be made.
Having heard these well-spoken words of Sugrīva, he, with a joyful heart, grasped his hand with his own.
4.005.013e Embracing him with heartfelt affection, she clasped him tightly.
4.005.014a Then Hanumān, the subduer of enemies, casting off the form of a mendicant, 4.005.014c produced fire from two pieces of wood by means of his own natural form.
Then, having worshipped the blazing fire with flowers and honored it,
he, being well-pleased and deeply concentrated, placed it between the two of them.
Then they both circumambulated the blazing fire.
Sugrīva and Rāghava entered into a state of friendship.
Then, both the monkey and the descendant of Raghu, their minds full of joy,
gazed at one another and could not reach satiety.
Then the radiant Sugrīva, with a focused mind, addressed these words to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha and knower of all things:
"O Rāma, this minister of mine, the best of counselors, tells me this."
"O Hanuman, for what reason have you come to this desolate forest?
While you were dwelling in the forest with your brother Lakshmana,
your wife Maithili, the daughter of Janaka, was abducted by a Rakshasa."
Separated from you and from the wise Lakṣmaṇa, she weeps;
yet that [Rāvaṇa], seeking an opportunity, having slain the vulture Jaṭāyu,
will before long release you from the sorrow born of separation from your wife.
"I shall bring her back, just as one recovers a lost Vedic revelation—
whether she is dwelling in the subterranean realm of Rasātala or in the expanse of the sky.
O subduer of enemies, having brought her back, I will give your wife to you."
"O Rāghava, know these words of mine to be the truth:
abandon your grief, O mighty-armed one, for I shall bring that beloved woman back to you.
By inference, I know with no doubt that she is Maithilī."
I saw her being carried away by a Rākṣasa of cruel deeds, crying out discordantly, "Rāma! Rāma! Lakṣmaṇa!
as she struggled in Rāvaṇa’s embrace like the consort of the king of serpents.
"Indeed, seeing me standing on the mountain slope as the fifth person including herself,
she cast off her upper garment and her beautiful ornaments;
those were taken by us and set aside, O Rāghava."
"I shall bring them; you ought to recognize them.
Then Rāma spoke to Sugrīva, who speaks kindly:
"Bring them quickly, my friend; for what reason do you delay?"
Thus addressed, Sugrīva then quickly entered a deep cave in the mountain out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Rāghava;
he took with him his upper garment and his auspicious ornaments.
"Look at this," the monkey said, showing it to Rāma.
Then, taking that garment and the beautiful ornaments,
he became choked with tears, like the moon obscured by mist.

Corrupted by tears flowing from his affection for Sītā, crying out "O my beloved! and casting aside his fortitude, he fell to the ground. Having repeatedly placed that most excellent ornament upon his heart, he wept.
He sighed deeply like an enraged serpent in its hole;
and beholding the son of Sumitrā by his side with an unceasing torrent of tears,
Rāma began to lament in distress.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this upper garment and these ornaments cast from her body onto the ground by Vaidehī as she was being carried away—
surely they were dropped by Sītā upon the grassy earth while she was being abducted."

"This ornament has been cast off; indeed, it appears exactly as it was. Tell me, Sugrīva, in what region was my beloved—my very life—seen by you as she was being carried away by that Rākṣasa of fierce form?"
"Where does that great Rākṣasa dwell, who has brought me such great calamity,
and on whose account I shall destroy all the Rākṣasas—
he who abducted Maithilī and has provoked me so intensely with his wrath?"
The door of death has been flung open for my life’s end,
for that one who was most dear to me has been carried away from the forest by a night-stalker after he had overwhelmed her.
"O Lord of Monkeys, tell me now of that enemy whom I shall lead into the presence of Yama.
Thus addressed by the distressed Rāma, the monkey Sugrīva [replied].
With palms joined in reverence, his voice choked with tears and trembling with emotion, he spoke these words:
"I do not know the dwelling place of that wicked Rākṣasa, nor his power, nor his prowess, nor even the lineage of that base-born wretch."

"I truly promise this: abandon your grief, O subduer of enemies. I shall make such an effort that you will recover Maithilī, having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts and satisfied your own manliness."
"In this way, I shall soon act so that you will be satisfied. Enough of resorting to despondency; remember the fortitude inherent in yourself.
Such lightness of mind is not befitting those like you."
I too have encountered a great calamity arising from the abduction of my wife;
yet I do not grieve in this manner, nor do I abandon my fortitude.
Even though I am but an ordinary monkey, I do not mourn for her.
"You are high-souled and disciplined; how much more so, then, you who possess such fortitude! You ought to restrain this falling tear through your steadfastness;
you should not abandon the composure that is the boundary of those endowed with inner strength."
In calamity, or in financial distress, or in fear that ends one's life,
a man of fortitude who reflects with his own intellect does not despair;
whereas a foolish man is one who constantly yields to despondency.
He sinks helplessly into grief like a heavily laden boat in the water.
Here I join my palms in supplication; I entreat you out of affection. Rely on your manly resolve; you ought not to give way to sorrow.
4.007.012a Those who follow after grief find no happiness;
4.007.012c their vital energy (tejas) is exhausted—therefore, you ought not to grieve. 4.007.013a I speak what is beneficial to you out of friendship; I am not merely instructing you.
"Out of respect for our friendship, you ought not to grieve for me. Thus consoled sweetly by Sugrīva, that Rāghava wiped his face, which was drenched with tears, with the hem of his garment.
But the lordly Kakutstha, remaining in his natural state at the word of Sugrīva,
embraced Sugrīva and spoke these words:
"That which must be done by a friend who is affectionate and well-wishing— "
"O Sugrīva, you have done what was both fitting and appropriate. And I, who was established in my natural state, have been won over by you, my friend;
for such a kinsman is indeed difficult to find, especially at a time like this."
"But you must exert yourself in the search for Maithilī and for the fierce,
evil-minded Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
And tell me with confidence what I, in turn, ought to do."

Just as everything prospers in a fertile field during the rainy season, so shall everything be accomplished for you. O tiger among monkeys, you should understand that these words which have been uttered by me out of self-confidence are indeed the truth.
"Never before have I spoken a falsehood, nor shall I ever speak one;
this I promise you, and I swear it to you by truth.
Thereupon Sugrīva was filled with joy, along with his monkey ministers.
Having heard the words of Rāghava, and especially his solemn promise,
the monkey, having listened to the speech of that high-souled bull among men, [acted accordingly].
Then that foremost of monkey heroes, being wise, felt in his heart that his own task was accomplished. Sugrīva, the monkey, was highly gratified by those words.
He spoke these words to Rāma, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa:
"Without a doubt, I am favored by the gods in every way,
since you, endowed with such excellent qualities, are my friend."

"O sinless Rāma, it would indeed be possible for you, with me as your companion, to attain even the sovereignty of the gods, O Lord; how much more so your own kingdom? Therefore, O Raghava, I am one who ought to be honored by my kinsmen and friends."
"Since you have obtained as a friend one born of the Raghava lineage, with fire as witness, I too shall be a worthy companion for you; you will come to know this gradually,
for I am not able to speak of my own inherent qualities myself."
But for high-souled ones like you who have perfected themselves,
affection becomes exceedingly steadfast, just as fortitude is constant in those who possess self-mastery.
[Whether it be] silver or gold, garments or ornaments—
The virtuous understand that the virtues of the virtuous are indivisible.
Whether one is wealthy or poor, suffering or happy, blameless or flawed— a friend is the supreme refuge.
"Seeing such affection as this, people will go so far as to renounce wealth, renounce happiness, or even renounce their own bodies for the sake of a friend.
To Sugrīva, who spoke so kindly, Rāma replied, "So be it."
In the presence of the wise Lakṣmaṇa, he was like the splendor of Vāsava himself.
Then, seeing Rāma standing there and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa,
Sugrīva cast his restless eyes all around the forest.
Then the lord of monkeys saw a *sāla* tree not far away,
beautifully flowering, rich with young leaves, and adorned by bees.
Breaking off a single branch of it, which was thick with foliage and in full bloom, he—
Having spread out the *sāla* branches, Sugrīva sat down together with Rāghava. Then, seeing that the two were seated, Hanumān also uprooted a *sāla* branch and seated Lakṣmaṇa in a humble manner.
Then Sugrīva, greatly delighted, spoke gently to Rāma with a sweet voice,
his words faltering with joy out of affection:
"I have been treated with contempt by my brother and wander about, afflicted by fear."
"O Raghava, having been robbed of my wife and being deeply distressed, I dwell on Ṛśyamūka, the best of mountains; terrified and submerged in fear, my mind is bewildered,
for I have been humiliated by my brother Vālin and have incurred his enmity."

"O granter of fearlessness to all the worlds, you ought to show favor even to me, who am protectorless and afflicted by the fear of Vālin. Thus addressed, the radiant one, who knows the dharma and is devoted to righteousness, [replied].
4.008.019c That descendant of Kakutstha replied to Sugrīva as if laughing:
4.008.020a "A friend is characterized by the fruit of assistance; doing harm is the mark of an enemy.
4.008.020c This very day I shall slay him who has carried off your wife."
"For these arrows of mine are of great speed and fierce brilliance; born from the forest of Kārttikeya, they are adorned with gold,
fletched with the feathers of herons, and resemble the thunderbolt of the great Indra."
With well-jointed joints and extremely sharp points, like angry serpents,
behold Vālin— your enemy known as your brother, who has committed an offense—
struck down by my arrows and lying there like a shattered mountain.
Having heard the words of Rāghava, Sugrīva, the lord of the army, attained incomparable joy and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! [He said:
"I am overwhelmed by grief for Rāma; you are the refuge for those afflicted by sorrow."
"Indeed, it is because you are my friend that I lament before you.
For by the joining of our hands in the presence of the sacred fire, you were made my friend;
you are held as dear as my own life, and I swear this by the truth."
"Considering you my friend, I speak to you with confidence about the sorrow within me that constantly consumes my mind. Having spoken these words, his eyes were clouded with tears.
With a voice choked by tears, he was unable to speak aloud; yet,
in the presence of Rāma, Sugrīva restrained with fortitude the sudden surge of tears that came upon him like the rushing current of a river.
4.008.030a Having restrained his tears and wiped his beautiful eyes,
4.008.030c the radiant one sighed and spoke again to Rāghava:
4.008.031a "Long ago, O Rāma, I was deposed from my own kingdom by Bali."
Having been made to hear harsh words, I have been cast out by one more powerful;
my wife, who is dearer to me than life itself, has been seized by him,
as have my friends who were confined in bonds.
O Rāghava, that evil-minded one has been striving many times for my destruction;
and the monkeys dispatched by him have been slain by me.
It is because of this suspicion, O Rāghava, that I looked even at you upon seeing you.
"I do not approach you out of fear, for everyone indeed fears when there is danger;
it is simply because these companions of mine, headed by Hanumān,
are here that I sustain my life even though I have fallen into such distress."
"For these affectionate monkeys protect me on all sides;
they go with me when I must go, and they always remain by my side when I stay. This, O Rāma, is my brief account; for what would be the use of speaking to you at length?"
"That elder brother of mine, Vālin, whose prowess is renowned, is my greatest enemy.
Indeed, with his destruction, my sorrow would immediately vanish;
my happiness and very life depend upon his death."
"O Rāma, this end of my sorrow has been related by me, who am afflicted by grief;
for whether one is suffering or not, a friend is always the refuge and the resort of a friend.
Having heard these words, Rāma spoke thus to Sugrīva.
"O monkey, I wish to hear the truth of what caused this enmity; for having heard the cause of your hostility,
I shall deliberate upon the relative strengths and decide upon immediate action."
"For my powerful indignation, having heard that you were insulted,
increases with a throbbing in my heart like the surge of waters in the rainy season.
Tell me with confidence, while the bow is being strung."
"For the arrow has indeed been released by me, and your enemy has been struck down.
When the high-souled descendant of Kakutstha had spoken thus, Sugrīva,
together with the four monkeys, experienced incomparable joy.
Then Sugrīva, with a joyful countenance, began to relate the true cause of the enmity to the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa:
"My elder brother, the destroyer of enemies, is named Vālī."
He was always highly esteemed by his father, and likewise by me in the past.
When our father had passed away, the ministers, considering him the eldest among us,
installed this highly honored one as the lord and king of the monkeys.
While he was ruling that great ancestral kingdom of his father and grandfather,
I remained at all times bowed down before him like a servant. I am the powerful one named Māyāvī, the elder brother and son of Dundubhi.
By him, a great enmity caused by a woman was formerly made famous.
But while the people were asleep at night, he came from Kiṣkindhā to the gate;
highly incensed, he roared and challenged Vālin to battle.
But my brother Vālī, while asleep, hearing that roar of terrifying sound, could not endure it; he then rushed out with speed. Having emerged in his fury, he set out to slay that foremost of asuras.
Though he was being restrained by the women and by me with a humble spirit,
that mighty one shook us all off and went forth;
then I also, out of friendship, went out together with Vālin.
But seeing my brother and me standing at a distance, that asura was seized with terror and then fled away most swiftly. As he fled in his fear, we both pursued him even more rapidly.
At that time, as the moon was rising, it illuminated the path.
The Asura entered with speed a great, difficult-to-traverse opening in the earth covered with grass; having reached us, he stood before us.
Seeing that enemy had entered the cave, Vālin fell under the sway of rage; with his senses agitated, he then spoke these words to me:
"Stay here, Sugrīva, concentrated at the entrance of the cave."
"4.009.013c As soon as I have entered here, I shall slay the enemy in battle.
4.009.014a But having heard these words of mine, that scorcher of foes entreated me; 4.009.014c and having made me swear an oath by his feet, he then entered the cave.
When he had entered the cave, more than a full year passed;
and while I remained at the entrance, that time slipped away.
But I, realizing that he was lost, became agitated with affection.

"I do not see my brother, and my mind is filled with apprehension of evil. Then, after a long time, I saw blood mixed with foam and red liquid issuing from that cave; seeing this, I was deeply distressed.
The sound of the roaring Asuras reached my ears,
as did the cry of my preceptor as he was being cast down in battle;
and by those signs, I perceived through my intellect that my brother had been slain.
Having covered the entrance of the cave with a boulder as large as a mountain,
and having offered water in mourning for my sake, O friend, you have come to Kiṣkindhā;
yet, despite my efforts to conceal the truth, it has been heard by my ministers.
4.009.020c Then, having come together with them all, I was consecrated by them.
4.009.021a O Rāghava, while I was ruling the kingdom with justice, 4.009.021c Vālī returned, having slain that foremost of asuras, his enemy.
But seeing me consecrated, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
he bound my ministers and spoke these harsh words.
O Raghava, although he was capable of punishing that wicked man, he did not do so.

My mind did not incline toward [the fight], restrained as I was by respect for my brother; honoring that high-souled one, I saluted him duly. And no blessings were uttered by him, for his inner self was already satisfied.

Then, desiring to do what was pleasing to him, I sought to appease my brother as he approached, overcome with anger and agitated. "By good fortune you have arrived safe and sound, and the enemy has been slain by you."

"For you alone are my protector, O delighter of the helpless, since I am indeed without a protector. Accept this umbrella, which has many ribs like the risen full moon, along with the fly-whisk, as it is held out by me."
"You alone are the king worthy of honor, and I shall always remain as I was before. I now restore this kingdom to you as a trust;
do not harbor anger toward me, O gentle one, O destroyer of enemies."
"I entreat you with my head bowed, O King; here I join my palms in supplication.
Having been brought here by force by the ministers and the city-dwellers, I have been appointed to the kingship with the desire to conquer a vacant region."
But that monkey, having rebuked me as I spoke so affectionately, said "Fie on you!
and addressed me with many such words. Then, having summoned the subjects and the esteemed ministers, he spoke.
In the midst of his friends, he spoke these most contemptible words to me:
"It is known to you how that great Asura, a master of illusion, cruel and evil-minded, challenged me at night while longing for battle."
4.010.010a Having heard that roar of his, I emerged from the king's palace;
4.010.010c and this most terrible brother of mine quickly followed after me.
4.010.011a But upon seeing me at night accompanied by another, that one of great strength—
Terrified with fear, he fled as we pursued him;
but being pursued with speed, he entered a great cave.
Knowing that he had entered that most formidable and vast cavern, [we followed].
4.010.012c Then this brother of mine, Krūradarśana, was addressed by me:
4.010.013a "Without killing him, I have no power to return from here to the city. 4.010.013c Wait at the entrance of the cave while I slay him."
Thinking, "He is staying here," I entered that place which was difficult to approach;
and as I was searching for him, a full year passed away.
Then, through perseverance, I beheld that formidable enemy.

And there, that asura was slain by me along with his kinsmen. By the torrent of blood flowing from his mouth, that cave became filled and difficult to enter, even as he lay groaning upon the surface of the earth.
Having slain that valiant enemy, the son of Dundubhi, as I was just emerging, I saw the mouth of the cave blocked. And as I cried out "Sugrīva! again and again, [I heard no answer].
When there was no reply, I became deeply distressed;
I struck it many times with kicks of my feet until it was torn open. Then, having emerged through that opening, I returned here once more.

"There, I was imprisoned by this cruel Sugrīva, who has forgotten his brotherly affection while seeking the kingdom for himself. Having spoken thus to me there, the monkey [covered me] with a single garment.
Then Vālin, free from fear, banished me;
by him I was cast out, O Rāghava, and my wife was taken away. Out of fear of him, I have traversed this entire earth with its forests and oceans.

"Afflicted by the grief of my wife's abduction, I entered the unassailable Ṛśyamūka, the best of mountains, for a specific reason related to Vālin. All this, a great account of our enmity, has been told to you."
"O Rāghava, behold this calamity that has befallen me,
though I am innocent. O hero, granter of fearlessness to all the worlds, you ought to show me favor by subduing Vālin."
Thus addressed, that radiant one, who knows the dharma,
began to speak words consistent with righteousness to Sugrīva, as if smiling:
"These sharp arrows of mine are unfailing and resemble the sun."
4.010.027c Upon that wicked Vālin, they shall fall with fury;
4.010.028a as long as I do not behold that thief of your wife,
so long shall that evil-souled Vālin, the defiler of conduct, continue to live.
"By means of inference from my own case, I see that you are submerged in an ocean of grief;
I shall deliver you, and you will obtain every abundant desire.
Having heard Rāma's words, which increased his joy and manliness...
Sugrīva honored Rāghava and praised him, saying:
"Without a doubt, when enraged, you could consume the worlds with your blazing, sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs, like the sun at the end of an eon."
Having heard with an undivided mind what was Vālī’s manliness, and what his prowess and fortitude were, decide what must be done next.
[He traversed] from the western ocean to the east, and from the south to the north.
Before the sun has risen, Vālin, free from fatigue, strides forth;
having climbed to the very tops of the mountains and even their great peaks,
the heroic one seizes them, lifting them upward with speed.
In the forests, there were many various trees full of strength,
which Vālin had shattered by his might, displaying his own prowess.
There was a buffalo named Dundubhi, who possessed the luster of a peak of Mount Kailāsa.
The heroic one possessed the strength of a thousand elephants;
yet that evil-minded one, deluded by the granting of the boon and intoxicated by his own prowess,
went toward the ocean, the lord of rivers, with his massive body.
"Having crossed the ocean, which is full of waves and a storehouse of jewels,
grant me battle," he said to that great sea.
Then the righteous and mighty Ocean rose up.
4.011.010c O King, he spoke these words to the Asura who was impelled by Time:
4.011.011a "O you who are skilled in battle, I am not capable of giving you battle;
4.011.011c listen, for I shall tell you who will grant you battle."
In the great forest, there is the king of mountains, the supreme refuge for ascetics,
known by the name Himavat, the father-in-law of Śaṅkara;
it is endowed with caves and springs, and possesses many mountain clefts and waterfalls.
"He is capable of bestowing incomparable joy upon you in battle. Perceiving that the ocean was afraid, the supreme asura went to the forest of the Himalayas like an arrow released from a bow.
Then Dundubhi hurled many white boulders from that mountain, as large as lordly elephants, onto the ground, and let out a great roar.
Then there appeared one whose form was pleasing and delightful, resembling a white cloud.
Standing upon his own peak, Himavat spoke these words:
"O Dundubhi, you who are devoted to dharma, you ought not to cause me distress;
for I am unskilled in the arts of war and am a refuge for ascetics."
Having heard those words of the wise king of mountains,
Dundubhi, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke these words:
"If you are incapable in battle, or if you have become inactive out of fear of me..."

"Tell me who it is that would give battle today to me, who am desirous of fighting. Having heard these words, the righteous Himavat, skilled in speech, spoke these words never before uttered out of anger to that best of asuras.
4.011.021a A highly wise monkey named Vālin, whose prowess is equal to that of Śakra, 4.011.021c the illustrious one, dwells in Kiṣkindhā, which is of incomparable splendor.
4.011.022a He is capable, highly wise, and skilled in battle.
"Like Vāsava [Indra] offering a great duel to Namuci,
go quickly to him if you desire battle here;
for he is ever invincible and a hero in the art of war."
Having heard the words of Himavat, Dundubhi, overcome with rage,
then went to that city of Vālin, Kiṣkindhā;
assuming the form of a buffalo, he was terrifying with his sharp horns.
Like a great cloud filled with water in the sky during the rainy season,
the mighty one then approached the gate of Kiṣkindhā and roared,
making the earth tremble like the sound of a kettledrum.
Breaking down the trees growing nearby and tearing up the earth with his hooves,
he scratched at that gate with his tusks out of pride, like an elephant;
hearing this sound, Vālin, who was within the inner apartments, became indignant.
He leapt forth with the women like the moon with the stars.
Vālī, the lord of the monkeys and of all forest-dwellers, spoke measured words with distinct syllables and phrases to Dundubhi:
"For what purpose do you roar, having blocked this city gate?
O Dundubhi, you are known to me; protect your life, O one of great strength!
Having heard those words of the wise lord of monkeys, [the demon replied:]
4.011.031c Dundubhi, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke these words:
4.011.032a "O hero, you ought not to speak such words in the presence of a woman. Give me battle; then I shall know your strength."

"Or rather, O monkey, I shall harbor my anger for this night; you may indulge freely in the pleasures of desire until sunrise. For he who [attacks] one who is intoxicated, heedless, asleep, or utterly unprotected—"
"He would be a killer of an embryo in this world who, like you, were deluded by pride.
Laughing, he then spoke softly out of anger to that best of asuras,
having dismissed all those women, including Tārā and Prabhiṛti.
"Do not think, 'He is intoxicated,' if you are not afraid in combat. This intoxication is for this encounter; let it be regarded as a hero's draught.
Having spoken thus to him, he became enraged and cast off his golden garland.
Given by his father Mahendra for the sake of battle,
Vālī seized that mountain-like Dundubhi by its two horns,
hurled it away, and let out a great roar.
In that life-ending battle, Dundubhi was then crushed;
as he was being struck down, blood flowed from both his ears,
and the giant-bodied one fell to the earth, having met his death.
Having weighed that lifeless and unconscious body with his two arms,
the impetuous Vālin hurled it with a single forceful thrust for a distance of one *yojana*.
As it was cast forth by that momentum, drops of blood fell from its mouth.

4.011.041c Tossed up by the wind, they fell toward Mataṅga’s hermitage. 4.011.042a Seeing those drops of blood fallen there, the sage 4.011.042c uttered a great curse against Vālin, who had thrown them.
"4.011.042e He must not enter here; for one who has entered, there shall be death.
4.011.043a Having approached the great seer, he entreated him with palms joined in reverence.
4.011.044a Then, terrified by the fear of a curse, [he fled] to the great mountain Ṛśyamūka."
"O lord of men, Hari does not wish to enter or even to look upon it. Knowing that he cannot enter, O Rāma, I roam this great forest with my ministers, free from all anxiety."

4.011.046a This heap of bones belonging to that Dundubhi appears here; 4.011.046c it is as large as a mountain peak, cast down by his excessive pride in his own prowess. 4.011.047a And here are these seven massive *sāla* trees, hanging with their branches.
"O Rāma, I have revealed to you this peerless valor of his, wherein Vālī alone was capable of stripping [a tree] of its leaves by his might. O King, how will you be able to slay that Vālī in battle?"

"O mighty-armed one, if you were to pierce these *sāla* trees with a single arrow, then I would know you to be capable of slaying Vālin. Having heard those words of the high-souled Sugrīva, [Rāma replied:]...
4.011.050c With his big toe, the mighty-armed Rāghava effortlessly lifted Dundubhi’s body and hurled it ten yojanas away. 4.011.051a Seeing the body thus cast forth, Sugrīva spoke again:
In front of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma spoke these meaningful words:
"O friend, formerly this body was moist, fresh with flesh, and cast [into the fire];
now, O Rāghava, it is light, devoid of flesh, and like a blade of grass."
"4.011.052e It is not possible here to know whether your strength or his is superior.
4.012.001a Having heard these well-spoken words of Sugrīva,
the immensely radiant Rāma took up his bow for the sake of providing proof.
Taking up his formidable bow and a single arrow,
that bestower of honor discharged it toward the *sāla* trees, filling the quarters with the sound of the bowstring.
That gold-adorned arrow, released by the powerful one, [flew forth].
4.012.003c Having split the *sāla* trees on the mountain slope, it entered the earth.
4.012.004a But having entered, that one of great speed pierced the subterranean realm (*rasā*) in a mere moment;
and having emerged again swiftly, it entered its own quiver.
Seeing those seven *sāla* trees pierced through by the velocity of Rāma’s arrow, that bull among monkeys was struck with supreme wonder;
with his ornaments dangling down, he fell prostrate upon the ground.
4.012.006c Sugrīva, supremely delighted and with palms joined in reverence to Rāghava,
4.012.007a spoke these words to the knower of dharma, who was gladdened by that deed—
to the heroic Rāma, the foremost among those skilled in all weapons, as he stood firm.

"O bull among men, O Lord, you are capable of slaying even all the gods led by Indra with your arrows in battle; how much more so Vālin? By him, seven great sāl trees, a mountain, and the earth itself were rent asunder."

"O descendant of Kakutstha, who could stand before you in the forefront of battle with even a single arrow? Today my grief has vanished; today I have supreme joy, having found you as a friend, equal to Mahendra and Varuṇa."
"O Kākutstha, slay this Vālī this very day for my sake—he who is my enemy in the form of a brother; here I join my palms in supplication to you. Then Rāma embraced the handsome Sugrīva.
The highly wise one replied with words approved by Lakṣmaṇa:
"Let us go from here to Kiṣkindhā; you go quickly ahead.
Having gone there, O Sugrīva, challenge Vālin, who is a mere brother in name."
4.012.014a All of them, having gone quickly to Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālin, 4.012.014c stood in the dense forest, concealing themselves behind trees.
4.012.015a Sugrīva let out a terrible roar for the purpose of challenging Vālin.
Tightly bound, he rushed forward with speed, as if splitting the sky with his roars.
Hearing that cry of his brother, the mighty Vālin, filled with rage and great agitation,
sprang forth like the sun from the western horizon.

Then a most tumultuous battle took place between Vālin and Sugrīva, as fierce as that between the two planets Mercury and Mars in the sky. They fought with palms like thunderbolts and fists like diamonds.
4.012.018c The two brothers, overcome with rage, struck each other in battle. 4.012.019a Then Rāma, bow in hand, beheld them both;
4.012.019c those two heroes, who resembled one another like the twin gods, the Aśvins.
Because Rāghava did not recognize whether it was Sugrīva or Vālin,
he did not then form the resolve to release the death-dealing arrow.
In that interval, Sugrīva was struck down by that Vālin.
Not seeing his lord Rāghava, he fled toward Ṛśyamūka;
exhausted, his limbs drenched in blood and shattered by blows,
pursued by Vālin in a rage, he entered the great forest.
Seeing that he had entered the forest, the mighty Vālin, out of fear of the curse, said,
"You are indeed released," and then turned back.
Rāghava, along with his brother and Hanumān, [proceeded further].

4.012.024c Sugrīva came to that very forest where the monkey [Hanumān] was. 4.012.025a Seeing that Rāma had arrived along with Lakṣmaṇa, 4.012.025c the modest Sugrīva, looking down at the ground, spoke these words in distress.
"Having said to me, 'Call for me,' and having displayed your prowess,
and having caused me to be slain by my enemy— what have you accomplished now,
O Rāghava? You should have spoken the truth at that very moment."
"If I do not slay Vālin, then I shall not depart from here. To the high-souled Sugrīva who was speaking thus,
Rāghava replied again in a piteous and distressed voice.
"O Sugrīva, my dear brother, listen and let your anger be dispelled. Hear the reason why this arrow was not released by me.
[It was because] in its ornamentation, its attire, its proportions, and its gait..."

4.012.030c And you and Vālin, O Sugrīva, are similar to one another. 4.012.031a By voice, by luster, and even by your gaze, O monkey, 4.012.031c as well as by your prowess and your speech, I cannot perceive a distinction between the two of you.
Then, O best of monkeys, deluded by the resemblance of his form,
I did not release that high-velocity arrow, the destroyer of enemies.
But behold, in this very moment, I have slain Vālin in battle.
"Struck by a single arrow and writhing upon the earth,
O Lord of Monkeys,
provide me with a token of recognition so that I may know you when we have entered into this duel."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, having plucked this blooming *gajapuṣpī* flower, which possesses auspicious characteristics, place it around the neck of the high-souled Sugrīva. Then,
having uprooted that flower-cluster growing on the mountain slope,"
Lakṣmaṇa placed that *gajapuṣpī* vine around his neck. Adorned with the vine clinging to his neck, the illustrious one shone like a rain-cloud at twilight encircled by a garland of cranes.
Radiant in body and focused on Rāma’s words,
he went with Rāma to Kiṣkindhā, which was protected by Vālin. From Ṛśyamūka, that righteous soul, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, departed for Kiṣkindhā.
Accompanied by Sugrīva, Rāma went toward the land protected by Vālin’s prowess;
raising his great bow adorned with gold,
he took up arrows that resembled the sun and were effective in battle.

4.013.003a Sugrīva, with his neck firmly set, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa went at the head of that high-souled Rāghava. 4.013.004a Behind them followed the heroic Hanumān, as well as Nala and the monkey Nīla.
And Tāra himself, of great splendor, along with the leaders of the monkey troops—
those leaders gazed upon the trees bending under the weight of their blossoms,
and upon the rivers flowing with clear waters as they journeyed toward the ocean.
Valleys, mountains, waterfalls, and likewise caves;
principal peaks and beautiful ravines;
with lotuses possessing leaves as pure as lapis lazuli and buds like the sky.
Along the way, they beheld beautiful, water-filled ponds,
resounding with the cries of kāraṇḍava ducks, cranes, swans, vañjūla birds, water-fowls, ruddy geese, and various other birds.
He saw deer roaming everywhere on the open grounds— fearless forest-dwellers whose food consisted of soft sprouts of young grass; and he also saw elephants,
the enemies of the ponds, adorned with white tusks.
Beholding fierce wild elephants that roam alone and destroy the riverbanks,
as well as other forest-dwelling creatures in the woods and birds flying in the sky,
those who were under Sugrīva’s command proceeded with haste.
4.013.012 As they were traveling there in haste, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus,
seeing a forest grove of trees, spoke to Sugrīva:
4.013.013 "This cluster of trees shines like a cloud in the sky."
"Vast as a mass of clouds and surrounded by plantain trees at its edge—what is this? I wish to know it, my friend; I have a great curiosity.
I desire that you dispel my curiosity."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Rāghava,
Sugrīva, even as he was proceeding, pointed out that great forest:
"O Rāghava, this is a vast hermitage that destroys all fatigue."
4.013.016c It was endowed with gardens and groves, and possessed sweet roots, fruits, and water.

4.013.017a There dwelt seven sages named Saptajanas, who were firm in their vows; 4.013.017c they were exactly seven in number, lying submerged in water with their heads turned downward in constant discipline.
Those forest-dwellers, subsisting on air for seven nights,
went to heaven with their physical bodies after seven hundred years.
By the power of those very [sages], it was enclosed by a wall of trees.
This hermitage is extremely difficult to assail, even for the gods and asuras led by Indra. Birds avoid it, as do other forest-dwellers;
those who enter here out of delusion do not return again.
4.013.021a And here the sounds of ornaments are heard with every syllable distinct;
4.013.021c there are also the sounds of musical instruments and songs, and a divine fragrance, O Rāghava.
4.013.022a The three sacrificial fires are also blazing, for this smoke is clearly visible.
"Enveloping the treetops as if to embrace them, the cloud, reddish like the body of a pigeon,
appeared. O righteous-souled Rāghava, together with your brother Lakṣmaṇa, being self-restrained and with palms joined in reverence, offer salutations directed toward those [ancestors]."
"For those who bow down to these seers of purified souls,
O Rāma, no inauspiciousness whatsoever is seen upon their bodies.
Then Rāma, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, joined his palms in reverence.
Having paid homage to those high-souled sages,
the righteous Rāma, his brother Lakṣmaṇa,
Sugrīva, and the monkeys departed with joyful hearts.
4.013.027a Having traveled a long distance from that hermitage of the seven sages,
they beheld that unassailable Kiṣkindhā, protected by Vālin.
4.014.001a They all proceeded swiftly toward Kiṣkindhā, which was ruled by Vālin.
Covering himself with trees, he stood in the dense forest;
having cast his gaze in every direction throughout the grove,
Sugrīva, the broad-necked one who is fond of the woods, summoned a great rage.
Then, letting out a terrible roar, he challenged him to battle,
surrounded by his followers as if splitting the sky with his shouts.
Then, resembling the rising sun and possessing the gait of a proud lion, he [advanced].
Having seen Rāma, who was skilled in action, Sugrīva spoke these words:
"We have reached Kiṣkindhā, the city of Vālin, which is ensnared by a net of monkeys, adorned with gateways of refined gold, and rich in banners and mechanical engines."
"O hero, that promise which was made by you long ago regarding the slaying of Vālin—
fulfill it quickly now, like the arrival of the season for a creeper.
Thus addressed by Sugrīva, that righteous Rāghava...
Then the slayer of enemies spoke these words to Sugrīva:
"You have been marked with this sign of recognition by her,
like the sun in the sky surrounded by a garland of stars."
"O monkey, today I shall, with a single discharge of an arrow in battle, liberate you from the fear and enmity arising from Vālin. Show me that enemy of Sugrīva who wears the form of a brother."
4.014.010c As long as Vālin lies struck down, wallowing in the dust of the forest, 4.014.011a If he comes within the range of sight and returns alive,
4.014.011c then you should not incur blame for this fault, and you should immediately reproach me.
"Directly before your eyes, those seven palaces of yours were shattered by me with my arrow.
Therefore, you shall know today that Vālin has been slain by my strength.
O hero, never before have I spoken a falsehood, even while standing in the midst of great distress."
"Overcome by a longing for righteousness, I shall not speak at all;
I will make my vow fruitful, so cast away your agitation.
[I am like] Śatakratu [making] the rice-sprout born in the field fruitful with rain."
"O Sugrīva, for the purpose of summoning Vālin, who wears a golden garland, make that sound by which the monkey will emerge— he who appears victorious,
who boasts of his triumphs, and who was never previously provoked by you."
Vālī, who is ever eager for combat, will emerge without hesitation; for heroes do not tolerate the provocation of their enemies in battle,
especially when they are aware of their own prowess, particularly in the presence of women.
Having heard Rāma’s words, Sugrīva, who was tawny like gold,
let out a cruel roar as if splitting the very sky.
Terrified by his sound, the cattle fled, their luster extinguished.
Afflicted by the king's faults, they are as agitated as noble women;
the deer flee swiftly like horses broken in battle,
and the birds fall to the ground like planets whose merit has been exhausted.
Then that son of the Sun, his splendor increased by valor, being confident, let out a roar with speed, like the thundering of a mass of clouds.
Then Vālin, the lord of rivers with waves restless from the wind, who was residing in the inner apartments, heard that roar of his high-souled brother Sugrīva; he was one who could not brook offense.

But having heard that roar which made all beings tremble, his intoxication vanished in an instant and a great rage fell upon him. With his limbs overwhelmed by fury, Vālin then shone with the radiance of the twilight sun.
Like the sun eclipsed by Rāhu, he instantly lost his luster;
Vālin, with his formidable fangs and blazing like a kindled fire in his rage,
shone like a lake from which the lotuses and their stalks have been uprooted.
4.015.005a Hearing that unbearable sound, the monkey then rushed forth, 4.015.005c with such speed that he seemed to tear the earth asunder with his footsteps.
4.015.006a But Tārā, embracing him out of affection, displayed her friendship;
Terrified and agitated, she spoke these words, which were destined for his welfare:
"O hero, it is well that you have arisen from your bed at dawn; cast off this anger, which has come upon you like the rush of a river, as one casts off a worn garland."
Your sudden departure does not yet please me;
listen, for I shall tell you the reason why you are being restrained.
Previously, overcome by anger, he has challenged you to battle.
Having fled, he was repulsed by you and, being struck, went in all directions.
That he has returned here to challenge you again— especially after having been so driven away and tormented by you— seems to me to arouse a sense of apprehension.
4.015.011 The pride and the resolve of that one who roars,
as well as the intensity of his clamor— this cannot have a trivial cause.
4.015.012 I do not believe that Sugrīva has come here without an ally.
Supported by his allies and relying upon him, this monkey roars; for he is naturally skillful and intelligent, Sugrīva will not come with one whose prowess has not been tested.
"O hero, I have already heard these words spoken by Prince Aṅgada; now I shall speak words for your benefit. For your brother is renowned as a companion who is fierce in battle."
Rāma, the crusher of enemy forces, has arisen like the fire at the end of an eon;
he is the sheltering tree for the virtuous, the supreme refuge for those in distress, the resort for the afflicted, and the sole vessel of glory.
Endowed with both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, devoted to his father’s command,
he is like the king of mountains among the elements— a great mine of virtues.
Therefore, it is not right for you to oppose that high-souled man.
"O hero, by Rāma—who is invincible and immeasurable in the arts of war—I shall say something to you, for I do not wish to speak with malice.
Listen, and let it be done; I shall tell you what is for your benefit."
"Quickly and properly consecrate Sugrīva as the crown prince;
O hero, O King, do not engage in conflict with your stronger brother. For I consider it appropriate for you to maintain friendship with Rāma."
"Cast enmity far away and cultivate friendship with Sugrīva;
for this younger monkey is indeed your brother and deserves to be cherished by you.
Whether he is there or staying here, he is in every way your kinsman."
"If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, and if you consider me to be well-disposed toward you, then,
being entreated with such effort, act upon my virtuous words.
To Tārā, whose face resembled the lord of the stars, as she was speaking thus—
Vālin rebuked him and spoke these words:
"O lady of beautiful countenance, for what reason would I tolerate the arrogance of this roaring brother, especially since he is my enemy?"
For brave men who have never been defeated and do not retreat in battles,
O timid one, the endurance of an insult is superior to death.
And I am not capable of enduring [an insult] from one who desires battle in combat.
"Behold the fury of Sugrīva, who roars even though his neck is severed! You must not feel despondency on account of me regarding Rāghava;
for how could he, who knows the dharma and is grateful, ever commit a sin?"
"Return with the women; why do you follow me further? O Tārā, you have shown me friendship and displayed devotion toward me.
Go and I shall fight Sugrīva in return; abandon your agitation."
"I shall humble his pride, yet he shall not be deprived of life. I adjure you by my own life: turn back with victory!
Having defeated him, I shall return; that brother of mine is no match for me in battle."

Then Tārā, speaking sweet words, embraced Vālin; weeping softly, that auspicious woman performed a circumambulation of him from left to right. Then, desiring his victory, she performed a rite for his well-being according to the sacred mantras.
4.016.010c Overwhelmed by grief and delusion, she entered the inner apartments together with the women.
4.016.011a But once Tārā had entered her own quarters along with the women,
he went forth from the city, hissing like a great serpent in a rage.
Sighing deeply, the immensely powerful Vālin, filled with supreme rage,
cast his gaze in every direction, longing for a sight of his enemy.
Then the illustrious one beheld Sugrīva, who was tawny like gold.

4.016.013c Well-encased and firmly grasped, he was like a blazing fire. 4.016.014a Seeing that Sugrīva standing there with great prowess, Vālī, exceedingly enraged, drew his garment tightly around him.
4.016.015a That valiant Vālin, tightly girded and raising his fist,
4.016.015c advanced directly toward Sugrīva, ready for battle. 4.016.016a Raising his clenched fist, he approached with even greater fury.
4.016.016c Sugrīva, too, having aimed at Vālin, who was adorned with a golden garland—
4.016.017a Vālin, his eyes copper-red with rage, spoke these words to Sugrīva, who was skilled in battle, as he approached with great speed: 4.016.017c [He spoke] this speech.
"This fist has been clenched by me, firm with well-placed fingers;
released by me with force, it shall depart taking away your life.
Thus addressed, Sugrīva, filled with rage, spoke to Vālī.
"And as he takes away your very life-breaths, let this fist fall upon your head.
Struck by him, he became enraged and, advancing with speed,
began to vomit blood like a mountain with its mineral ores gushing forth.
4.016.021a But by Sugrīva, who with his splendor uprooted a *sāla* tree without hesitation,
Vālī was struck on his limbs as if a great mountain were struck by a thunderbolt.
4.016.022a And that Vālī, overwhelmed by the blow from the *sāla* tree, began to wander about.
Overwhelmed by that heavy burden, he became like a ship upon the ocean.
Those two, possessing formidable strength and prowess, and endowed with a speed equal to that of Suparṇa,
grew in stature with terrible forms like the sun and moon in the sky.
But Sugrīva, his pride shattered by Vālin and his prowess dulled,
was filled with indignation toward Vālin and displayed his agility.
Then, having fixed an arrow resembling a venomous serpent upon his bow—
4.016.025c A great arrow was struck by Rāghava into Vāli’s chest; 4.016.026a Struck with force, Vāli fell to the surface of the earth.
4.016.027a Then he was drenched by streams flowing from his blood.
Like a well-flowered *aśoka* tree shaken by the wind,
the son of Vāsava, deprived of consciousness in battle,
fell to the earth like the banner of Indra cast down.
Then, struck by Rāma’s arrow, Vālī, fierce in battle, suddenly fell like a tree that has been cut down. With all his limbs cast upon the ground, he lay there adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
He fell like the banner of the King of the Gods when its ropes have been released.
When that lord of the hosts of monkeys had fallen to the earth,
the surface of the ground no longer shone, like the sky when the moon has vanished.
Even as that great-souled one fell upon the ground,
neither his splendor, nor his life-breaths, nor his radiance, nor his prowess left his body.
The excellent golden garland, adorned with jewels, which had been given by Śakra, remained [upon him].
She sustained the life-force, the splendor, and the fortune of that foremost of monkeys.
With that golden garland, the hero, the leader of the monkey hosts,
appeared like a cloud whose edges are touched by the twilight.
His garland, his body, and the arrow that struck his vital organs— though he had fallen, these three elements combined made his splendor appear as if fashioned in three parts;
that weapon of the hero illuminated the path to heaven.
4.017.008c Discharged from Rāma’s bow, it attained the supreme state. 4.017.009a As he lay thus fallen in battle like a fire whose flames have gone out,
4.017.009c he was like Yayāti falling from the world of the gods at the exhaustion of his merit.
Like the sun fallen to earth at the end of an eon by the power of Time,
like the invincible Mahendra, like the unbearable Mahendra—
Vālin, the son of Mahendra, adorned with a golden garland, lay there fallen.
4.017.011c With the chest of a lion, mighty arms, a blazing face, and tawny eyes—
4.017.011e Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, beheld him and drew near.
4.017.012a Having seen Rāghava and the exceedingly powerful Lakṣmaṇa, Vālī...
He spoke these words, which were humble yet harsh and consistent with righteousness:
"What merit have you gained by killing one who had his back turned to you,
that I, having been intent on battle, should meet my death because of you?"

Rāma is of noble birth, endowed with courage, radiant, and firm in his vows; he is compassionate, sensitive to the suffering of his subjects, and devoted to their welfare. He is merciful, possessed of great energy, knowledgeable of the proper time, and steadfast in his resolve.
"Thus all beings proclaim your glory upon the earth. Having considered those virtues and your preeminent lineage,
I was forbidden by Tārā and have come here to meet Sugrīva."
"You ought not to strike me while I am distracted and preoccupied with another"—
this thought arose in me when you were out of my sight. [But now] you have slain one whose soul was already destroyed, a hypocrite who bears the banner of dharma yet is unrighteous.

I know you to be one of evil conduct, like a well covered over with grass— a wicked man wearing the garb of the virtuous, like a fire hidden beneath the ashes. I do not recognize you, for you are shrouded in the disguise of righteousness.
Whether in your kingdom or in your city, I have never done you any harm; nor do I acknowledge you as my master—why then do you strike me, who am innocent?
I am but a forest-dwelling monkey, always subsisting on fruits and roots.
"O son of a lord of men, you are renowned and of pleasing appearance; though I am here not fighting back and have encountered another,
O King, even your outward signs are seen to be consistent with righteousness."
Who, born in a kṣatriya family, learned in the scriptures, and free from doubt,
would perform a cruel deed while disguised under the outward marks of dharma? O Rāma, you are born in a royal lineage and are renowned as one who possesses righteousness.
"Why do you run about in the guise of one who is capable, when you are actually incapable?
O King, conciliation, generosity, forgiveness, righteousness, truthfulness, fortitude, prowess, and the rod of punishment against wrongdoers— these are the virtues of kings."
"O Rāma, we are forest-dwellers, deer who subsist on roots and fruits;
this is our nature. You, however, O lord of men, are a man.
Land, gold, and silver are the grounds for [confiscation] and for punishment."

4.017.027c What desire do you have for my forest, or for my fruits? 4.017.028a Both policy and discipline, as well as restraint and favor, constitute the unadulterated conduct of kings; kings do not act according to their whims.

But you are dominated by desire, prone to anger, and unstable; you are muddled by the conduct of kings and devoted solely to the bow. You have no reverence for dharma, nor is your intellect established in artha.
O lord of men, being driven by the senses and acting out of desire, you are dragged away. O descendant of Kakutstha, having slain me here with an arrow though I am innocent,
what will you say in the midst of the virtuous after committing such a loathsome deed?
The regicide, the slayer of a Brahmin, the killer of a cow, the thief, one intent on taking life,
the atheist, and the younger brother who marries before his elder— all these go to hell.
My hide is not to be worn by the virtuous, nor my hair, nor my bones, for they are shunned.
4.017.033c And meats that are not to be eaten [should be avoided] by those like you who practice dharma.
4.017.034a O Rāghava, five five-nailed animals may be eaten by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas:
4.017.034c the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the hare, and the tortoise as the fifth.

"O King, wise men do not touch my skin or my bones; furthermore, my meats are unfit for consumption. Thus have I, though a five-clawed beast, been slain by you, O Kakutstha—by you as its protector, the earth is no longer truly protected."
Just as a woman endowed with virtuous character might fall for a rogue, how could you—
a rogue, deceitful, mean-spirited, and falsely humble in mind—
be born of the great-souled Daśaratha?

"O prince, I have been struck down by the elephant that is Rāma, whose girth-rope of good conduct has been snapped, who transcends the dharma of the virtuous, and who has cast away the goad of righteousness;
had you been visible, O son of a king, you would have fought with me in battle."
"Today, once slain by me, you shall see the god Vaivasvata;
yet I, though difficult to approach, have been struck down in battle by you while you were invisible—
like a man overcome by drink who falls asleep after being bitten by a serpent."
"Since I was slain by you while desiring to do what was pleasing to Sugrīva,
I would have given you Rāvaṇa unslain in battle, having bound him by the neck;
or I would have delivered Maithilī to you, even if she were cast into the waters of the ocean or into the netherworld (pātāla)."
By your command, I would have brought forth a white female mule as if it were born of a mare;
it would have been fitting had Sugrīva obtained the kingdom upon my passing into heaven,
but it was improper that I was slain in battle by you through unrighteousness.
"Indeed, the world is thus brought to its end by Time; if a suitable reply has been reached by you, let it be considered well. Having spoken thus, his mouth became parched.
Pained by the impact of the arrows, the high-souled son of the King of the Gods,
beholding Rāma who resembled the sun,
became silent.
Having been addressed with these humble words— beneficial, consistent with dharma and artha—
by the lifeless Vālin, who was now senseless after being slain, Rāma beheld him like the sun deprived of its luster or a cloud that has released its water.
When the best of monkeys, who was like a fire extinguished after its words had been spoken, had finished speaking—
that unsurpassed lord of monkeys endowed with the virtues of dharma and artha— Rāma, having been insulted, then spoke back to Vālin.
"Without understanding dharma, artha, kāma, and even worldly convention, how can you today, out of childishness, reproach me here?
Without having consulted those endowed with wisdom— the elders esteemed as teachers— "
"O gentle one, out of the fickleness of a monkey, you wish to speak to me here.
This land, with its mountains, forests, and groves, belongs to the Ikṣvākus;
it is also the domain for the punishment and favor of beasts, birds, and men."

The righteous Bharata— truthful, upright, and knowing the true essence of dharma, desire, and wealth— protects that kingdom, devoted as he is to both restraint and favor. In him, both statesmanship and discipline, as well as truth, are firmly established.

And his prowess has been witnessed; that king is a knower of place and time. By his command, which is rooted in righteousness, we and other kings wander over the entire earth, desiring the continuity of dharma.
4.018.010a While that tiger among kings, Bharata, who is devoted to righteousness,
4.018.010c protects the entire earth, who could possibly practice the suppression of dharma? 4.018.011a We, established in our own supreme duty, [shall oppose] him who has strayed from the path.

4.018.011c Placing Bharata’s command foremost, we shall restrain you according to the law. 4.018.012a But you are one whose dharma is corrupted and whose actions are censurable; 4.018.012c devoted primarily to the pursuit of pleasure, you do not abide on the path of kings.
The eldest brother, the father, and he who imparts knowledge—
these three should be known as fathers for one who walks the path of dharma. Furthermore, a younger brother, one’s own son, and a disciple endowed with virtue [should be regarded as sons].
"If righteousness is the motive here, then those three should be regarded by you as your own sons.
O monkey, the dharma of the virtuous is subtle and extremely difficult to discern;
the Self, dwelling in the hearts of all beings, knows what is auspicious and what is inauspicious."
4.018.016a Like a fickle man with fickle monkeys who have not disciplined themselves,
4.018.016c like one blind from birth deliberating with those blind from birth— what indeed will you see?
4.018.017a But I shall explain to you the clarity of this matter.
Indeed, you ought not to reproach me out of mere anger alone;
rather, behold this very reason for which you have been slain by me:
that you have abandoned eternal dharma and are consorting with your brother’s wife.

"While that great-souled Sugrīva is still alive, you, a doer of evil deeds, have out of lust taken Rumā as your wife— though she is his daughter-in-law. Therefore, O monkey, since you have transgressed dharma and acted according to your own desires,"
4.018.020c This punishment has been prescribed for this violation of a brother’s wife.
4.018.021a For one who acts contrary to dharma and departs from the ways of the world, O leader of the monkey hosts, I see no means of restraint other than punishment.

If a man, out of lust, should have sexual intercourse with the natural sister or even the wife of his younger brother, his punishment is declared to be death. But Bharata is the protector of the earth, while we are merely those who abide by his commands.
"And how can you, who have transgressed dharma, remain indifferent?
