A wise man, protecting the dharma according to dharma, must restrain one who has violated the weightiest duties;
Bharata is thus resolved to suppress those who act according to their own lusts."

"O Lord of Monkeys, having carried out the command of Bharata as our duty, we are here prepared to restrain those like you who have transgressed the bounds of propriety. My friendship with Sugrīva is just as it is with Lakṣmaṇa."
He is devoted to my ultimate welfare, even for the sake of his wife and kingdom.
Furthermore, a promise was made by me at that time in the presence of the monkeys;
how could a promise such as this be disregarded by one like me?
Therefore, for all these great reasons consistent with righteousness,
may you grant your approval to this command of yours which is appropriate;
in every respect, your restraint must be regarded as being solely for the sake of dharma.
4.018.029c One who regards it as his duty must assist a friend.
4.018.030a But men who have committed sins, once they have been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
"By my noble Māndhātṛ, a terrible calamity was sought when a sin was committed against a śramaṇa, just as the sin has been committed by you; likewise,
sins have been committed by other lords of the earth who were heedless."
4.018.032c And they perform an expiation; by that, this passion is pacified.
4.018.033a Therefore, enough with this distress; according to dharma, [this] execution has been ordained, O tiger among monkeys. We are not acting of our own free will.
With snares, nooses, and various traps—
both concealed and visible— men capture very many deer,
whether they are running away, terrified, trusting, or standing still.
Whether they are heedless or heedful, men who are intensely seeking meat pierce them even when they have turned their faces away; yet no fault is found in this.
Furthermore, royal sages who are experts in dharma go hunting here.

Therefore, O monkey, you have been slain by me in battle with this arrow, whether you were fighting back or not, because you are but a forest-dweller (śākhāmṛga). And [you have lost] that dharma which is difficult to attain, as well as your auspicious life.
"O best of monkeys, kings are undoubtedly givers;
one should not harm them, nor revile them, nor insult them, nor speak unpleasant words to them.
These are gods moving upon the surface of the earth in human form."
"But you, not understanding dharma, have resorted solely to anger;
you revile me, who am established in the dharma of my fathers and grandfathers.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Vālī was deeply distressed.
Then the lord of the monkeys, with palms joined in reverence, replied to Rāma:
"O best of men, that which you have said is exactly so; there is no doubt in this matter.
For one who is superior is able to respond, whereas one who is inferior cannot."
"O Raghava, you ought not to find fault with me for whatever improper or unpleasant words I previously spoke out of negligence;
for you are one who knows the truth of reality and are devoted to the welfare of your subjects."

Since you have established the relationship between cause and effect, your intellect has become serene and immutable. O knower of dharma, protect me as well— who, though understood [by you], have been set aside by transgressing dharma— with words consistent with dharma.
But Vālin, his throat choked with tears and uttering a cry of distress,
slowly spoke to Rāma while looking at him, like an elephant stuck in the mud:
"I do not grieve for myself, nor for Tārā, nor even for my kinsmen."
Just as my son Aṅgada, the best of those endowed with virtues and adorned with golden armlets—
whom I cherished from his very childhood— is now dejected at not seeing me,
he will wither away like a pond whose water has been drained.
"Direct your highest attention toward Sugrīva and Aṅgada;
for you are both the ruler and the protector, established in the knowledge of what ought and ought not to be done.
Whatever conduct you maintain toward Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa, O Lord of Men,"

O King, you ought to consider Sugrīva and Aṅgada in such a way that Sugrīva does not disregard the ascetic Tārā, whose fault was caused by my own transgression. You must conduct yourself so that he does not hold her in contempt.
"For by you, being favored, it is possible to rule the kingdom—
remaining under your control and following your will.
Rāma consoled Vālī, who had regained his clarity of vision.
"O best of monkeys, neither you nor ourselves should be worried;
for, according to dharma, we have reached a firm resolve that distinguishes us from you.
He who inflicts punishment upon one deserving of it, and he who is punished when deserving of punishment—"
"Since both the cause and the purpose have been accomplished, neither of us shall suffer. Therefore, through this application of punishment, you are cleansed of sin;
you have returned to your own righteous nature by way of the path perceived by Dharma."
Having heard those sweet, composed words of the high-souled Rāma, the crusher of foes in battle, who follows the path of dharma;
The monkey spoke these well-reasoned words:
"O Lord, because I was tormented by arrows and deprived of my senses, I reviled you out of ignorance."
"O Lord of the Earth, you whose formidable prowess is like that of Mahendra, you have been propitiated by me; forgive me.
That great king of monkeys, lying there wounded by arrows, [spoke thus].
Rebuked by his reasoned arguments, he could offer no reply;
with his limbs shattered by stones and severely struck by trees,
and overwhelmed by Rāma’s arrow, he lost consciousness at the end of his life.

Tārā heard that Vālin, the tiger among monkeys, had been slain in battle by the discharge of an arrow from his wife, bestowed by Rāma. Having heard this unpleasant news of her husband’s most terrible death, she, together with her son, [was overcome].
Terrified, she leapt out from the various mountain caves.
But as for those mighty monkeys who were Aṅgada’s followers,
seeing Rāma with his bow, they fled in terror.
Then she saw the monkeys rushing forward in haste, terrified,
like deer strayed from their herd whose leader has been slain. Approaching those who were distressed, she herself, being sorrowful, spoke to them.
"O Rāma, why do you all flee in great terror, like those pursued by arrows, having abandoned that lion among kings before whom you were once leaders? Why do you run away, fallen into such distress?"
"If that brother was struck down by his fierce brother Rāma for the sake of the kingdom,
with arrows discharged from afar that travel long distances,"—
having heard these words of the monkey's wife, the monkeys, who could assume any form at will, [prepared to act].
At that opportune moment, they spoke these unambiguous words to the woman:
"Live on, O son! Return and protect your son, Aṅgada.
Rāma, in the form of Death, has slain Vālin and is carrying him away."
Having struck down the trees and likewise the massive rocks that were hurled at him,
Vālin was felled as if by a thunderbolt with arrows equal to the thunderbolt itself. This entire army, having been rushed upon, has fled and scattered.
Now that this tiger among monkeys, whose splendor was equal to Śakra’s, has been slain,
let the city be protected by the heroes, and let Aṅgada be consecrated;
for once the son of Vālin is established in his position, the monkeys will pay him their allegiance.
"Or rather, O lady of lovely countenance, this place is pleasing to you;
for the monkeys will soon enter difficult terrains, even today. Among them are forest-dwellers both without wives and with their wives."
"From our own greedy kinsmen who have turned against us, we face a tumultuous fear.
Hearing these words from those who were close to her,
that woman of lovely smiles spoke in a manner suited to herself:

"What use have I for my son, what use for the kingdom, or what use for myself, now that my illustrious husband, that lion among monkeys, is perishing? I shall go to the very feet of that great-souled one."
"He who was struck down by the arrow discharged by Rāma"—
having spoken thus, she fled away, weeping and emaciated by grief,
striking her head and chest with both arms in her sorrow.
Then, as she was returning, she saw her husband fallen upon the ground—
the slayer of the lords of the Dānavas who never retreat in battles,
and the hurler of great mountains like Vāsava hurls his thunderbolts.
Filled with a great wind and possessing a roar like a mass of mighty clouds,
he was equal to Śakra in prowess; like a rain-cloud that has ceased after its downpour,
that terrible hero, who used to roar among those who roar, has been struck down by another hero.
Just as a tiger might slay the king of beasts for the sake of its prey,
so has this shrine— honored by all the world, adorned with banners and altars—
been destroyed for the sake of a serpent, like the *caitya* shattered by Suparṇa.
She saw the powerful bow standing there, grasped and held firm;
she saw Rāma, as well as Rāma’s younger brother, and her husband’s younger brother.
Having passed them by and reached her husband, she found him slain in battle.
Beholding him, she fell to the ground in distress, bewildered;
then, as if waking from sleep, she rose again, crying out, "O noble son!
Seeing her husband bound by the nooses of death, she wept.
Beholding her crying out like a female osprey, Sugrīva fell into deep distress; and seeing Aṅgada arrived,
he was overcome with grief upon perceiving him struck by that world-ending arrow discharged from Rāma’s bow.
Seeing him slain upon the ground, Tārā, whose face was like that of the lord of stars,
approached her husband and embraced him, O passionate lady,
beholding Vālin struck down by the arrow and resembling a fallen elephant.
With a mind tormented by grief, the distressed Tārā lamented for the lord of monkeys, who resembled Mahendra,
like a tree uprooted from its base:
"O hero of terrible prowess in battle, O foremost of leapers!"
"Why do you not speak today to me, who am dejected and standing before you? Arise, O tiger among monkeys, and resort to your excellent bed;
for the best of kings do not lie upon the bare ground in such a manner."

"O lord of the earth, this earth is indeed exceedingly dear to you, since even though I am dead, you attend to her with your limbs while abandoning me. Clearly, O hero, as you proceed according to dharma, another woman has been favored by you."
This beautiful city of Kiṣkindhā, constructed on the path to heaven, is like that very place.
Whatever pleasures we enjoyed together with you in the honey-scented forests during those times have now come to an end through you.

Deprived of joy and deprived of hope, I am submerged in an ocean of grief now that you, the leader of great leaders of the herd, have met your death. Seeing you slain upon the earth, my heart remains strangely steadfast.
That it has not burst asunder today in a thousand pieces, though tormented by grief,
is because you have carried off Sugrīva’s wife and he has been driven into exile; this is the retribution for that which you have received from him, O Lord of Monkeys.
Out of delusion, you have censured me, who am devoted to your supreme welfare;
for I spoke these beneficial words, desiring the well-being of the lord of monkeys.
Without a doubt, the time has surely come that will bring an end to your life.

"By whom you were forcibly brought under the power of Sugrīva against your will— now, though previously unaccustomed to suffering, I, a miserable woman, shall endure this state of widowhood and the torment of grief like one who is helpless."
4.020.015a And what state will the heroic Aṅgada endure— he who is cherished, delicate, and accustomed to comfort— when my paternal uncle is overwhelmed by rage?
4.020.016a O son, take a final look at your father, who is devoted to righteousness.
"O child, it will be difficult for you to behold him again. Comfort your son and give him a message;
for you are now about to depart on your journey, having smelled his head in blessing."
Indeed, by striking you down, Rāma has performed a great deed;
he has attained freedom from his debt regarding his promise to Sugrīva. Be fulfilled in your desire, O Sugrīva; you shall regain Rumā.
"Enjoy the kingdom without anxiety; your brother, who was your enemy, has been slain. Why do you not speak with affection to me as I lament thus?
Look, O Lord of Monkeys, at these many excellent wives of yours."

4.020.021 Having heard her lamentation, all those female monkeys from every side took hold of the dejected Angada and wailed, afflicted with grief. 4.020.022 "O hero, O Angada, O you with powerful arms! What [has happened] to Angada?"
Leaving behind a long exile today is not at all fitting for one so endowed with virtues; O you who love your son, it is not right to depart, leaving your son behind.
"O Lord, O you of lovely and pleasing appearance, what displeasure has been caused to you by me, or by your son? O Hero, having abandoned your companion today..."
O long-armed one, if you go to the abode of Yama because of some unpleasant thing done by me without due reflection, and if it was ill-behaved of me, [then consider this].
"Forgive me for that, O Lord of the Harivaṃśa;
I go to your feet with my head bowed, O Hero.
Thus Tārā, weeping piteously, spoke.
In the presence of her husband, she of blameless complexion resolved, together with the female monkeys,
to sit down upon the ground where Vālin lay to fast unto death.

Then Hanumān, the leader of the monkey hosts, slowly comforted Tārā as she lay fallen, like a star fallen from the sky. "A living being experiences what is produced by virtues and faults, caused by the fruit of its own actions."
One who is undistracted attains all that—both auspicious and inauspicious—after death.
You grieve for those who are to be pitied; you, being miserable yourself, show compassion to the miserable.
And who is there to be pitied by whom, in this body that is like a bubble?
"This prince Aṅgada must be looked after by you, whose son is still living;
consider what effective measures should be taken for his future. You know that the coming and going of beings is indeed thus uncertain."
Therefore, a wise person should indeed perform auspicious deeds for this world; for he,
upon whom thousands, millions,
and billions of monkeys subsist by the portions they have been assigned, has now met his end.
4.021.007 Since he has perceived the truth through right reasoning and is devoted to conciliation, generosity, and forbearance,
and has attained the state of those who have conquered through dharma, you ought not to grieve for him.
4.021.008 Moreover, O tiger among monkeys, all these [monkeys] and this son of yours, Aṅgada, [are here].
"O blameless one, the sovereignty over the lions and the rishabha-beasts is now under your protection.
O beautiful lady, gently urge these two who are consumed by grief;
let this Angada, supported by you, rule the earth."
4.021.010a Let the lineage be maintained as it has been seen, and let whatever duty is immediate be performed; O King, let all that be done—this is the certainty of the time.
4.021.011a King Hari must be consecrated with the purificatory rites, and Aṅgada must be anointed.
"Beholding your son seated upon the lion-throne, you shall attain peace.
Hearing those words of his, Tārā, afflicted by the calamity that had befallen her husband, spoke this reply to Hanumān, who stood before her.

"Even if he were slain, it would be better for me to have the embrace of this hero's body than to have a hundred sons resembling Aṅgada born to me from one [husband]. Furthermore, I am not the mistress of the King of the Monkeys, nor of Aṅgada."
"Sugrīva is his paternal uncle and is next to him in all affairs.
O Hanumān, best of monkeys, you should not entertain such thoughts regarding Aṅgada; for a father is the true kinsman of a son, not a mother."
For there is nothing more conducive to my welfare, either in this world or the next, than being attended by heroes slain while facing the enemy, through my reliance upon Hari, the King.
"This bed is fit for me to occupy," he thought; yet, with his strength failing and breathing faintly from all sides,
he first beheld Sugrīva standing before his son.
Having addressed Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, who had achieved victory, Vālī spoke these words with clear speech and affection:
"O Sugrīva, you ought not to blame me for this transgression."
"O father, as I am being forcibly dragged away by the delusion of my future destiny,
I do not believe that happiness is ordained for both of us at once;
for this brotherly affection has indeed turned into its opposite."
"Having taken over the kingdom of these forest-dwellers this very day,
know that I too am departing this very day for the abode of Vaivasvata;
for both life and this vast sovereignty and prosperity [are transient]."
"I shall indeed quickly abandon this great and irreproachable fame. O hero, in this state of affairs, I shall say these words;
though they may be difficult to perform, O King, you ought nevertheless to do them."
Behold this child Aṅgada, who deserves happiness and was raised in comfort, yet is now no longer childish; see him fallen upon the ground with his face filled with tears—
this son who is dearer to me than my own life, like a son born of my own body.
Protect in every way this one who is bereft of me, yet whose purpose is unimpaired;
for you too are his giver and his protector in every respect,
and the bestower of fearlessness in times of danger, just as I am, O Lord of Monkeys.
"This illustrious son of Tārā, whose prowess is equal to yours,
shall stand at the forefront of you in the slaughter of those rākṣasas,
performing deeds worthy of himself through his valor in battle."
This swift and youthful Aṅgada, the son of Tārā, will accomplish this;
and this daughter of Suṣeṇa is thoroughly proficient in every way in determining subtle matters of state and in interpreting various portents.
4.022.014a Whatever she may say is "right," that task should be carried out without doubt.
4.022.014c For the opinion of Tārā never turns out otherwise. 4.022.015a And you must perform this service for Rāghava without hesitation.
For there would be unrighteousness in failing to do so, and he, being insulted, might even harm you.
Put on this divine golden garland of Sugrīva;
for noble fortune resides within it, yet she would surely depart if I were to die.

Thus addressed by Vālin out of brotherly affection, Sugrīva abandoned his joy and became dejected once more, like the lord of stars seized by a planet; yet, pacified by those words of Vālin, he remained vigilant and performed what was appropriate.
Having been granted permission, he took that very golden garland.
Having given that golden garland and seeing his son standing there, Vālin,
having attained perfection for his state after death, spoke out of affection to Aṅgada:

4.022.020a Attend now to place and time, enduring both the pleasant and the unpleasant; 4.022.020c bearing joy and sorrow in their due season, remain under the authority of Sugrīva. 4.022.021a For as you have been constantly cherished by me, O mighty-armed one, [so must you now act].

Sugrīva will not hold you in high regard if you continue to behave in such a manner. O subduer of enemies, do not go with his foes, nor with his enemies; devoted to your master's interests and self-controlled, remain under Sugrīva’s authority.
"One should not show excessive intimacy, nor should one show a lack of intimacy;
for both are great faults. Therefore, remain an observer from within.
Having said this, his eyes rolled back as he was severely tormented by the arrow.
With his terrifying teeth bared, he was deprived of life. When that heroic lord of the monkeys had been slain,
the monkeys there found no peace.
Like cows wandering in a great forest filled with lions when their leader has been slain,
Tārā was then submerged in an ocean of calamity.
Beholding the face of her deceased husband,
she fell to the ground embracing Vālin,
like a creeper clinging to a great tree that has been severed.
Then Tārā, smelling the face of the king of monkeys—
her husband fallen from the world and dead— spoke these words:
"You lie here in misery upon the uneven ground, having failed to heed my words."
O hero, upon this surface of the earth, strewn with stones and filled with great suffering,
the ground must surely be dearer to you than I am, O Lord of Monkeys;
for you lie there embracing it, yet you do not answer me.
"O hero, lover of daring deeds, it is Sugrīva alone who is truly valiant;
the leaders of the bears and monkeys attend upon you, the mighty one.
[Consider] this lamentation of theirs and the distress of Aṅgada as he grieves."
4.023.005c Having heard these words of mine, why do you not awaken?
4.023.006a This is that bed of heroes where you lie slain in battle; 4.023.006c it is here that in the past your enemies were laid low and killed by you alone.
"O you of pure character and noble birth, lover of battle, my beloved!
O giver of honor, you have departed, leaving me alone and protectorless. Indeed, a wise man should never give his daughter to a mere warrior."
Behold me, the wife of a hero, now slain and suddenly made a widow! My pride is shattered, and my eternal refuge is broken;
I am submerged in a vast and bottomless ocean of grief.
4.023.010a Surely this heart of mine is made of the essence of stone and is firm, 4.023.010c since, having seen my husband slain, it has not today shattered into a hundred pieces.
4.023.011a For he was indeed my friend and my husband, and by nature dear to me.
A hero who has displayed his prowess in battle and met his death there,
though he may have been the lord of a woman, she is called a "widow" by the wise— even if she possesses sons and is fully provided with wealth and grain. (4.023.011c–4.023.012)
O hero, you lie upon a pool of blood produced from your own limbs, as if upon a bed covered with a rug dyed with red lac; your body is entirely enveloped on all sides by dust and gore.
"O bull among monkeys, I am unable to embrace you with my arms.
Today, Sugrīva has accomplished his purpose in this most terrible enmity,
for the fear caused by Rāma has been removed by a single arrow released by him."
"Because of the arrow lodged in your heart, I am prevented from touching your body;
I can only gaze at you as you have passed away. Then Nīla extracted that arrow which was embedded in his body.
Like a blazing venomous serpent hidden in a mountain cave,
the brilliance of that arrow as it was being drawn forth shone like a ray of light from the sun obstructed by the peak of the setting mountain.
Streams of blood flowed from all his wounds like torrents of liquid copper and red chalk falling from a mountain.
As she wiped her husband covered in the dust of battle, [she saw him thus].
She drenched the hero, who had been struck down by weapons, with tears born from her eyes.
Seeing her husband slain, his entire body drenched in blood,
the woman Tārā spoke to her tawny-eyed son, Aṅgada.
"O son, behold this most terrible final state of your father;
having engaged in enmity, he has reached his end through his evil deeds—
departing for the abode of Yama with a body like the rising morning sun."
"Pay homage, my son, to the king, your father, who bestows honor. Thus addressed, he rose and grasped his father's feet with his thick, rounded arms, saying, "I am Aṅgada."
Why do you not address Aṅgada, who salutes you as before, saying, "May you live long, my son"? I,
accompanied by my son, wait upon you who have lost consciousness.
Slain instantly by the lion like a cow with her calf by a bull,
he has performed the sacrifice of battle with various weapons for its waters;
having bathed in this final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*), how can he be without me, his wife?

"O giver of honor, why do I not see here that garland made of gold which was given to you by the King of the Gods, pleased with you in battle? Royal splendor does not abandon you, even though your life has departed."
Like the radiance of the revolving sun upon the king of mountains,
this wholesome word of mine has been disregarded by you;
indeed, I am not capable of restraining you.
"Slain in battle along with my son, Fortune herself deserts me here, together with you. Having seen Vālin lifeless, Rāghava immediately thereafter—
The scorcher of enemies spoke these humble words to Sugrīva:
"A dead man is not joined with any benefit through the torment of grief;
you ought to attend to that which must be done next."
4.024.003a The conduct of the world must be followed; you have shed your tears.
4.024.003c No action whatsoever can be undertaken beyond the power of time.
4.024.004a Destiny is the cause in the world; necessity is the instrument of action.
4.024.004c Destiny is the cause for all beings in their various assignments here.
4.024.005a No one is the agent of anything, nor is anyone the master over another’s assignment;
4.024.005c the world proceeds according to its own nature, and time is its ultimate resort.
Time does not bypass time, nor does time ever fail;
having encountered one's own nature, no one can transcend it.
Time possesses neither kinship, nor cause, nor prowess.

Neither friendship, nor kinship, nor relationship is the cause, nor is it one's own will; rather, the transformation of time must be seen by one who perceives correctly. For virtue, wealth, and pleasure are all established through the sequence of time.
"From here, Vālin has gone to his own nature, having attained the fruit of his actions;
O Lord of the Monkeys, he was purified by his union with dharma, artha, and kāma. And through his adherence to his own duty, that great-souled one has conquered [the realms]."
4.024.010c Heaven has been secured by him who did not cling to his own life.
4.024.011a This indeed is the supreme destiny which the leader of the monkey-hosts has attained. 4.024.011c Therefore, enough with lamentation; attend now to what the occasion demands.
At the conclusion of Rāma’s speech, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
spoke these humble words to Sugrīva, who was distraught:
“O Sugrīva, perform for him immediately the funeral rites.”
"Accompanied by Tārā and Aṅgada, go toward the cremation fire for Vālī.
Order that many dry logs and divine sandalwood be prepared for the sake of Vālī’s funeral rites."

4.024.015a "Console this Aṅgada, whose mind is dejected; 4.024.015c do not be of such childish intellect, for this city is dependent upon you. 4.024.016a Let Aṅgada bring garlands and various garments."

"Bring ghee, oil, perfumes, and whatever else is required for this occasion; O Tāra, come quickly with haste to fetch the palanquin. Indeed, speed is a virtue and especially appropriate at a time such as this."
"Let the monkeys who are accustomed to carrying palanquins prepare themselves;
being capable and strong, they shall carry Vālin away. Having spoken thus to Sugrīva, the enhancer of Sumitrā’s joy—
Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, stood near his brother.
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, Tāra, his mind agitated,
quickly entered the cave with his thoughts fixed upon the palanquin.
4.024.021a Tāra, having taken that palanquin, caused it to be carried once more;
4.024.021c it was borne by heroic monkeys who were accustomed to carrying such loads.
4.024.022a Then Sugrīva, lifting Vālin up, [placed him] upon the palanquin.
"Place him upon [the bier] while he still cries out, together with Aṅgada.
Having thus placed the lifeless Vālin upon the palanquin,
they adorned him with various ornaments, garlands, and garments.
Then King Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, commanded:
"Let the funeral rites for my noble brother be performed in a fitting manner.
As they distributed many various kinds of jewels, he continued: [4.024.025a] "Distributing many diverse gems..."
"Let the monkeys go in front, and let the palanquin follow immediately after them.
For whatever kinds of extraordinary royal splendors are seen on earth,
they quickly prepared such [a display] for Vālin’s funeral rites."
Then Aṅgada, Tāra, and the others, having quickly taken hold of him, all the monkeys whose kinsmen had been slain went forth wailing; likewise,
all the female monkeys, headed by Tārā, whose troop-leader had been killed, followed.
Crying out with piteous sounds, they indeed followed their lord. By the sound of those female monkeys weeping within the forest,
all the woods and mountains seemed to cry out in every direction.
On a secluded sandy bank of a mountain river, shaded by water,
many forest-dwelling monkeys prepared a funeral pyre.
Then, those accustomed to carrying palanquins lowered the litter from their shoulders.
4.024.031c All of them, overcome with grief, stood apart, having retreated to a secluded spot.
4.024.032a Then Tārā, seeing her husband lying upon the floor of the litter,
placed his head upon her lap and lamented, deeply afflicted by sorrow.
"And why do you look upon these people so oppressed by grief? O giver of honor, even though he is dead, your face appears as if delighted;
it bears the hue of the setting sun, as if he were still alive."
"O monkey, this Time, in the form of Rāma, drags you away—
he by whom all [these women] were made widows in battle with a single arrow.
These are those very female monkeys, O king of kings, who have always been dear to you."
"Do you not realize that we have come along this long, arduous path on foot?
Are these moon-faced wives of yours not indeed dear to you?
Why do you not look now upon Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys?"
"O King, these ministers of yours, headed by Tāra, as well as these city-dwellers, sit here surrounding you, O sinless one. O subduer of enemies, dismiss these powerful men as is appropriate."
"Then we shall all sport in the forests, intoxicated with wine.
To Tārā, who was thus lamenting and overwhelmed by grief for her husband,
the female monkeys, themselves emaciated by sorrow, then raised her up.
Then, together with Sugrīva, Aṅgada, his senses overwhelmed by grief, weeping, placed his father upon the funeral pyre. Then,
having offered the fire according to the prescribed rites, he performed the circumambulation from right to left.
With his senses overwhelmed, he [saw] his father set out upon the long journey.
Having performed the funeral rites for Vālin according to the prescribed rules,
those monkeys went to a beautiful river of cool water to offer the water libation.
Then, having placed Aṅgada at their head,
they gathered together there along with Sugrīva and Tārā and offered water for Vālin.
Having become dejected himself, the mighty Sugrīva, in his own distress, performed the rite.

4.024.044c Śarabhaṅga, the son of Kakutstha, shared his grief and performed the funeral rites. 4.025.001a Then, the high ministers of the monkeys gathered around and stood by Sugrīva, who was tormented by grief and wearing wet garments.
Having approached the mighty-armed Rāma, the doer of effortless deeds,
they all stood with palms joined in reverence, like sages before their Grandfather [Brahmā].
Then he appeared, resembling a mountain of gold, with a face like the rising sun.

4.025.003c With palms joined in reverence, Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, spoke these words: 4.025.004a "O Lord, through your grace, Sugrīva has obtained this great ancestral kingdom of his fathers and grandfathers, which is so difficult for the monkeys to attain."
"With your permission, having entered the auspicious city, he will,
together with his circle of friends, attend to all necessary duties.
He has already bathed according to the prescribed rites with various perfumes and medicinal herbs."
He will honor you especially with jewels and garlands.
You ought to come from here to this delightful mountain cave;
O Lord, establish this alliance, bringing great joy to the monkeys.
Thus addressed by Hanumān, Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
wise and skilled in speech, replied to Hanumān:
"O gentle one, for fourteen years— whether in a village or a city— "
"O Hanumān, as one who obeys the command of my father, I shall not enter [the city].
Let Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, enter that divine and most prosperous cave;
once he has entered according to the prescribed rites, O hero, let him be swiftly consecrated in the kingdom."
Having spoken thus to Hanumān, Rāma said to Sugrīva:
"O hero, consecrate this Aṅgada as well in the position of crown prince.
This is the first month of the rainy season, Śrāvaṇa, the time when the waters arrive."

"O gentle one, the four months known as the rainy season have begun. This is not the time for exertion; enter the auspicious city. O gentle one, I shall dwell on this mountain together with Lakṣmaṇa."
"This mountain cave is delightful, spacious, and well-ventilated;
it abounds in water, O gentle one, and is filled with lotuses and water-lilies.
Now that the month of Kārttika has arrived, you must strive for the slaying of Rāvaṇa."
"O gentle one, this is our agreement: enter your own abode, be consecrated in the kingdom, and gladden your friends.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, [acted accordingly].
He entered the beautiful city of Kiṣkindhā, which had been protected by Vālin. As the lord of monkeys entered, thousands of monkeys greeted him with joy and surrounded him on all sides.
Then all the subjects, having seen the lord of the monkey hosts,
bowed with their heads and fell prostrate upon the earth with concentrated minds.
The valiant Sugrīva, having addressed all the subjects, raised them up.
The immensely powerful one entered his brother’s pleasant inner apartments.
Having entered, he found Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, had already departed;
then his friends consecrated him, just as the immortals consecrated the Thousand-Eyed One.
They brought for him a white parasol adorned with gold,
and two glorious white yak-tail fans with golden handles;
likewise, they brought all kinds of jewels, as well as all types of seeds and medicinal herbs.
The sprouts and flowers of milky trees,
white garments, white unguents,
fragrant garlands, and both land-born and water-born lotuses.
And divine sandalwood, many various perfumes,
unbroken grains, gold, priyaṅgu, honey, and clarified butter;
curd, tiger-skin, and sandals made of boar-leather.
Taking fragrant unguents, yellow pigment (rocanā), and red arsenic (manaḥśilā), sixteen excellent maidens arrived there joyfully. Then,
at the proper time and according to the prescribed rite, they [honored] that best of monkeys.
Having gratified the best of the twice-born with jewels, garments, and food,
those people learned in the mantras then offered oblations purified by sacred formulas into the kindled fire of Jātavedas, which was strewn with *kuśa* grass.
Then, on the delightful summit of the palace— which was established in gold, covered with excellent carpets, and adorned with various garlands—
he had him seated facing east upon an excellent throne with various mantras.
Having gathered water from rivers and streams, from bathing places on every side,
and having brought it from all the oceans, those bulls among monkeys placed the pure and auspicious waters into golden jars.
With auspicious bull-horns and golden jars,
according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures and ordained by the great seers,
[the consecration was performed]. Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana—
Mainda, Dvivida, Hanumān, Jāmbavat,
and Nala consecrated Sugrīva with clear, fragrant water,
just as the Vasus consecrated the thousand-eyed Vāsava.
When Sugrīva had been consecrated, all those high-souled bulls among monkeys,
thousands in number, shouted for joy there.
And Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, carried out the word of Rāma.
Having embraced Aṅgada, he consecrated him as the crown prince. When Aṅgada had been consecrated, the high-souled monkeys, filled with compassion, honored Sugrīva, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Crowded with happy and well-fed people, adorned with banners and flags,
the lovely city of Kiṣkindhā lay within the mountain cave.
Then, having reported this to the high-souled Rāma;
Having received the great consecration and regained his wife Ruma, the heroic lord of the monkey host obtained a kingdom just like the lord of the thirty gods.
When Sugrīva had been consecrated and the monkey had entered his cave,
Rāma, together with his brother, went to Mount Prasravaṇa,
which resounded with the cries of tigers and deer and was filled with lions of terrible roar.
4.026.002c Hidden by various shrubs and creepers, crowded with many trees;
4.026.003a Haunted by bears, monkeys, gopucchas, and wildcats;
4.026.003c A mountain resembling a mass of clouds, which was a constant refuge for pure waters.

On the peak of that mountain, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, took up residence for the sake of dwelling in a large and extensive cave. There the righteous-souled descendant of Raghu lived along with Lakṣmaṇa.
On that mountain Prasravaṇa, amidst its many caves and groves,
though it was most pleasant and abounded in resources,
Rāma found not even the slightest pleasure while dwelling there.
For as he remembered his wife— who had been carried away and was dearer to him than life itself—
he could not find sleep at night when he lay upon his bed, especially upon seeing the moon risen at dawn.
To that descendant of Kakutstha, whose mind was overwhelmed by tears arising from that grief and who was constantly mourning, wholly surrendered to sorrow,
his brother Lakṣmaṇa— sharing the same suffering— spoke these words of consolation.
"Enough, O hero; do not fall into distress, for you ought not to grieve.
For it is well known to you that all purposes fail for one who grieves. You are devoted to action in this world, and you are dedicated to the gods."
"O Rāghava, you are a believer, virtuous in character,
and resolute. For one who is not determined is not capable of slaying that enemy, the Rākṣasa, especially in battle— that deceiver, by means of your heroic exploits."
4.026.012a Uproot your grief and make your resolve firm;
4.026.012c then, together with his followers, utterly destroy that Rākṣasa.
4.026.013a O descendant of Kakutstha, [you shall likewise conquer] even the earth, along with its oceans, forests, and mountains.
If he is capable of overturning even me, how much more so Rāvaṇa? Indeed, I shall awaken your dormant prowess,
like a fire covered in ashes being rekindled at the proper time with blazing oblations.
Having honored those beneficial and auspicious words of Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava spoke these words to his affectionate friend: "That which ought to be said by one who is devoted, affectionate, and well-wishing— "
"O Lakṣmaṇa of true valor, what you have said is appropriate.
This grief, which brings all undertakings to ruin, has been cast aside. I shall now rouse that energy of yours which is unimpeded in its prowess."
"I shall await the autumn season; this rainy season has now arrived.
Then, I will slay that Rākṣasa along with his kingdom and his hosts.
Hearing those words of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa was filled with joy.

4.026.019c Again, the son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends, spoke these words: 4.026.020a "O destroyer of enemies, these words you have spoken are worthy of you; 4.026.020c now, O descendant of Kakutstha, you have returned to your true nature."
"Having recognized your own prowess, you ought to act accordingly;
this which you have spoken is worthy of your learning and your noble lineage.
Therefore, O tiger among men, consider the means of subduing the enemy."
"O Raghava, let this night of the rainy season pass by. Controlling your anger, wait for the autumn;
endure these four months with me."
On this mountain Vasācala, frequented by the king of beasts,
he grew strong, intent upon the destruction of his enemy.
Having then slain Vālī and consecrated Sugrīva, he—
4.027.001c While dwelling on the ridge of Mālyavat, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
4.027.002a "This very time has arrived; today is the season for the coming of the rains. Behold the sky covered with clouds that resemble mountains."
Having drunk the essence of the oceans with its rays, the sky brings forth as an elixir the embryo held for nine months;
it is possible to ascend to the vault of heaven by means of a flight of stairs made of clouds.
With garlands of *kuṭaja* and *arjuna* flowers, they sought to adorn the sun;
the sky appeared as if its wounds were bandaged by glistening veils of cloud-patches— coppery from the glow of twilight and increasingly pale at their edges.
With the gentle breeze as its sighs and colored by the sandalwood of twilight,
the sky, with its pale clouds, shines like one afflicted by love. This [earth],
oppressed by the heat and now drenched with fresh water—
Like Sītā tormented by grief, the earth sheds tears.
Released from the bellies of the clouds, the winds— cool and pleasant as white lotuses and fragrant with the scent of *ketakī* flowers— can be drunk in cupped palms.
4.027.009a This mountain, its *arjuna* trees in full bloom and perfumed by *ketaka* flowers,
4.027.009c is being consecrated by showers of rain, like Sugrīva whose enemies have been quelled.
4.027.010a The clouds, wearing black antelope skins and bearing the rain-showers as sacred threads, [are present].
With their caves filled by the Maruts, the mountains seemed as if they were reciting aloud;
struck by lightning as if by golden whips,
the sky, with its internal rumbling, seemed to be in pain.

4.027.012a To me, lightning flashing against the dark blue clouds appears like the wretched Vaidehī flashing in the lap of Rāvaṇa. 4.027.013a These quarters of the sky, though obstructed, are favorable to those possessed by love.
4.027.013c Like nights when the moon has vanished and are smeared by thick clouds;
4.027.014a In some places, O Saumitri, behold the *kuṭaja* trees on the mountain ridges, their buds closed by dew and eager for the arrival of the rains.
For me, who am overwhelmed by grief, these things that inflame desire remain present; yet today the dust has been stilled by a cool breeze,
and the spreading afflictions of the summer heat have subsided.
For the expeditions of the lords of the earth have indeed been halted;
men who were traveling abroad are returning to their own lands,
having set out with the desire to dwell at Lake Mānasa.
Now that the cakravāka birds are united with their beloveds, vehicles no longer pass along the roads, which have been ravaged by the incessant downpour of rain.
In some places bright and in others dim,
the sky, with its scattered clouds, shines forth; in some places and in others it is obstructed by mountains.
The appearance was like that of the great ocean when it is stilled,
with its fresh water mixed with the blossoms of the *sarja* and *kadamba* trees and reddened by the minerals of the mountains.
The mountain streams flow even more swiftly, followed by the cries of peacocks;
they are filled with water and resemble the humming of bees.
The jambu fruit is enjoyed to one's heart's content— multicolored and shaken by the wind—
while the ripe mango fruit falls to the ground.
The clouds, resembling the peaks of the king of mountains, adorned with banners of lightning and garlands of cranes,
roar with a thunderous sound.
Like lordly elephants in rut standing in battle, the row of cranes, eager for the clouds and flying about,
shines with joy.
Shaken by the wind, the excellent *pauṇḍarīka* lotus is like a long garland upon the sky;
sleep slowly approaches Keśava.
The river swiftly approaches the ocean;
the joyful crane approaches the cloud;
the longing beloved approaches her lover.
The forest edges have come to life with peacocks dancing beautifully;
the kadamba trees have blossomed along with their branches;
and the bulls, sharing the same desire, have become enamored with the cows.
The earth has become delightful with its crops and forests;
they carry, rain, roar, and shine;
they meditate, dance, and take heart.
The rivers, the clouds, the intoxicated elephants, the forest edges,
the peacocks with their charming cries, the monkeys, and the fragrance of the *ketaka* flowers— all were filled with great joy.
Having smelled the forest waterfalls, the lordly elephants, thrilled and agitated by the sound of the cascades,
trumpet lustily along with the peacocks.
Struck by the falling torrents and clinging to the branches of the *kadamba* trees,
they [drank] the honey-nectar they had gathered for a moment.
The bees gradually abandon their intoxication with fruits that are richly endowed with abundant juices and resemble heaps of powdered charcoal.
The branches of the *jambū* trees shine forth,
as if being settled upon by swarms of bees;
they are adorned with banners of lightning.
The forms of the clouds, with their surging and deep great roars, shine like elephants prepared for battle.
Following the path and traversing mountains and forests, he set out upon hearing the roar of a cloud,
desiring battle and suspecting it to be a rival elephant.
The lordly elephant, having turned back from me,
let fall water from his trunk which, being perfectly pure, clung to the hollows of the leaves.
Delighted birds with pale plumage, being thirsty, drink from that water bestowed by the Lord of the Gods;
dark blue birds drink from the dark blue waters filled with fresh rain.
Clouds cling to clouds,
like those scorched by forest fires to other fires so scorched;
they are rooted fast, like mountains upon mountains.
The lordly elephants are intoxicated, the lordly bulls are joyful,
and the lions in the forests are most at ease; the great mountains are beautiful, and the great trees are tranquil.
The Lord of the Gods has sported with the clouds;
the expeditions of the kings have ceased and their armies are returning; both hostilities and the roads have been leveled by the water.

In the month of Prauṣṭhapada, for Brāhmaṇas desiring to speak of the Veda, this time for study has arrived for the chanters of the Sāmaveda. Having ceased from ritual action and having surely accumulated his stores, [he should remain thus].
Bharata, the lord of the treasury, has arrived at the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
surely the current of the swelling Sarayū increases as it hears the sound of my approaching Ayodhyā.
"These rains, rich in virtues, Sugrīva enjoys in happiness;
having conquered his enemies, he remains with his wife established in a great kingdom. But I, on the other hand, have had my wife stolen away and have been cast down from my great kingdom."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, I am sinking like a riverbank that has become saturated;
my grief is vast, the rains are exceedingly difficult to traverse,
and the great enemy Rāvaṇa appears to me as boundless."
Having seen this lack of provisions and these extremely difficult paths,
and since Sugrīva was already bowed down [in submission], I said nothing at all.
Furthermore, he had been greatly distressed for a long time before being reunited with his wife.
"Because my own duty is more important, I do not wish to speak to the monkey myself.
For Sugrīva will understand the service that has been rendered once he has rested and realized that the time has arrived; there is no doubt in this."
Therefore, O one of auspicious marks, I remain here awaiting the proper time, biding my time while waiting for the clearing of Sugrīva and the rivers.
For a hero is indeed joined with a return favor by means of a service rendered.
"An ungrateful person who has not returned a favor strikes at the hearts of the virtuous.
Then, having been addressed in this way, Lakṣmaṇa composed himself and,
with palms joined in reverence, honored those words in return.
He, whose appearance was most delightful, spoke to Rāma,
manifesting his own auspicious vision:
"All this that you have desired has been accomplished exactly as you requested."
O Lord of Men, O Lord of Hari, you who are intent on the destruction of the enemy may wait for this autumn; may you endure this downpour of rain for a short while.
Having observed the cloudless sky, from which the lightning and clouds had departed,
resounding with the cries of cranes and anointed by the lovely moonlight;
and having observed Sugrīva, whose purposes were fulfilled yet who was negligent in the accumulation of dharma and artha.
His mind was entirely intent upon the path of the wicked;
his duties were abandoned and his goals accomplished; he was constantly devoted to women;
and he had attained every single desire of his heart.
He was sporting day and night with his own beloved wife and also with Tārā, whom he desired; having accomplished his purpose, his fever had subsided,
and like the Lord of the Gods sporting with hosts of Apsarases in the Nandana grove.
One who has entrusted all affairs to his ministers, yet pays no heed to those ministers;
one whose royal administration has fallen into ruin, remaining addicted to sensual pleasures—
[such a king] may be approached by one who has ascertained the facts, knows the true nature of objectives, and understands the specific requirements of time and circumstance.

Having propitiated the Lord of Monkeys— who was himself a master of speech and knew the true essence of discourse— with sweet, reasoned, and delightful words, the son of the Wind-god spoke that which was beneficial,
truthful, wholesome, and endowed with conciliation, righteousness, purpose, and policy.
Approaching the Lord of Monkeys with words joined by affection and love, and certain in his confidence, Hanumān spoke these words:
"The kingdom has been attained, as well as fame; the ancestral glory has increased."
The remaining task is the gathering of friends; you ought to perform that.
For the kingdom, fame, and power of one who always conducts himself virtuously toward his friends and knows the proper time increase.
4.028.011 O protector of the earth, he whose treasury, army, allies, and his own person are all united shall enjoy a great kingdom.
4.028.012 You, however, are endowed with such conduct and remain established on the path that is free from danger.

One ought to act appropriately to fulfill the purpose of a friend for whom one has undertaken a task. But he who attends to a friend's business only after the proper time has passed does not truly serve the friend's interest, even if he accomplishes great objectives.
"O Raghava, let this search for Vaidehi be undertaken.
O hero, subduer of enemies, this task of yours has now passed its proper time;
yet the one who knows the timing does not inform you that the time has elapsed."
O King, even though he is in a hurry, the wise Rāghava remains obedient to your will; he is the banner of his prosperous lineage, a kinsman for a long time,
possessed of immeasurable power, and himself peerless in his virtues.
"You must indeed perform for him that service which he previously performed for you.
O Lord of Monkeys, you ought to command the foremost of monkeys;
for time will not pass by without such an exhortation."
For there may be a lapse of time regarding a task that has been urged;
yet, O Lord of Monkeys, you are the performer of even a task for which you have not acted as an agent—
how much more so for one who has repaid your kindness with both kingdom and wealth?
"O lord of the hosts of monkeys, you are powerful and valiant;
why do you hesitate to carry out the command that will bring joy to the son of Daśaratha?
Indeed, you are capable of slaying with your arrows the gods, asuras, and great serpents at will."
The son of Daśaratha desires to bring [the world] under his control, yet he awaits the fulfillment of your promise.
Without hesitation regarding the sacrifice of his own life, he has done what is pleasing to you; therefore, let us search for Vaidehī upon the earth and even in the sky.
Neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Asuras, nor the hosts of Maruts,
nor Yakṣas shall cause him fear, much less Rākṣasas;
for he is thus endowed with power and has previously performed what was pleasing [to the Lord].

O Lord of the Monkeys, you ought to do what is pleasing to Rāma with all your soul. By your command, O Lord of the Monkeys, no one among us shall be obstructed— neither on the ground below, nor in the waters, nor above in the sky.
"Therefore, command who among them shall stay somewhere for your sake;
for you have monkeys, O sinless one, numbering more than ten million, who are invincible.
Having heard those words of his, spoken at the proper time and with virtuous intent, [Rāma replied:]
4.028.027c Sugrīva, endowed with great courage, formed an excellent plan. 4.028.028a He commanded his trusted Nīla, who was ever-exerting himself,
to gather all the troops from every direction.

"Act in such a way that my entire army and all the troop-leaders assemble together without delay, just as the vanguards of an army do. As for those monkeys who are frontier-guards— swift-moving and resolute— "
"Let them quickly assemble your army at my command.
You yourself must immediately inspect the troops.
Any monkey who does not arrive here within fifteen nights shall [face punishment]."
His punishment shall be the loss of life; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
And you, accompanied by Aṅgada, should approach the elder monkeys, acting upon my firm command.
Having thus established this arrangement with the lord of the foremost monkeys,
the valiant one entered his dwelling. When Sugrīva had entered his cave and the sky was freed from clouds, [Rāma spoke].
Having spent the rainy season and nights there, Rāma, oppressed by desire and grief,
beheld the pale sky and the stainless orb of the moon,
and gazed upon the autumnal night anointed with moonlight.
Having learned of Sugrīva’s devotion to sensual pleasures, the disappearance of Janaka’s daughter,
and that the appointed time had passed, he fainted, overcome with extreme distress. But after a moment, that wise one regained consciousness once more.
Seated upon the mountain peak adorned with gold and minerals, Rāghava, beholding the autumnal sky, thought of Vaidehī, who remained within his mind,
and went to his beloved in spirit.
And seeing the cloudless sky, from which the lightning and clouds had departed,
and which resounded with the cries of cranes, she lamented with a voice of distress; she,
who had previously echoed the calls of the cranes, now cried out with the very sounds of those cranes.
"How can that young girl, who used to delight in the hermitage, find joy today without me? Seeing the flowering *āsana* trees, as pure as if they were made of gold,
how can that young girl find pleasure while not seeing me?"
She who formerly, speaking with sweet accents, would wake at the sound of the kalahamsa geese—
she whose every limb was beautiful, how does she wake today?
Having heard the cry of her companions, the cakravaka birds...
"How will she, whose eyes are as wide as lotuses, survive? Without that fawn-eyed woman, I find no pleasure today as I wander among the lakes, rivers, ponds, groves, and forests."
"Will not desire, intensified by the qualities of autumn, afflict that beautiful woman excessively because of her separation from me and her delicate nature?
Thus did the prince, the best among men, lament.
Like a *sāraṅga* bird seeking water from the Lord of the Gods,
and having then wandered among the delightful mountain peaks in search of fruit,
the fortunate Lakṣmaṇa, upon returning, beheld his elder brother.
Overwhelmed by unbearable anxiety,
the wise one sat alone in the desolate place, distressed and dejected by his brother’s despair.
Having reflected, the son of Sumitrā said to Rāma:
"O Noble One, why [act] by falling under the sway of desire?
Why [yield] to the defeat of one's own manliness?"
4.029.016c This concentration is always withdrawn; what is the use here of yoga that has been practiced? 4.029.017a [One should cultivate] application to action and serenity of mind;
O one of undaunted spirit, attend to the time favorable for the practice of concentration, rely on the strength of your companions,
and make your own past actions the cause for your success.
O Lord of the human race, Jānakī,
having you as her protector, cannot easily be won by another; nor can she be approached by one who has drawn near to a blazing crest of fire.
"O one worthy of the best of heroes, no one can burn Lakṣmaṇa,
who is accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and is invincible," Rāma spoke these words born of his own nature.

One should examine the task to be performed without doubt, ensuring it is beneficial, wholesome, consistent with political wisdom, and properly aligned with the principles of conciliation, virtue, and material interest.
For one who has set out on a difficult and unassailable task, the specific course of action must indeed be followed; the fruit of such a youth's undertaking is not to be deliberated upon.
Then, brooding over Maithilī, whose eyes were like lotus petals,
Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with a parched face:
"The thousand-eyed Indra has refreshed the earth with water."
Having brought the crops to fruition and completed his task, he stood at rest.
O Prince, having discharged their water— emitting smooth and deep sounds and preceded by mountains and trees— the clouds became exhausted.
Dark as the petals of the blue lotus, they turned the ten directions a deep shade of blue; the clouds, their momentum stilled like elephants deprived of their pride,
were heavy with water and possessed great speed, fragrant with the scent of *kuṭaja* and *arjuna* flowers.
"O gentle one, having performed their course, the rains and winds have ceased; O sinless Lakṣmaṇa, the roar of the clouds, the elephants, and the peacocks,
as well as that of the waterfalls, has suddenly become quiet."
Drenched by great clouds, the mountains with their variegated ridges appear stainless; they shine as if anointed by the rays of the moon.
The autumn rivers gradually reveal their sandy banks.

O gentle one, the reservoirs of water shine with their clear waters, resounding with the cries of female ospreys and crowded with flocks of ruddy geese, like the hips of women bashful at their first union.
"O prince, O gentle one, the time for mobilization has arrived for the kings who harbor mutual enmity and desire victory. O prince,
this is that first expedition of the kings."
"And yet I do not see Sugrīva, nor any such exertion as that. O gentle one, the four months of the rainy season have passed like a hundred years for me,
who am tormented by grief at not seeing Sītā."

"O Lakṣmaṇa, King Sugrīva shows no compassion toward me, who am bereft of my beloved, afflicted by grief, deprived of my kingdom, and exiled. This king is now without a protector, his realm has been taken away, and he has been humiliated by Rāvaṇa."
"Dejected, far from home, and full of longing, he has come to me for refuge. O gentle one, for these reasons, I have been treated with contempt by that evil-minded Sugrīva,
the king of the monkeys, O scorcher of foes.

Having calculated the time for the search for Sītā and having made an agreement, that evil-minded one, thinking his purpose was accomplished, did not realize [the danger]. And you, having entered Kiṣkindhā, speak to the bull among monkeys.
"O Sugrīva, you are a fool, vulgar, and addicted to pleasure; by my word, [know that] he who,
having promised his hope to those who have approached him as supplicants and who were formerly his benefactors, yet destroys that hope, is the lowest of men in this world."
Whether it be auspicious or even sinful, he who upholds with truth the word that has been spoken is a hero, the best among men.
For those who do not act for their friends when they have achieved their own ends are not true friends.

Even when dead, those ungrateful wretches do not serve as food for carnivorous beasts. Surely they wish to behold the form of my gold-backed bow, drawn by me in battle, resembling a flash of lightning.
He wishes to hear once more the terrible sound of my bowstring and palms in battle when I am enraged— a sound like the crash of a thunderbolt—
even though his prowess has been thus recognized and he has come to this state.
"O hero, O prince, son of a king, conqueror of enemy cities, as long as I have you as my companion, I shall have no anxiety regarding the purpose for which this undertaking was begun;
for the lord of the monkeys, having achieved his goal, does not recognize the proper time."
Having pledged himself to the time of the rainy season, the lord of monkeys did not realize that four months had passed while he was sporting;
surrounded by his ministers and assembly, he indulged only in play and drink.
"Sugrīva shows no compassion for us, who are so wretched with grief.
Go, my child, O mighty one, and speak to Sugrīva;
tell him the nature of my wrath and say these words to him."
"The path by which Vālin, who was slain, departed is not yet closed. Abide by your agreement, O Sugrīva; do not follow the path of Vālin.
Vālin alone was slain by me with a single arrow in battle."
"But I shall slay you, along with your kinsmen, once you have transgressed against the truth.
Therefore, O bull among men, since this task has been thus ordained, tell me whatever is beneficial for it, O best of men; hurry, for there is no time to lose."
O Lord of Monkeys, having regard for the eternal dharma, make true your promise to me;
do not let Vālī, having gone to the abode of Yama after death, [be deprived of his due].
Today you shall see him with my arrows impelled [at him],
as he gazes upon his elder brother, who is wretched, lamenting, and possessed by an intensely increased rage.
4.029.052c He of fierce splendor formed a resolute resolve;
the lord of the lineage of the monkey and the man. 4.030.001a He of undaunted spirit [beheld] that lover who was miserable;
To the son of a king of men who was overcome by grief and possessed by rising anger— the son of a god among men—
Rāma’s younger brother spoke thus to his elder brother.
The monkey will not abide in virtuous conduct;
he will not consider the consequences of his actions;
nor will he enjoy the royal fortune of the monkeys.
For thus his intellect does not advance,
being attached to vulgar pleasures due to the decay of his wisdom, and his mind is intent on not returning your favor.
"Let him, once slain, behold his elder brother Vālin;
the kingdom must not be given to one so devoid of virtue. I cannot restrain my rising wrath."
Today, along with the foremost heroes of the monkeys, I shall slay the untruthful Sugrīva; let the son of Vālin search for the wife of the king of men.
To him, who had taken up his bow and was springing forward,
having announced his purpose and being fierce with rage for battle, Rāma, the slayer of enemy heroes, spoke:
"Look upon yourself with self-reflection and speak words full of conciliation;
for indeed, one such as you would never commit such an evil act in this world. He who destroys evil through noble means is a hero, the best of men."
"O Lakṣmaṇa of virtuous conduct, you must not accept this today;
rather, follow that former affection and our long-standing association. Avoid harsh words and speak with speech tempered by conciliation."
"You ought to speak to Sugrīva, for the appointed time has passed. Having been thus instructed in the matter by his elder brother, that bull among men,
the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy warriors, entered the city exactly as directed.
Then the wise Lakṣmaṇa, of auspicious mind, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of his brother, being highly incensed, went to the dwelling of the monkey; he,
resembling Yama the Destroyer at the end of time, carried a bow that was like the rainbow of Śakra.
Seizing [the bow] which resembled a mountain peak like Mount Mandara with its ridges,
the younger brother of Rāma, who was equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence, then considered the words spoken and provided a reply that was both fitting and superior.
Enveloped by the fire of his brother’s anger, which had arisen from desire and wrath,
Lakṣmaṇa then set forth like a displeased tempest,
violently felling many sāl, tāla, and aśvakarṇa trees.
4.030.014c Casting aside mountain peaks and other trees by his speed,
4.030.015a And shattering rocks into fragments with his feet like a swift elephant,
4.030.015c He went quickly for the sake of his mission, covering great distance in a single stride.
4.030.016a He beheld that great city of the king of monkeys, crowded with troops;
4.030.016c Kishkindha, difficult to access in its mountain fastness, did the tiger among the Ikshvakus behold.
4.030.017a With his lips quivering in rage toward Sugriva, Lakshmana looked upon it.
He saw terrifying monkeys roaming outside Kiṣkindhā;
those monkeys, resembling elephants, seized hundreds of mountain peaks and massive trees within the mountains.
Seeing those monkeys who had seized their weapons, Lakṣmaṇa became twice as enraged, like a fire fed with abundant fuel.
Seeing him angry, those monkeys, their limbs overcome with fear, [stood before him].
Resembling the end of time, death, or the dissolution of an eon, the quarters of the sky fled in hundreds of directions.
Then, having entered Sugrīva’s palace, those foremost of monkeys reported both the arrival and the wrath of Lakṣmaṇa.
Accompanied by Tārā, the lustful bull among monkeys was absorbed in private;
he did not then hear the words of those monkey heroes.
Thereupon, the hair-raising monkeys were dispatched by his ministers.
Then, resembling mountain caves and clouds, they emerged from the city;
all were terrible, with claws and fangs as their weapons, and possessed hideous appearances. All were as proud as tigers, and all had deformed faces.
Some possessed the strength of ten elephants, some were ten times stronger than that,
and others were equal in prowess to a thousand elephants.
Indeed, the entire region was filled with mighty monkeys holding trees in their hands.
Enraged, Lakṣmaṇa beheld that unassailable Kiṣkindhā. Then all those monkeys, possessed of fierce courage, emerged from within the walls and moats and stood forth openly.
Perceiving Sugrīva’s negligence and his elder brother in distress,
the self-possessed hero once again fell under the sway of anger.
With long, hot, and deep sighs, his eyes bloodshot with rage, he [proceeded].
That tiger among men became like a fire enveloped in smoke;
with the quivering arrow-heads for his flickering tongue and the bow for his body,
he was like a five-headed serpent whose venomous mass was his own fiery energy.
Approaching him, who was like the blazing fire of time or an enraged king of serpents,
Aṅgada fell into deep despondency out of fear.
With eyes copper-red with rage, that highly illustrious one gave instructions to Aṅgada.
"O child, let Sugrīva be told of my arrival.
This younger brother of Rāma, the subduer of enemies, has arrived in your presence;
tormented by his brother's misfortune, Lakṣmaṇa stands at the gate."
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, Aṅgada, overcome with grief, said:
"This son of Sumitrā has come into the presence of our father.
Seeing him resembling a great flood and possessing a voice like a thunderbolt, they [approached].
In the vicinity of Lakṣmaṇa, they simultaneously let out lion-like roars.
By that great sound, the monkey was awakened;
his eyes were copper-red and unsteady with intoxication, and his garlands and ornaments were disarrayed.
Then, having heard the words of Aṅgada, the two ministers of the lord of monkeys— who were esteemed, noble-minded, and possessed of far-reaching vision— arrived together with him;
these two ministers were Plakṣa and Prabhāva, who were experts in matters of worldly profit and righteousness.
They informed Lakṣmaṇa, who had arrived to speak various words,
after they had propitiated Sugrīva with speech determined by conciliation; and as he sat there, they attended upon him just as the Maruts attend upon Śakra, the lord of the gods.
The two highly fortunate brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who are true to their word, have attained the state of being my friends; they are worthy of the kingdom and are the givers of the kingdom.
Of those two, Lakṣmaṇa stands at the gate with bow in hand.
"Terrified by whom the monkeys tremble and let out cries—
this is that very Lakṣmaṇa, the brother of Rāghava, whose charioteer is his speech.
Having made resolve his chariot, he has arrived here by the command of Rāma."
4.030.043a Bowing your head before him, O King, together with your sons and kinsmen, 4.030.043c remain steadfast in your own duty and be true to your promise.
4.031.001a Having heard the words of Angada, Sugriva, along with his ministers, [acted accordingly].
4.031.001c Hearing that Lakṣmaṇa was angry, the self-possessed king rose from his seat.

4.031.002a Having weighed the relative gravity of the situation, he spoke these words to his ministers— men skilled in counsel, experts in deliberation, and thoroughly established in the art of consultation.
"I have uttered no harsh word, nor have I committed any wrongful act;
yet I wonder why Rāghava’s brother Lakṣmaṇa is angry. This must be the work of my enemies and unfriendly foes who constantly look for my vulnerabilities."
4.031.004c The younger brother of Rāghava has been made to hear of faults that do not exist in me.
4.031.005a In this matter, therefore, you all must, according to your understanding and in accordance with the rules, skillfully and gradually ascertain his firm resolve.
Indeed, I have no fear of Lakṣmaṇa, nor even of Rāghava;
however, a friend who is provoked out of place certainly causes agitation.
In every respect, a friend is easy to find, but difficult to maintain.
Because the mind is impermanent, joy is shattered even by a slight cause; for this reason, I am terrified of the high-souled Rāma,
for that which he has done for me cannot be repaid by me.
Thus addressed by Sugrīva, Hanumān, the bull among monkeys,
spoke according to his own reasoning in the midst of the monkey ministers:
"In every respect, O Lord of the monkey hosts, it is no wonder that you [have done this]."
Do you not forget the beautiful and auspicious favor performed with great affection?
By the heroic Rāghava, casting fear far behind,
Vālin— whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra— was slain for the sake of your welfare.
4.031.012a Rāghava is angry with you for some reason; there is no doubt about this.
4.031.012c He has dispatched his brother Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity.
4.031.013a You, being heedless, do not realize that this is the time, O best among those who know the proper seasons.
The auspicious autumn has set in, darkened by blossoming *saptacchada* trees; the sky is free of clouds and filled with stainless planets and stars;
and all the quarters, as well as the rivers and lakes, have become clear.
"O bull among monkeys, you do not perceive that the time for exertion has arrived;
it is evident that you are negligent, for here is Lakṣmaṇa come,
[to hear] the harsh words of one who is distressed and whose wife has been abducted from another man."
"You must endure the words of the high-souled Rāghava;
for since you have committed an offense against him, I see no other course open to you than to propitiate Lakṣmaṇa by joining your palms in salutation."
4.031.018a Appointed ministers must certainly speak what is beneficial to the king;
4.031.018c for this very reason, casting aside all fear, I speak these firm words.
4.031.019a For Rāghava, when provoked to anger, is capable of raising his bow.
In order to bring the world— including its gods, asuras, and gandharvas— under his control,
he is not one to be provoked to anger, for once he has been propitiated, he returns [to favor];
especially so by one who remembers past kindness and is grateful.

4.031.021a Having bowed your head to him, O King, together with your sons and your circle of friends, 4.031.021c remain under his authority at the proper time, like a wife under the power of her husband.
4.031.022a You must not disregard the command of Rāma and his younger brother;
Even with the mind, it is impossible to set aside that which is yoked to the lord of monkeys;
for your mind will surely recognize the human strength of this Rāghava, who possesses the splendor of the lord of the gods.
Then, having been thus commanded, Lakṣmaṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes,
entered the formidable cave-city of Kiṣkindhā by the order of Rāma.
There stood at the gate monkeys of massive body and great strength.
Upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa, they all stood with their palms joined in reverence.
But seeing the son of Daśaratha sighing and filled with rage,
the monkeys became terrified and did not attempt to restrain him.
The illustrious one beheld that great cave, made of jewels, divine, filled with flowering groves, delightful, strewn with gems,
crowded with mansions and palaces, and adorned with various kinds of merchandise.

It was adorned with flowering trees that bore the fruits of all desires, and graced by the sons of gods and gandharvas who had taken the form of monkeys— beings of lovely appearance wearing divine garlands and garments, capable of assuming any form at will.

The great highways were made fragrant by the scents of sandalwood, agallochum, and lotuses, all possessing sweet perfumes; they were further enlivened by the aroma of *maireya* wines and honey-liquors.
The city was adorned with multi-storied palaces resembling the plateaus of the Vindhya and Meru mountains.
There Rāghava beheld clear mountain rivers and the beautiful dwellings of Aṅgada, Mainda, Dvivida,
Gavaya, Gavākṣa, Gaja, and Śarabha.
Of Vidyunmālī and Saṃpāti, of Sūryākṣa and Hanumān, of Vīrabāhu and Subāhu, and of the high-souled Nala;
of Kumuda and Suṣeṇa, as well as Tāra and Jāmbavān.
On the royal highway, Lakṣmaṇa beheld the magnificent and highly substantial residences of these great-souled monkey leaders— of Dadhivaktra, Nīla, Supāṭala, and Sunetra.
Resembling pale white clouds, adorned with divine garlands,
abundant in wealth and grain, and graced by jewels among women—
[the city] was surrounded by a pale-white mountain and was difficult to approach.
The lovely residence of the lord of monkeys was like the abode of Mahendra;
it was adorned with white palace pinnacles resembling the peaks of Mount Kailāsa and with flourishing trees that bore the fruits of all desires.
It was surrounded by majestic trees, bestowed by Mahendra, resembling dark clouds, bearing divine flowers and fruits, and providing cool, delightful shade;
its gates were guarded by powerful monkeys, weapons in hand.

The mighty Saumitri, unimpeded like the sun entering a great cloud, entered the beautiful palace of Sugrīva, which was radiant, adorned with celestial garlands, and featured an archway of refined gold.
Having entered through seven courtyards filled with vehicles and seats, that righteous-souled one beheld the vast and well-guarded inner apartments,
which were furnished with many couches of gold and silver and numerous excellent thrones.
It was adorned here and there with highly precious coverings;
as he entered, he constantly heard sweet sounds filled with the music of stringed instruments and the singing of perfectly articulated words and syllables.
That one of great strength beheld many women of various forms in Sugrīva’s palace, who were proud of their beauty and youth;
seeing them, well-born and adorned with wreaths of variegated garlands.

Lakṣmaṇa also observed Sugrīva’s followers, who were busily engaged in preparing choice garlands, adorned with the finest ornaments, neither overly satiated nor excessively distracted, and dressed in noble attire.
Then he beheld Sugrīva seated upon a supreme golden throne covered with costly rugs, resembling the sun;
his limbs were adorned with wonderful celestial ornaments, and he was illustrious and possessed of divine form.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, he was as invincible as the great Indra,
surrounded by women adorned with divine ornaments and garlands;
then the hero embraced Rumā firmly.
Seated upon an excellent throne, possessing a noble golden complexion and wide eyes, he beheld the son of Sumitrā, who was undaunted in spirit and possessed of very large eyes.
Seeing that bull among men, Lakṣmaṇa, who was unassailable, enraged, and had entered [the city], Sugrīva’s senses became distressed. He was furious,
sighing heavily, and blazing as if with fiery energy.
Seeing the son of Daśaratha tormented by his brother’s calamity,
the best of monkeys leapt up from his golden seat,
like the great and well-adorned banner of Mahendra.

As he leaped up, the women led by Rumā followed him into the sky, like clusters of stars following the full moon. The illustrious Sugrīva, his eyes bloodshot, moved forward with his hands joined in reverence.
There stood a great *kalpa* tree, as if it were a mountain. To Sugrīva, who was standing there with Rumā in the midst of the women like the moon accompanied by the stars, the enraged Lakṣmaṇa spoke:
A king who is endowed with noble birth and lineage, compassionate, self-controlled,
grateful, and truthful, is honored in the world. But that king who stands in unrighteousness toward his friends and benefactors—
Who is more cruel than he who makes a false vow?
One kills a hundred horses by lying about a horse, but one kills a thousand cows by lying about a cow;
by lying about a man, a person kills himself and his own kin.
4.033.010a He who, having previously achieved his purpose through his friends, does not repay them in kind—
4.033.010c that ungrateful man, O Lord of Monkeys, deserves to be slain by all living beings.
4.033.011a This verse was sung by Brahmā, who is honored by all the worlds:
4.033.011c Having seen that ungrateful man, listen, O monkey, to what was done by the enraged one.

4.033.012a For the slayer of a Brahmin, for the drinker of liquor, for a thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow, atonement has been ordained by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
"You are ignoble, ungrateful, and a liar, O monkey!
Having previously achieved your purpose through Rāma, you do not repay him for it.
Indeed, O monkey, having accomplished your goal through Rāma—"
"Effort must be made to search for Sītā by one who desires what has been done.
You, however, are attached to vulgar pleasures and have made a false promise;
Rāma does not recognize you as a serpent croaking like a frog."

"By the illustrious Rāma, who is compassionate and high-souled, you, a wicked and evil-minded soul, have been granted the kingdom of the monkeys. If you do not acknowledge what has been done for you by Rāma, whose deeds are effortless,"
"Immediately, struck by my sharpened arrows, you shall see Vālin. The path by which the slain Vālin departed has not yet closed;
abide by your agreement, O Sugrīva, and do not follow the path of Vālin."
Surely you do not behold the arrows, resembling thunderbolts, released from the bow of the best of the Ikṣvākus;
therefore, you enjoy what is called happiness as one who is happy.
"You do not consider Rāma’s duty even in your mind.
To the son of Sumitrā, who was speaking thus as if blazing with splendor,
Tārā, whose face resembled the lord of the stars, replied to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Lakṣmaṇa, you must not speak thus; this lord of the monkeys does not deserve such harshness from your mouth,
especially since he is not ungrateful, nor is he deceitful, nor cruel."
O hero, the lord of monkeys is neither a speaker of falsehood nor is he crooked; furthermore,
this heroic monkey has not forgotten the favor rendered by Rāma, O hero, which was difficult for others to achieve in battle.
O scorcher of enemies, through the grace of Rāma, Sugrīva has obtained here eternal fame, the sovereignty of the monkeys, Rumā,
