and me; having previously lain in great misery, he has now attained this supreme happiness.

4.034.006c Viśvāmitra, like the sage [who failed to recognize] the time that had arrived, did not perceive it. 4.034.007a O Lakṣmaṇa, being indeed deeply attached to Ghṛtācī for ten years, 4.034.007c the righteous-souled great sage Viśvāmitra thought, "Alas! (that so much time had passed).
"For even Viśvāmitra, the possessor of great splendor and the best among those who know the timing of time, did not perceive that the appointed hour had arrived; how much less so an ordinary person,
O Lakṣmaṇa, when he has reached the state of physical dissolution and is exhausted?"

"Rāma deserves forgiveness here for one who is not yet satiated with desires. O dear Lakṣmaṇa, you ought not to fall under the sway of anger like an ordinary man, acting impulsively without understanding the true purpose."
"For men like you, O bull among men,
who are endowed with goodness, do not fall under the sway of anger so hastily without reflection. O knower of dharma, I, being composed, seek to appease you for the sake of Sugrīva."
4.034.012c This great anger that has arisen—let this agitation be abandoned.
4.034.013a Rumā, myself, the kingdom of the monkeys, and wealth, grain, and treasures— 4.034.013c Sugrīva would renounce all these for the sake of Rāma’s pleasure; such is my conviction.
4.034.014a Sugrīva will reunite Rāghava with Sītā,
4.034.014c just as the moon is joined with Rohiṇī, after he has slain Rāvaṇa in battle.
4.034.015a It is said that there are thousands of ten billion Rākṣasas in Laṅkā.
Thirty-six thousand, six hundred, and ten thousand—
without slaying those invincible Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will,
it is impossible to kill Rāvaṇa, by whom that princess of Mithilā was abducted.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, they cannot be slain in battle by one who is unaided;
this is especially true of Rāvaṇa, the performer of cruel deeds, and Sugrīva.
Thus did Vālī speak, for he was the lord of monkeys and possessed of such knowledge."

But the traditional account is not clear to me; I speak of it only from what I have heard. Indeed, these foremost of monkeys have been dispatched for the purpose of assisting you, to bring many monkey leaders to the battle.
"And waiting for those valiant and exceedingly powerful ones,
the Lord of Monkeys does not set forth for the sake of accomplishing Raghava's purpose.
O Saumitri, the arrangement made by Sugriva is exactly as it was before."
"Today all those mighty monkeys must arrive;
thousands of crores of bears and hundreds of golangulas shall come to you today. Cast off your anger, O subduer of enemies!"
O descendant of Kakutstha, many millions of monkeys of blazing splendor,
beholding this face of yours and observing these eyes resembling blood due to your anger, [stand before you].
"The women of the Harivaras find no peace,
for they all remain apprehensive of that first danger.
Having been addressed with these humble words by Tārā, which were consistent with righteousness, [he replied:]

4.035.001c The son of Sumitrā, being gentle by nature, accepted those words. 4.035.002a When that speech had been accepted by him, the lord of the monkey hosts cast off his great terror, as one might discard a wet garment.
Then Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, being free from intoxication, tore away the large, variegated, and many-stranded garland that had been around his neck; he,
the best of all monkeys, [then addressed] Lakṣmaṇa of terrible strength.
Sugrīva, gladdening him, spoke these humble words:
"O son of Sumitrā, my lost fortune, my fame, and my eternal kingdom as king of the monkeys have all been regained by me through the grace of Rāma."
"O hero, subduer of enemies, who is capable of countering such prowess of that god-like being renowned for his own deeds?
The righteous-souled one shall recover Sītā and slay Rāvaṇa."
With me as merely his companion, Rāghava, by his own splendor,
performed the work of an ally; for by him, with a single arrow, seven great trees, a mountain, and even the earth itself were pierced.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, when the earth with its mountains trembled at the sound of his stretching the bow, what need is there for companions?
O bull among men, I shall indeed follow as the escort of that lord of men."
As I go forth to slay my enemy Rāvaṇa along with his followers,
if I have transgressed anything out of confidence or affection,
it must be forgiven in me as a servant; for there is no one who does not commit an offense.
While the high-souled Sugrīva was speaking thus,
Lakṣmaṇa became delighted and, out of affection, spoke these words:
"O Lord of Monkeys, my brother is indeed protected in every way."
4.035.013c With you as our protector, O Sugrīva, especially since you are so humble;
4.035.014a Whatever power you possess, O Sugrīva, and whatever supreme purity you have— 4.035.014c You deserve to enjoy that unsurpassed glory of the kingdom of the monkeys.
O Sugrīva, with you as his ally, the majestic Rāma will slay his enemies in battle before long; of this there is no doubt.
[He is] one who knows the dharma, who is grateful, and who never retreats in battles.
"O Sugrīva, what you have spoken is both appropriate and logical. Who else, knowing the faults [of others] yet possessing the necessary capability, would dare to speak thus—
save for my elder brother and yourself, O best of monkeys?"
"O bull among monkeys, you are equal to Rāma in prowess and strength;
you have been granted by the gods as an ally for a long time.
However, O hero, depart from here quickly with me."
Console your companion, who is suffering from the loss of his wife;
and you ought to forgive those harsh words I spoke to you upon hearing Rāma’s speech when he was overwhelmed by grief.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
Sugrīva spoke these words to his minister Hanumān, who was standing at his side:
"On the peaks of Mahendra, Himavat, Vindhya, and Kailāsa..."
Those who dwell on Mount Mandara with its pale peaks, and those situated upon the five mountains that shine in every direction with the color of the rising sun,
as well as those on the mountains at the edge of the ocean in the western quarter.
And on the mountain resembling the twilight clouds, in the very abode of Āditya,
those bulls among monkeys took refuge in a formidable forest of lotuses and palmyra trees;
they resembled dark clouds and possessed the strength of elephants.
And those monkeys who dwell on Añjana and Parata, the Vanaras with golden luster who live in caves and use red arsenic as pigment,
as well as those situated on the slopes of Meru and those who have taken refuge on Mount Dhūmra.
And on the great mountain Mahāruṇa, those monkeys of terrible speed, possessing the hue of the rising sun, were drinking honey-wine (*madhu-maireya*) in vast,
fragrant, and most delightful forests.
"Bring quickly all those monkeys on earth from the delightful forest regions of the ascetics on every side;
dispatch the monkeys at once by means of conciliation, gifts, and other appropriate methods."
"The swift messengers whom I previously dispatched for the purpose of urging haste— send yet other monkeys,
those who are addicted to pleasures and are procrastinating."
"Bring them all here quickly by my command. Those who do not arrive within ten days at my order must be slain— those evil-minded ones who have violated the king's decree."
"By my command, let hundreds, thousands,
and even crores of lion-like monkeys set out in all directions, abiding by my will,
resembling clouds and mountains as they seem to cover the very sky."

4.036.014c Let the best of monkeys, of terrible form, go forth from here at my command. 4.036.015a Having traveled every path on earth, those monkeys who know the way must quickly bring back all the forest-dwellers at my order.
Having heard the words of that king of monkeys, the son of Vāyu dispatched monkeys who were valiant in all directions. Those travelers,
moving through the path of birds and celestial lights, sought the place where Viṣṇu had stepped.
4.036.017c Dispatched by the king, those monkeys indeed set out at that very moment.
4.036.018a In the oceans, on the mountains, in the forests, and along the rivers,
4.036.018c those monkeys urged all other monkeys to action for the sake of Rāma.

4.036.019 Upon hearing the command of Sugrīva, the king of kings, which was like the time of death itself, the monkeys, perceiving the danger posed by Sugrīva, approached him. 4.036.020 Then those monkeys,
who were as dark as collyrium and possessed great speed, [leapt] from that mountain.
Three crores of monkeys set forth where Rāghava was;
they were devoted to that excellent mountain where the sun goes to its setting. From there, ten crores more emerged, possessing a luster like molten gold.
And from the peaks of Kailāsa, thousands of crores of monkeys, possessing the luster of a lion’s mane, arrived;
they subsisted on fruits and roots and had taken refuge in the Himavat mountains.
A thousand times ten million of them gathered together—
terrible beings of fearsome deeds, resembling glowing embers.
From the Vindhya mountains, thousands of crores of monkeys descended swiftly.
Those who dwell on the shores of the Ocean of Milk, those who inhabit the tamāla forests,
and those who subsist on coconuts— their number is beyond reckoning;
they emerge with great speed from the woods, the caves, and the rivers.
The monkey army arrived, as if drinking up the sun itself.
Those heroic monkeys who had gone out to urge on all the other monkeys beheld that great mountain, the Himavat, with its massive trees.
On that beautiful, excellent mountain, in ancient times, the sacrifice of Maheśvara shone forth—
divine and captivating, bringing satisfaction to the minds of all the gods. There, roots and fruits grew in abundance, produced by the overflowing of food.
There the monkeys beheld fruits and roots that were as delicious as nectar; whoever ate even once of those divine and heart-pleasing provisions remained satisfied for a month.
Those leaders of the monkey troops, subsisting on fruit, gathered those divine roots and fruits, as well as divine medicinal herbs,
from that sacrificial ground and fragrant flowers.
Having gone forth for the sake of doing what was pleasing to Sugrīva, the monkeys brought [the news].
Then all those foremost of monkeys, having urged on all the other monkeys upon the earth, went quickly at the head of the troops.
In that very moment, those swift-acting troop-leaders reached Kiṣkindhā with haste, where the monkey Sugrīva was;
having taken all the medicinal herbs, fruits, and roots, the monkeys—
They caused him to accept it and spoke these words:
"All the mountains, the oceans, and the forests have been searched;
all the monkeys on earth are coming to you at your command."
Having heard this, Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, was then delighted; and being pleased, he accepted all their offerings. Having accepted all those presented gifts, he [honored them].
Having consoled all the monkeys, he dismissed them all.
Having sent away those heroic monkeys who had accomplished their task,
he considered himself and the mighty Rāghava to have achieved their purpose.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, gladdening Sugrīva, spoke these humble words to him of terrible strength, the best of all monkeys:
"O gentle one, if it pleases you, depart from Kiṣkindhā."
Having heard those well-spoken words of Lakṣmaṇa, Sugrīva was exceedingly pleased and spoke these words:
"So be it; let us go, for I must abide by your command."
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, who bears auspicious marks, Sugrīva then dismissed him, as well as Tārā and the other women. "Come! Sugrīva called out loudly to the foremost of the monkeys.
Having heard those words of his, the monkeys quickly arrived; all those who were capable of looking upon women came with their hands joined in reverence.
Then the king, whose splendor was like that of the sun, spoke to them as they had arrived.
"O monkeys, quickly bring a palanquin for me. Having heard his words, the monkeys of swift prowess brought forward a beautiful palanquin.
Seeing that palanquin brought forward, the lord of the monkeys said to the son of Sumitrā,
"Lakṣmaṇa, ascend quickly. Having spoken thus, Sugrīva [prepared] the golden vehicle, which resembled the sun.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he ascended [the chariot] yoked with large bay horses;
with a white parasol held over his head and white yak-tail fans being waved on all sides.
Honored by the sounding of conchs and kettledrums and by bards, Sugrīva went forth after attaining unsurpassed royal splendor. He was accompanied by many hundreds of fierce monkeys, weapons in hand.
Scattered about, he went to where Rāma was stationed. Having reached that excellent place frequented by Rāma, the one of great splendor, together with Lakṣmaṇa, descended from the palanquin.
Then, having approached Rāma, he stood with his palms joined in reverence;
and while he stood thus with joined palms, the monkeys likewise did so.
Seeing them like a pond filled with lotus buds, Rāma—
The great army of monkeys was filled with joy toward Sugrīva. Raising up that lord of monkeys who had fallen at his feet with his head bowed, Rāghava embraced him out of affection and great respect.
Having embraced him, the righteous-souled one said, "Please sit down.
Seeing that he was seated upon the ground, Rāma then spoke these words:
"He who pursues virtue, wealth, and pleasure at their proper times..."
O hero, O best of monkeys, that king constantly divided [his time] thus; yet he who abandons dharma and artha to indulge only in kāma awakens only after falling,
like one who has fallen asleep on the top of a tree.
"Intent on the destruction of enemies and devoted to the gathering of friends,
a king who enjoys the fruits of the three aims of life is united with righteousness.
O destroyer of foes, this very time for exertion has now arrived."
"O Lord of the Tawny Ones, let it be considered together with the monkeys and the ministers.
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke these words to Rāma:
"My fortune, my fame, and my eternal kingdom as king of the monkeys have been lost."
"O mighty-armed one, by your grace this has been regained by me once more;
and through your divine favor and that of my brother, O best among victors—
he who does not repay a kindness received is a defiler of men."
"O slayer of enemies, these hundreds of monkey chiefs have arrived,
O Raghava, bringing with them all the powerful monkeys from across the earth—
brave bears and golangulas who are ever-vigilant."
4.037.028c They are familiar with wildernesses and forest fastnesses, and they are of fearsome appearance.
4.037.029a These monkeys, sons of gods and gandharvas, who can assume any form at will, 4.037.029c proceed along the path, O Rāghava, each surrounded by his own respective army.
O scorcher of enemies, those heroic monkeys were surrounded by hundreds, hundreds of thousands, and tens of millions; they were covered by tens of thousands and by *śaṅkus*;
and the vanaras were accompanied by *arbudas*, hundreds of *arbudas*, *madhyas*, and *antas*.

O King, monkeys who are leaders of monkey-troops, equal in prowess to Mahendra, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara, and making their home on the Vindhya and Meru mountains, will come to you by the hundreds of millions and even by the parārdhas.
They will come to you, those who, having slain Rāvaṇa along with his kinsmen in battle, shall bring back Maithilī. Then, observing that exertion, the wise one—
Obedient to the command of the hero among monkeys,
the son of the lord of the earth became filled with joy,
his appearance resembling a blossoming blue lotus.
To Sugrīva, who was speaking thus with palms joined in reverence, Rāma— the best among the upholders of dharma— embraced him with both arms and replied:
"That Indra should pour down rain is nothing remarkable on this earth."
The sun, with its thousand rays, may indeed make the sky free from darkness;
the moon, with its beams, may make the earth pure and pleasant, O gentle one;
or even one such as you might repay the kindness of friends, O scorcher of foes.
"O gentle one, it would not be surprising if such auspiciousness were found in you;
for I know you, Sugrīva, to be one who always speaks kindly.
With you as my ally, O friend, I shall conquer all enemies in battle."
"You alone are my well-wisher and friend; you ought to provide me with assistance.
That lowest of Rākṣasas has carried off Vaidehī for his own destruction, just as Anuhlāda abducted Śacī, the daughter of Puloman, after deceiving her."
"Before long, I shall slay that Rāvaṇa with sharpened arrows,
just as Śatakratu, the destroyer of foes, did to the arrogant father of Paulomī.
In the meantime, a cloud of dust arose."
It shrouded the hot, intense, and thousandfold radiance of the sun in the sky;
the quarters of the world became agitated and overwhelmed by that dust,
and the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Then the entire earth was covered by those innumerable monkeys, who resembled the lords of mountains, possessed sharp fangs, and were endowed with great strength;
this was accomplished by those leaders of the monkey hosts in the mere twinkling of an eye.
She was surrounded by hundreds of millions of followers who could assume any form at will—
mighty monkeys from the rivers, the mountains, and the sea,
as well as others dwelling in the forests, all possessing voices like the roar of thunderclouds.

Then the illustrious one was surrounded by ten thousand crores of monkeys— some with the color of the rising sun, some as white as the moon, some with the hue of lotus filaments, and some white ones who made their home on Mount Meru.
The heroic monkey named Śatabali appeared;
then Tārā’s powerful father, who resembled a mountain of gold,
appeared with many tens of thousands of crores.
Resembling the filaments of a lotus, with a face like the rising sun,
he was wise, the best of monkeys, and the most excellent among all vanaras;
accompanied by many thousands of monkey troops.
The glorious Kesarī, the father of Hanumān, appeared;
and Gavākṣa, the great king of the golāṅgūlas, possessed of terrifying prowess,
was seen surrounded by ten billion monkeys.
Dhūmra, the destroyer of enemies among the bears of fearsome speed,
advanced surrounded by two thousand crores.
Then the leader of the host named Panasa, who was like a great mountain and terrible to behold, [advanced].
The immensely powerful one arrived, surrounded by thirty million [monkeys].
Then the troop-leader named Nīla, who had the appearance of a mass of black collyrium,
was seen with a massive body, surrounded by one hundred million.
Then the powerful troop-leader Darīmukha approached,
surrounded by ten billion followers, and presented himself before Sugrīva.
Both Mainda and Dvivida, the two sons of the Aśvins and possessors of great strength, also arrived.
With a thousand times ten million monkeys, he became invisible;
then, followed from behind by a hundred thousand times ten million monkeys, he reached Mount Gandhamādana.
Then the crown prince Aṅgada, whose prowess was equal to his father’s, arrived accompanied by a thousand lotuses and a hundred spikes.
After him came the monkey Tāra, who possessed the radiance of Tārā and formidable valor.
Accompanied by five crores of monkeys,
the heroic monkey Indrajānu, the leader of the host, appeared from afar;
he was the lord of eleven crores and was surrounded by them.
Then Rambha arrived, resembling the rising sun,
surrounded by ten thousand, a thousand, and a hundred [monkeys].
Then there was the heroic monkey leader named Durmukha.
The powerful one was seen surrounded by two crores [of monkeys];
Hanumān was seen surrounded by a thousand crores of monkeys of terrifying prowess, who resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa.
And the immensely powerful Nala also arrived, surrounded by a hundred crores, a thousand, and a hundred of tree-dwelling monkeys—
namely Śarabha, Kumuda, Vahni, Rambha, and others.
These and many other monkeys, capable of assuming any form at will, covered the entire earth, the mountains, and the forests; leaping, bounding, and roaring, those forest-dwellers surged forward.
They approached Sugrīva like masses of clouds approaching the sun;
making many sounds and filled with joy, those powerful ones announced themselves to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, by bowing their heads.
Other foremost monkeys,
having assembled appropriately and approached Sugrīva, then stood with palms joined in reverence.
Sugrīva, in haste, [reported] all those bulls among monkeys to Rāma.
Having announced this, the knower of dharma stood with palms joined in reverence and said:
"O lords of monkeys, may you dwell at your ease among the mountain cascades and in all the forests."

Having stationed the forces according to rule, he who knows the nature of strength was able to proceed with his own army. Then King Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, having achieved his purpose, [prepared for departure].
He spoke to Rāma, that tiger among men and crusher of enemy forces:
"The powerful lords of the monkeys, who dwell within my domain and possess the splendor of Mahendra, have arrived and taken up their positions; they are able to assume any form at will."
These formidable monkeys, resembling Daityas and Dānavas, have arrived with many thousands of tawny monkeys of terrifying prowess;
they are renowned for their deeds and exploits, powerful, and have conquered all fatigue.
Renowned for their prowess and supreme in their resolve,
O Rāma, these monkeys— who range over the earth and the waters and dwell upon various mountains—
have arrived as your servants by the tens of millions.
All of them will abide by your instructions, and all are devoted to the welfare of their preceptor; they will be able to carry out what you desire, O subduer of enemies.
O tiger among men, let that which you deem appropriate for the present moment be spoken.
4.039.007c That army is under your control; you ought to command it.
4.039.008a This purpose of theirs is indeed known to me in its true essence; nevertheless, you ought to command them according to what is truly right.
To Sugrīva, who was speaking thus, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
embraced him with both arms and spoke these words:
"O gentle one, let it be known whether Vaidehī is alive or not."
O one of great wisdom, that is the region where Rāvaṇa dwells. Having reached Vaidehī and the abode of Rāvaṇa, I shall, at that time, act as the occasion demands together with you.

"O Lord of Monkeys, neither I nor Lakṣmaṇa am the master in this matter; you alone are the cause and the master of this task, O Lord of the Vanaras. Therefore, O Sovereign, you yourself must issue the command regarding the determination of my duty."
"For you surely know what must be done for me, O hero; of this there is no doubt.

Accompanied by a friend, you are valiant, wise, and a knower of the specific requirements of time. You are devoted to our welfare, accomplished in your purpose, and the best among those who understand worldly affairs."
Thus addressed, Sugrīva spoke to the troop-leader named Vinata— mighty,
resembling a mountain, with a voice like the roar of clouds— in the presence of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa.
O best of monkeys, together with the monkeys who are the sons of Soma and Sūrya,
you are endowed with the knowledge of place, time, and policy in determining what ought and ought not to be done;
you are surrounded by a hundred thousand swift monkeys.
Go toward the eastern direction, with its mountains, forests,
and groves. There, search for Sītā, the princess of Videha, as well as the dwelling place of Rāvaṇa, in mountain fastnesses, in forests, and by rivers.
The delightful river Bhāgīrathī, as well as the Sarayū and the Kauśikī;
the Kālindī, the beautiful Yamunā, and the great mountain on the Yamunā;
the Sarasvatī, the Sindhu, and the Śoṇa with its jewel-like waters.
He traversed the great earth, including Kālamahī, adorned with mountains and forests;
he passed through Brahmamāla, Videha, Mālava, Kāśi, Kosala,
and likewise the Magadhas, Mahāgrāma, Puṇḍra, and Vaṅga.
The city of the silk-weavers and the land containing silver mines—
all this must be searched from place to place by those seeking Rāma’s beloved wife Sītā, the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha.
They saw mountains plunging into the ocean and various cities; some were settled upon the long peaks of Mount Mandara,
while others had ears as large as hoods and lips reaching to their ears.
Terrible, with iron-like faces, swift, and one-legged;
inexhaustible, powerful, and man-eating men;
as well as Kirātas with ear-lobes like crests, golden-limbed and pleasing to behold.
There dwell Kirātas who live on islands and subsist on raw fish; they are known as fierce "tigers among men" who move within the waters. All their dwellings must be searched by you forest-dwellers.
Those regions which are accessible by mountain paths, by swimming, and by boat;
Yavadvīpa, abounding in jewels and adorned with seven kingdoms;
and Suvarṇarūpyaka, embellished with gold mines.
4.039.029c Beyond Yavadvīpa lies a mountain named Śiśira,
4.039.030a which touches the heavens with its peak and is frequented by gods and dānavas;
4.039.030c in the mountain fastnesses, the ravines, and the forests of these [regions]...
Rāvaṇa, together with Vaidehī, must be searched for here and there; thereafter, you ought to see the most terrifying islands of the ocean. There, the great-bodied asuras constantly seize the shadows.
Permitted by Brahmā, though they had been hungry for a long time,
they approached that great ocean— which resembled a dark monsoon cloud and was frequented by mighty serpents— by way of the sacred ford, uttering a great roar.
Then you will go to the terrible ocean of red water named Lohita,
and there you shall see that great Śālmalī tree with its thorny peaks,
as well as the abode of Vainateya, adorned with various jewels.
There, a place resembling Mount Kailāsa was constructed by Viśvakarman. There, terrifying Rākṣasas named Mandehas,
who resemble mountains and possess various forms, hang from the mountain peaks, inspiring fear.
They fall constantly into the water facing the rising sun;
scorched by the sun, they hang there again and again.
Then [there is] the ocean named Kṣīroda, which has the appearance of white clouds.
Having gone there, you shall behold that unassailable ocean, its mouths appearing like necklaces of waves. In its midst stands a great white mountain named Ṛṣabha,
surrounded by silver trees in full bloom with celestial fragrances.
And there was a lake named Sudarśana, filled with silver lotuses possessing blazing golden filaments and crowded with royal swans;
it was frequented by gods, *cāraṇas*, *yakṣas*, *kiṃnaras*, and hosts of *apsarases*.

4.039.041c Delighted and desiring to sport, they approach that lotus pond. 4.039.042a O monkeys, having crossed the Ocean of Milk, you will then behold 4.039.042c Jaloda, the best of oceans, which brings fear to all living beings.

There, that great horse-headed fire born of his wrath was created; they say it devoured the entire world of moving and non-moving beings with its immense velocity. There arose the sound of the creatures dwelling in the ocean crying out in distress.
And it is heard that those who are powerless, having seen that submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha),
[perish]; thirteen yojanas to the north of Svādu is a great golden mountain named Jātarūpaśila.
He saw the god seated on the mountain peak, saluted by all beings— the thousand-headed Ananta, clad in blue garments;
the golden palm tree was the banner of that great-souled one, possessing three peaks.
Established upon the summit of the mountain, it shines forth together with its altar;
that construction was made by the lords of the thirty gods in the eastern direction.
Beyond that lies the glorious Udaya mountain, composed of gold.
Its peak, extending for a hundred yojanas, touches the heavens;
made of gold and divine, it shines brilliantly along with its altar-platform.
It is adorned with flowering sāla, tāla, tamāla, and karṇikāra trees.
It shines with divine objects made of gold, resembling the sun. There stands the peak named Saumanasa, made of gold, ten *yojanas* high and one *yojana* wide, and it is eternal.
In ancient times, during the three strides of Viṣṇu, that Supreme Person first placed his foot there and made the second step upon the peak of Meru; thereafter,
the Sun-god circumambulated Jambūdvīpa by way of the north.
That peak of great height is mostly visible;
there, the great seers named Vaikhānasas and Vālakhilyas are seen, radiant ascetics with the brilliance of the sun.
This is the island of Sudarśana, which shines before him; in it resides the splendor and the sight of all living beings. Within its mountain groves, caves, and forests—
Rāvaṇa, together with Vaidehī, must be searched for here and there. And the morning twilight, entered by the splendor of the golden mountain and the great-souled sun, shines forth red.
Then the eastern quarter, surrounded by the gods, became utterly impassable;
deprived of the moon and the sun, it was invisible and shrouded in darkness.
Among all those mountains, in their caves and forests, [the same occurred].

"O bulls among monkeys, Janaki must be sought in those regions which have not been mentioned by me; this much can be traveled by the monkeys. Beyond that, we do not know the sunless and boundless realm."
"But having found Vaidehī and the dwelling of Rāvaṇa, you must return upon reaching Mount Udaya when the month is complete.
You must not stay beyond a month; anyone staying longer shall be put to death by me."
"O monkeys, having searched the direction beloved by Mahendra and adorned with forest groves with great skill, return now as successful ones, having found Maithilī."
"Having recovered Sītā, the beloved of the scion of Raghu's lineage,
you shall then return and be happy.
Then Sugrīva dispatched that great army of monkeys.
4.040.001 He dispatched as messengers certain distinguished monkeys:
4.040.002 Nīla, the son of Agni, and the monkey Hanumān,
4.040.002 as well as the great ape Jāmbavān, the son of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Suhotra, Śarīra, and likewise Śaragulma; Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Suṣeṇa, and Ṛṣabha;
as well as Mainda, Dvivida, Vijaya, and Gandhamādana.
The heroic lord of the monkey hosts, who was skilled in discerning distinctions, commanded both Ulkāmukha and Asaṅga— the two sons of Hutāśana— as well as the heroes headed by Aṅgada,
all of whom were endowed with speed and prowess.

Having appointed those foremost among the monkey heroes as the leaders of a great and irresistible force, he assigned them to the southern direction. "Whatever regions there may be in that quarter that are difficult to traverse," [he commanded].
4.040.007c That lord of monkeys recounted those [regions] to the leaders of the monkeys:
4.040.008a "The thousand-peaked Vindhya mountain, covered with various trees and creepers,
and the difficult-to-access river Narmadā, frequented by great serpents."
Then [he went] to the delightful Godāvarī, the great river Kṛṣṇaveṇī,
and the highly fortunate Varadā, frequented by great serpents;
as well as the Mekhalas, the Utkalas, and the cities of Daśārṇa.
Behold Avantī and Abhravantī in their entirety; Vidarbha and Ṛṣika, as well as the delightful Māhiṣaka lands;
and likewise the Baṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Kauśikas on all sides.
Having surveyed the Daṇḍaka forest with its mountains, rivers, and caves,
he beheld everything, including the Godāvarī River.
Likewise, he saw the Andhras, Puṇḍras, Colas, Pāṇḍyas, and Keralas.
And the mountain Ayomukha, adorned with minerals, must be traversed;
that glorious great mountain, with its variegated peaks and forests of diverse blossoming trees, and regions of sandalwood groves, must be searched.
Then you shall see that divine river Kāverī, with its clear and auspicious waters, sporting there with throngs of Apsarases. On the summit of that Malaya mountain sits one of great majesty.
"You shall behold Agastya, the best of sages, who resembles the sun. Then,
permitted by that gracious and high-souled one,
you shall cross the great river Tāmraparṇī, which is infested with crocodiles."
Covered by divine sandalwood forests and adorned with islands,
that land plunges into the ocean like a young woman approaching her beloved.
Then [he saw] a divine golden [palace], decorated with pearls and gems.
"O monkeys, you shall see the closed gate of the Pāṇḍyas.
Then, having reached the ocean and deliberated upon the determination of your purpose,
[the sea] was made to recede there in its midst by Agastya."
The glorious Mahendra, the best of mountains, abounding in various and variegated trees,
is made of gold and majestically plunges into the great ocean;
it is adorned with diverse blossoming trees and creepers.
It is frequented by the foremost of divine sages, yakṣas, and apsarases;
it is filled with throngs of siddhas and cāraṇas and is exceedingly beautiful.
The thousand-eyed Indra always resorts to it on every auspicious occasion.
On its opposite shore lies an island extending for a hundred yojanas;
inaccessible to humans and blazing, search it thoroughly on all sides. There, in particular, Sītā must be sought with all your soul.
For that region is the abode of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who possesses a splendor equal to the thousand-eyed Indra;
it lies in the midst of the southern ocean. And there, O Rākṣasī, is his dwelling.
Known as Aṅgārakā, she subsists by seizing the radiance [of others]. Having passed beyond her, one hundred yojanas out at sea,
there is a mountain named Puṣpitaka, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, which is endowed with splendor.
Resembling the rays of the moon and sun, and surrounded by the waters of the ocean,
it shines with its vast peaks as if scraping the very sky.
Of that mountain, there is one golden peak which the sun frequents.
The moon honors that single white mountain made of silver;
neither the ungrateful, nor the cruel, nor the atheists behold it.
O monkeys, bowing your heads to that mountain, search for it!
Having passed beyond that, there is a mountain named Sūryavān, difficult to assail,
extending for fourteen *yojanas* along a path hard to traverse. Then, having passed beyond that as well, there is a mountain named Vaidyuta.
4.040.032c With trees that yield the fruit of every desire and are enchanting at all times,
4.040.033a having there eaten the excellent roots and fruits,
and having drunk the finest honey, go on further, O monkeys!
There stands a mountain named Kuñjara, pleasing to the eye and the mind,
where the abode of Agastya was constructed by Viśvakarman;
there, it is one yojana in width and ten yojanas in height.
There is a divine golden refuge, adorned with various jewels;
there lies the city named Bhogavatī, the abode of the serpents,
with its wide streets, invincible, and protected on all sides.
It is guarded by terrible serpents with sharp fangs and potent venom;
there dwells Vāsuki, the most fearsome king of snakes. Having departed [from the city], that city of Bhogavatī must be sought out.

And having passed beyond that region, there stands a great mountain named Ṛṣabha, shaped like a bull, majestic and composed of all kinds of jewels. There grows gośīrṣaka, padmaka, and hariśyāma sandalwood.
There, a divine sandalwood tree arises, possessing a radiance equal to fire;
yet, having seen that sandalwood, it must never be touched.
Fierce Gandharvas named Rohitas guard that forest.
There, the lords of the Gandharvas, possessing a radiance equal to five suns—
namely Śailūṣa, Grāmaṇī, Bhikṣu, Śubhra, and likewise Babhru—
stand at the edge of the earth, invincible, having conquered heaven.
"Beyond this, the world of the ancestors (Pitṛloka), most dreadful, must no longer be frequented by you;
it is the capital city of Yama, shrouded in painful darkness.
This much alone, O heroes, O bulls among monkeys, is to be known by you."
It is impossible to discern or to go beyond this; therefore, it is not the destination of those who possess a path.
Having surveyed all of this and whatever else is seen, and having understood the course of Vaidehī, you ought to turn back.
But he who, having returned after the months have passed, shall say, "Sītā has been seen," and who possesses enjoyments equal to my own, shall dwell in happiness; indeed,
there is no one dearer to me than him, even more so than my own life.
"Though he has committed many offenses against me, he shall become my kinsman. You possess immeasurable strength and prowess,
and you are born of families endowed with vast virtues."
4.040.047c "Exert yourselves with even greater effort so that you may find the daughter of the lord of men.
4.041.001a Then Sugrīva dispatched those monkeys toward the southern direction.

Then the king of great splendor, having summoned the troop-leader named Suṣeṇa— the father of Tārā and father-in-law of Bhīma, endowed with intelligence and prowess, and equal to the wind in speed— [spoke].
Approaching him and bowing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words:
"Render assistance to Rāma now that this task has arisen.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand swift-moving monkeys, [he stood there].
"Go, O gentle lord, toward the western quarter presided over by Varuṇa;
[there you will find] Surāṣṭra along with Bāhlīka, as well as the Śūras and the Ābhīras— prosperous regions, delightful, and filled with vast cities."
"O leaders of the monkey troops, search the thickets of *puṃnāga* trees, the interior filled with many *uddālaka* shrubs, as well as the groves of *ketaka* flowers; and likewise,
search the auspicious rivers of cool water that flow toward the west."
Having searched the forests of ascetics, the wildernesses, and the mountains,
as well as the difficult terrain covered by mountain ranges in the western direction,
you should then proceed to see the western ocean.
Then the monkeys will sport in waters unagitated even by tens of thousands of *timi* and *nakra* monsters,
amidst groves of *ketaka*, thickets of *tamāla*,
and forests of coconut palms.
There, search for Sītā and the dwelling place of Rāvaṇa;
likewise, search Marīcipattana, the beautiful Jaṭīpura,
Avantī, Aṅgalopā, and the forest of Alakṣita.
There were vast kingdoms and cities here and there;
and at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean,
there stood a great mountain named Hemagiri, possessing a hundred peaks and massive trees.
On its lovely plateaus dwell winged lions;
they carry whales, fish, and elephants up into their nests.
Those lions who reside upon the mountain peaks have those very nests as their dwellings.
4.041.014c Arrogant and yet contented, the elephants, whose trumpeting sounds like the roar of clouds,
4.041.014e roam everywhere throughout this vast expanse filled with water. 4.041.015a Its golden peak, touching the heavens, is adorned with variegated trees.
4.041.015c Everything must be searched quickly by the monkeys, who can assume any form at will.
4.041.016a O monkeys, you shall see there in the ocean a golden peak extending for a hundred yojanas, difficult to behold, which has gone beyond the Paripātra mountain range.

Twenty-four crores of powerful Gandharvas dwell there— beings as radiant as fire, fierce, and able to assume any form at will. They must not be approached too closely by the monkeys of terrible prowess.
Therefore, no fruit from that region should be taken by the monkeys;
for those heroes are difficult to approach, full of courage, and possessed of great strength—
they of terrifying prowess guard the fruits and roots there.
In that matter, effort must be exerted and Jānakī must be sought;
for there is no fear whatsoever from them for one who maintains his status as a monkey.
On the fourth quarter of the ocean is a mountain named Cakravān.
There, a thousand-spoked discus was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Having slain Pañcajana and the Dānava Hayagrīva there,
Puruṣottama then took up that discus and the conch shell.
4.041.023 On its variegated ridges and in its vast caves,
Rāvaṇa must be searched for here and there along with Vaidehī.
4.041.024 Sixty-four yojanas away is the mountain named Varāha.
4.041.024c There, in the unfathomable abode of Varuṇa, is a most glorious mountain with golden peaks.
4.041.025a Therein lies the city named Prāgjyotiṣa, made entirely of gold;
4.041.025c within its caves dwells the evil-minded one named Naraka.
On its variegated ridges and in its vast caves, Rāvaṇa must be searched for here and there along with Vaidehī. Having passed beyond that lord of mountains, there is one with golden inner caverns.
The mountain was entirely golden, with tens of thousands of cascades and springs.
Elephants, boars, lions, and tigers roared constantly from all sides, emboldened by that sound.

On that mountain named Meghavat, the glorious Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka and possessor of bay horses, was consecrated as king by the gods. Having passed beyond that lord of mountains protected by Mahendra, [he proceeded].
You shall go to sixty thousand golden mountains,
shining on all sides with the color of the rising sun,
adorned with trees made of gold that are in full bloom.
Standing in their midst is King Meru, the supreme mountain;
in ancient times, this mountain was granted a boon by the gracious Āditya.
Thus addressed, the lord of mountains said: "All of you indeed have me as your refuge."
By my grace, they shall become golden by day and by night;
and those gods, gandharvas, and dānavas who dwell with you shall also become red in hue, possessing a radiance like that of gold.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Maruts, the dwellers of heaven,
having arrived at Mount Meru, the supreme mountain, for the evening twilight,
wait upon the Sun; and by them, Sūrya is worshipped.
Invisible to all beings,
the sun descends to the mountain; in half a *muhūrta*, the maker of day swiftly traverses those ten thousand *yojanas* to that peak.
On its peak is a great, divine palace, radiant as the sun,
crowded with the excellence of palatial halls, and constructed by Viśvakarman;
it is adorned with variegated trees teeming with various birds.
4.041.039c It is the abode of the high-souled Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand.
4.041.040a Between Mount Meru and the setting mountain stands a great ten-headed palmyra tree;
4.041.040c made of gold, glorious, and with a variegated pedestal, it shines resplendently.
In all those inaccessible places, lakes, and rivers,
Rāvaṇa must be searched for here and there along with Vaidehī—
wherever that righteous soul dwells, purified by his own ascetic power.
"He who is renowned as Merusāvarṇi is indeed equal to Brahmā himself.
That great seer Merusāvarṇi, who resembles the sun, should be questioned regarding the news concerning Maithilī; bowing his head to the ground, he should be asked."
4.041.044 Just as the sun, at the end of the night, having dispelled all darkness from the world of the living, goes to the mountain of setting;
4.041.045 so too, O bulls among monkeys, is it possible for monkeys to go only this far.
Beyond that point, we know nothing further— neither of the sun nor of any boundaries.
Having found Vaidehī and the dwelling of Rāvaṇa,
and having reached the Setting Mountain (Asta), return when the month is complete.
"One must not stay for more than a month; anyone staying longer shall be put to death by me. My heroic father-in-law will depart together with you.
All of this must be obeyed by you who act according to my command."

"This mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful man is my preceptor and my father-in-law; you too are valiant and the authority in all undertakings. Having established him as our authority, look toward the western direction."
"When the wife of the lord of men, who possesses immeasurable splendor, has been seen,
we shall have accomplished our purpose by repaying what was done for us.
Furthermore, whatever else may be beneficial for this task should be undertaken."
"Having deliberated together, you must act in accordance with the requirements of place, time, and purpose.
Then, having heard Sugrīva’s prudent words, the monkeys led by Suṣeṇa [prepared to depart].
4.041.052c Having addressed the lord of the monkeys, they all departed for that direction guarded by Varuṇa.
4.042.001a Then Sugrīva, having dispatched his father-in-law to the western direction, [proceeded further].
The king, that bull among monkeys who was skilled in counsel and esteemed by all the monkeys, spoke these words— beneficial both to himself and to Rāma— to the heroic monkey named Śatabali.
Surrounded by a hundred thousand forest-dwellers like yourself,
set forth together with your own ministers and the sons of Vaivasvata toward the northern quarter, which is renowned for its prowess and adorned by the Himālaya mountains.
"Search everywhere for Rāma’s blameless wife.
When this task is accomplished and the beloved wish of the son of Daśaratha is fulfilled, we shall be freed from our debt; we are the best among those who know how to achieve their goals."
"For a great service has indeed been rendered to us by the high-souled Rāghava;
if there is a way to repay him, our lives would become fruitful.
Adopting this resolve, we shall see how Jānakī may be found."
Therefore, you who desire our pleasure and welfare must act accordingly; for this Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, is worthy of honor by all beings, and he has conceived affection for us.
"Search these forest fastnesses, the rivers, and the mountain ranges with the excellence of your intelligence and prowess. There you will find Mlecchas, Pulindas, and likewise Śūrasenas."
The Prasthālas, the Bharatas, and the Kurus along with the Madrakas;
the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, and the Āraṭṭakas;
as well as the Bāhlīkas, the Ṛṣikas, the Pauravas, and the Taṅkaṇas.
Search repeatedly for Cīna, Paramacīna, and Nīhāra; then seek out Darada and explore the Himavat mountains,
amidst the thickets of *lodhra* and *padmaka* trees and the forests of *devadāru*.
4.042.013c Rāvaṇa, along with Vaidehī, must be searched for here and there.
4.042.014a Then, having gone to the hermitage of Soma, which is frequented by gods and gandharvas,
you shall go to that mountain named Kāla, which possesses great peaks.
"Search for the illustrious and highly fortunate wife of Rāma upon his great peaks, in the clefts, and in the caves.
Having passed beyond that lord of mountains, the great mountain Hemavarga,"
4.042.016c Therefore, you ought to go to the mountain named Sudarśana. 4.042.017a In its forest groves, on its precipices, and in its caves,
Rāvaṇa must be searched for here and there along with Vaidehī.
Having traversed that space extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction—
devoid of mountains, rivers, and trees, and abandoned by all living beings—
they quickly crossed that hair-raising wilderness.
Having reached Mount Kailāsa, white as snow, you shall be filled with joy. There lies the divine abode of Kubera, shining like a pale cloud and adorned with gold, constructed by Viśvakarman.
There is a vast lotus-lake, abounding with many lotuses and water-lilies,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and frequented by hosts of *apsarases*.
Therein dwells King Vaiśravaṇa, who is saluted by all beings.

The glorious Dhanada, the king of the yakṣas, delights there together with the guhyakas. Rāvaṇa, along with Vaidehī, must be searched for here and there among his sandalwood trees and in the mountain caves.
Having reached Mount Krauñca, one must enter its most difficult cave with vigilance; for it is remembered as being hard to penetrate. Indeed, high-souled beings, radiant as the sun, dwell there.
The great seers, who possess divine forms and are duly honored even by the gods,
must search here and there through the other caves of Krauñca, as well as its plateaus, peaks, caverns, and slopes.
Having also gazed here and there at the peak of Krauñca,
as well as the treeless Kāmaśaila and Mānasa, the abode of birds,
no passage exists there for beings— neither gods, dānavas, nor rākṣasas.

And he must be searched for by all of you throughout the mountain ranges, including their peaks and plateaus. Beyond Mount Krauñca lies the mountain named Maināka; there is the abode of the Dānava Maya, built by himself.
But Maināka, with its peaks, plateaus, and caves, must be searched;
for there, in various places, are the dwellings of the horse-faced women. Having passed beyond that region, one will find a hermitage frequented by the Siddhas.
There dwell the Siddhas, the Vaikhānasas, and the Vālakhilya ascetics. Those ascetics, perfected through austerity and free from all stain, are worthy of your homage;
you should also question them with humility regarding news of Sītā.

4.052.010a But those high-souled monkeys, with their faces then held by her hands,
were raised up from the cave by her in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Then that ascetic woman, who practiced righteousness, comforted all those monkeys who had emerged from that perilous place and spoke as follows:
"This is the glorious Vindhya mountain, endowed with various trees and creepers."
"This is Mount Prasravaṇa, and this is the great ocean, Sāgara. May it be well with you; I shall now depart for my own abode, O bulls among monkeys.
Having spoken thus, Svayaṃprabhā entered that glorious cave.
Then they beheld the terrible ocean, the abode of Varuṇa,
shoreless and roaring, agitated by fearsome waves; and as they searched for the mountain fortress constructed by the magic of Maya, [they saw it].
The month that had been fixed as the deadline by the king passed for them. Then,
at the foot of the Vindhya mountain where the trees were in full bloom,
those illustrious ones sat down and fell into deep reflection.

Then, seeing the spring trees covered by hundreds of creepers and their tops weighed down with an abundance of flowers, they became apprehensive with fear. Having informed one another that spring had arrived, they...
With their messages, purposes, and the appointed time lost, they fell to the surface of the earth.
But that monkey, whose shoulders were like those of a bull lion and whose arms were thick and long—
the highly wise crown prince Angada— spoke these words.
"By the command of the king of monkeys, we have all departed from our place in the cave;
a full month has passed—O monkey, do you not realize this?
When that time appointed by Sugrīva himself has elapsed..."
4.052.021c It is appropriate for all of us forest-dwellers to sit in fasting unto death.
4.052.022a Sugrīva is fierce by nature, and having established himself in his position as our master, 4.052.022c he will not forgive us all when we have returned as offenders.
If Sītā does not return, he will surely commit an evil deed;
therefore, it is appropriate for us to fast unto death right here this very day,
abandoning our sons, wives, wealth, and homes.
4.052.024c As long as the king does not have all those who have returned from here executed, 4.052.024e death right here would be better for us than an ignominious execution.
4.052.025a Furthermore, I was not consecrated to the position of crown prince by Sugrīva.
"I have been consecrated by Rāma, the lord of men, whose actions are untiring. Yet that king, harboring a long-standing enmity, will see my transgression and,
having made his decision, will have me executed with a severe punishment."
"What use have I for friends who witness my calamity until the end of my life? Right here on this holy shore of the ocean, I shall sit in the vow of fasting unto death.
Having heard these words spoken by the prince, the crown prince, [the charioteer replied:]
4.052.028c All those best of monkeys spoke these piteous words:
4.052.029a "Sugrīva is fierce by nature, and Rāghava is devoted to his beloved;
4.052.029c and since Vaidehī has not been found, they will see us gathered here."
"He will undoubtedly have them killed for the sake of pleasing Rāghava. Furthermore,
it is not appropriate for those who have committed an offense to go back to their master's side,
especially when these monkeys are afflicted by fear."
Having heard these words, Tāra spoke thus:
"Enough with despair! If it pleases you all, let us enter the cave and dwell there."
For this place, created by Māyā, is very difficult to traverse,
yet it abounds in trees, water, food, and drink;
here we have no fear at all from Purandara.
Neither from Rāghava, nor from the king of the monkeys, nor even upon hearing the favorable words of Aṅgada,
did all the monkeys speak with confidence.
"Let that be arranged for us this very day so that we may not be slain by such [beings].
While Tārā, who possessed the splendor of the lord of stars, was speaking thus, [the gods spoke].
Then Hanumān considered that the kingdom had been seized by Aṅgada;
for he regarded Vālin’s son as endowed with the eightfold intelligence, possessed of the four powers, and possessing fourteen virtues.
Constantly being filled with splendor, strength, and prowess,
like the moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight increasing in beauty;
equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence and resembling his father in valor.
Then Hanumān began to deceive Aṅgada, who was listening to Tāra as Indra once did to Śukra, and who, though exhausted for the sake of his master, was learned in all the scriptures.
Describing the third of the four expedients,
he sowed dissension among all those monkeys with a wealth of speech.
When they had all been divided, he then terrified Aṅgada.
With many terrifying words, accompanied by methods of provocation, he said:
"O son of Tārā, you are indeed more capable than your father in battle;
you are able to firmly uphold the burden of the monkey kingdom just as your father did."
"O bull among monkeys, these monkeys are by nature of unsteady mind;
they will not endure being commanded while deprived of you, their son and husband. Indeed, they would not question you; I tell you this as a direct truth."
"Just as this Jāmbavān, Nīla, and the great monkey Suhotra—
none of these can indeed be drawn away from Sugrīva by you through conciliation, gifts, or other such means, nor even by force."

4.053.012a They say that even a weak king may resort to a defensive posture against one who is stronger; 4.053.012c therefore, one who seeks self-protection should not engage in conflict with the weak.
4.053.013a And as for this nurse whom you consider to be this cave, it is so heard.
4.053.013c This is but a minor task for Lakṣmaṇa’s arrows in terms of tearing it apart. 4.053.014a For what Indra did in the past, by hurling his thunderbolt, was indeed slight;

4.053.014e And Lakṣmaṇa possesses many iron arrows of that same kind. 4.053.015a O scorcher of enemies, as soon as you take up your position, 4.053.015c then all the monkeys, having made their resolve, will abandon [their hesitation].
Constantly anxious and hungry for their children and wives,
exhausted by beds of suffering, they will leave you behind. Thus, you are deprived of both friends who desire your welfare and your kinsmen.
"You will become intensely agitated even by a blade of grass that is quivering; moreover,
the terrible arrows of Lakṣmaṇa, which possess great velocity and are difficult to withstand, will surely not fail to strike you as they seek to kill you when you have turned away."
"We have come together with you and attended upon you with humility;
however, Sugrīva will duly establish you in the kingdom. Your paternal uncle, who desires righteousness, is firm in his vows and wishes for your happiness."
Pure and true to his promise, he will never wish you harm;
he desires the welfare of your mother, and his very life is for her sake.
Since he has no other offspring, O Aṅgada, you must go back to him.
Having heard the humble speech of Hanumān, which was consistent with dharma and endowed with respect for his master, Aṅgada spoke these words:
"Steadfastness with one's whole being, purity, compassion, and likewise straightforwardness— "
Neither prowess nor fortitude is found in Sugrīva,
who, while his elder brother is still alive, has taken for himself by right his elder brother’s wife— the beloved queen—
and thus acts as a contemptible son toward his mother.
4.054.004a How can he understand righteousness when his evil-minded brother,
having been urged to battle, has blocked the entrance to the cave? 4.054.005a And that highly illustrious one, who took her hand in marriage according to truth, has fulfilled his duty.
By whom Rāghava has been forgotten— who would he remember as having done him a good deed? Since he,
who was not afraid of unrighteousness, commanded Lakṣmaṇa to search for Sītā out of fear, how can there be any dharma in him?
Who that is noble, well-born, and desirous of life would ever place his trust in such a sinful, ungrateful, forgetful, and fickle-souled man—
whether he be virtuous or devoid of merit— after having installed his son in the kingdom?
"How will Sugrīva allow me, born of an enemy's lineage, to live? For how could I— my counsel betrayed, having offended him, and stripped of my power—
live after reaching Kiṣkindhā, weak and like one who is helpless?"
For the deceitful, cruel, and ruthless Sugrīva might subject me to imprisonment by means of secret punishment for the sake of the kingdom; therefore,
fasting unto death is better for me than captivity and exhaustion.
"Grant me your permission, all you monkeys; let us go to our homes.
I promise you this: I shall not go to the city.
Right here I will sit in fasting unto death; for me, death alone is better."
"First, after offering salutations, the king should inquire about his welfare;
then he should say: 'Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, is younger than I.
My mother Rumā should also be asked about her health and well-being."
"You ought to comfort my mother Tārā as well; for she,
who is compassionate and naturally fond of her son,
will surely give up her life upon hearing that I am lost here."
Having spoken these words and having saluted even the elders,
Aṅgada, dejected and weeping, lay down upon the darbha grass on the ground.
As he lay there, the bull-like monkeys wept around him.
Distressed by grief, they shed warm tears from their eyes;
some censuring Sugrīva and others praising Vālin, they all gathered around Aṅgada, resolving to sit in fasting unto death.
Having understood that intention of Vāli’s son, all those bulls among monkeys sipped water and sat down facing the east,
taking their place upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, situated on the northern bank.
With many monkeys, as large as the peaks of great mountains, lying down upon it, that mountain,
with its interior waterfalls echoing with their noise, became resounded.
While all those monkeys were seated on that mountain plateau where they had resolved to fast unto death, like formidable clouds roaring intensely,
the king of vultures approached that place.
There was a bird named Sāmpāti by name, long-lived and glorious,
the brother of Jaṭāyu, renowned for his strength and prowess;
having emerged from a cave of the great mountain Vindhya, he—
Seeing the monkeys seated, he spoke these words with a joyful heart:
"In this world, it is said that destiny follows a person according to its own ordinance;
for just as this food was ordained, it has come to me after a long time."
"I shall eat the monkeys one after another, as each dies," the bird said,
looking at those forest-dwellers. Having heard these words of that bird who was greedy for food, [the monkeys...]

4.055.006c Then Aṅgada, extremely distressed, spoke to Hanumān: 4.055.007a "Behold! Under the pretext of Sītā, Yama, the son of Vivasvat himself, has arrived at this place for the destruction of the monkeys."
"Rāma’s task has not been accomplished, nor has the king’s word been followed;
this unforeseen calamity has suddenly befallen the monkeys.
Jaṭāyu has performed this deed out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Vaidehī."
4.055.009c Whatever was heard there by the king of the vultures, all of that you shall hear in its entirety.
4.055.010a Likewise, all beings, even those born of the animal realm,
perform what is pleasing to Rāma, having renounced their lives just as we have.
"Exhausted for the sake of Rāghava and having renounced our very lives,
we have entered these wildernesses, yet we do not see Maithilī.
That king of vultures, however, is happy, even though he was slain by Rāvaṇa in battle."
Released from the fear of Sugrīva, Jaṭāyu has attained the supreme goal;
yet, due to the death of Jaṭāyu, the passing of King Daśaratha,
and the abduction of Vaidehī, the monkeys have fallen into a state of uncertainty.
The dwelling of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in the forest together with Sītā;
the slaying of Vālī by the arrow of the descendant of Raghu;
and likewise, the destruction of all the Rākṣasas through Rāma’s wrath.
"Indeed, this calamity has been brought about by Kaikeyī’s granting of the boons.
Having heard those words then, as they issued from the mouth of Aṅgada,
the sharp-beaked vulture spoke these words in a loud voice.

"Who is this that proclaims with his voice the death of my brother Jaṭāyu, who was dearer to me than life itself, as if shaking my very heart? How did the battle between the Rākṣasa and the vulture take place in Janasthāna?"
"O bulls among monkeys, after a long time I have today heard this name of my younger brother,
who was a knower of virtues and praiseworthy for his heroic deeds; therefore,
I wish to hear about his destruction."
How was it that Daśaratha, the friend of my brother Jaṭāyu— who dwelt in Janasthāna— and indeed the friend of my own brother,
came to have as his beloved eldest son Rāma, who is dear to his elders?
"O subduers of enemies, because my wings have been scorched by the rays of the sun, I am unable to glide away; I wish to descend from this mountain.
Having heard him, even though his voice was broken with grief, those leaders of the monkey troops [responded].

They did not believe his words at all, for they were suspicious of his actions. Seeing the vulture, those monkeys sat down to fast unto death and then formed a fierce resolve: "He will devour us all."
"If he should devour us while we are seated here in the fast unto death, we shall have accomplished our purpose; having attained perfection, we shall quickly depart from here.
Then all those bulls among monkeys formed this resolution.
Having brought the vulture down from the mountain peak, Aṅgada then said to him:
"O bird, there was a powerful lord of monkeys named Kṣaraja;
he was my noble father, and he had two righteous sons."
Sugrīva and Valī were both sons of Oghabala;
my father was King Vālī, whose deeds are renowned throughout the world. He was the king of the entire earth and a great chariot-warrior among the Ikṣvākus.
The illustrious Rāma, son of Daśaratha, has entered the Daṇḍaka forest together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and his wife Vaidehī;

Having deprived Rāvaṇa of his chariot and having rescued Maithilī, the vulture—

was thus slain by that exceedingly powerful one.
He was consecrated by Rāma and attained the supreme goal.
Then, the high-souled Rāghava formed a friendship with my paternal uncle Sugrīva, and he [Rāghava] slew my father.

"The king of the monkey chiefs by whom we were dispatched— thus directed by Rāma, we have searched here and there,
yet we have not found Vaidehī, who is like the radiance of the sun in the night."
"Having thoroughly searched the Daṇḍaka forest with focused minds,

"The month that was agreed upon by the king has passed for us there. All of us, acting according to the command of the king of monkeys, have transgressed the established limit and, out of fear, are now sitting in fasting unto death."
"When that descendant of Kakutstha, along with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, is enraged,
there is no life left for any of us there, even those who have already departed.
Thus was he addressed by the monkeys who had renounced their lives, as they spoke these piteous words.
Tearful and with a great voice, the vulture replied to the monkeys:
