"Because of my old age and lack of allies, even while hearing this, I must endure it;
for I have no power today to avenge the enmity against my brother.
Long ago, when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred, both he and I were seekers of victory."
Having reached the sun, which was blazing and garlanded with rays,
they traveled swiftly through the path of the sky; but when the sun reached the meridian, Jaṭāyu grew exhausted.
Seeing my brother tormented by the rays of the sun and utterly overwhelmed by distress, I covered him with my wings out of affection.
O best of monkeys, with my wings burnt away, I fell upon the Vindhya mountains.
"Living here, I have not perceived any news of my brother.
Thus addressed by his brother Sampāti,
the highly wise crown prince Angada then replied.
"O Jaṭāyus, if you are my brother as I have told you,
tell me if you know the dwelling place of that Rākṣasa,
or of that short-sighted Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas."
"Whether near or far, if you know [her], tell us.
Then the highly energetic elder brother of Jaṭāyu spoke words suited to himself, gladdening the monkeys.
"O monkeys, my wings have been burnt away and my strength is gone;
nevertheless, with mere words, I shall provide the greatest assistance to Rāma.
I know the worlds of Varuṇa and even those of Viṣṇu attained through his three strides."
The battles between the gods and the asuras, and the churning for the nectar of immortality—
this task of Rāma must first be performed by me;
yet my splendor has been taken away by old age, and my vital breaths have grown feeble.
I saw a young woman, endowed with beauty and adorned with every ornament, being carried away by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa;
that beautiful lady was crying out, "O Rāma! O Rāma! O Lakṣmaṇa!"
Casting off her ornaments and shaking her limbs,
her exquisite silken garment shone upon the dark Rākṣasa like the radiance of the sun upon a mountain peak, or like lightning amidst a dark cloud.
I believe that Sītā is indeed there because of Rāma’s mention of her name. Listen as I tell you the location of that *rākṣasa*:
he is the direct son of Viśravas and the brother of Vaiśravaṇa.
A Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa dwells in the city of Laṅkā.
One hundred yojanas from here, on an island in the middle of the ocean,
that beautiful city of Laṅkā was constructed by Viśvakarman.
In that place dwells Vaidehī, dejected and clad in silk; confined within Rāvaṇa’s inner apartments, she is closely guarded by rākṣasīs. There you shall see Maithilī, the daughter of King Janaka.
Then, when Laṅkā is protected on all sides by the ocean,
having reached the end of the sea at its full extent of a hundred yojanas,
and having arrived at the southern shore, you shall then behold Rāvaṇa.
"O monkeys, proceed with haste and speed right there!
Indeed, through my knowledge I see that you shall return after having seen [her]. This is the path of the kuliṅga birds and others who live on grain."
The second [group] consists of those that eat offerings and those that feed on the fruits of trees; the hawks go to the third, along with the *krauñca* birds and the ospreys;
the falcons go to the fourth, and the vultures go to the fifth.
O bulls among monkeys, for us who are endowed with strength and vigor and possessed of beauty and youth,
the sixth path— that of the swans— is supreme, yet the gait of Vainateya is even higher; and our birth, O leaders of monkeys, was from Vainateya.
"Because of the contemptible deed committed by him, we have become flesh-eaters;
yet, remaining here, I behold Rāvaṇa as well as Jānakī. For us too, there is likewise the power of divine, golden vision."
"Therefore, by the power of our food and by our very nature,
we can always see beyond more than a hundred yojanas. Our livelihood is ordained for us from afar by our innate disposition."
A livelihood at the feet [of the enemy] has been ordained for those who fight with their feet. Let some means be found for crossing the salt sea;
having approached Vaidehī, you shall depart with your purpose accomplished.
"I wish to be led by you to the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa,
so that I may offer water for my high-souled brother who has gone to heaven.
Then, having been led to that place on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, he spoke.
Having brought back the lord of birds, Sampāti, whose wings had been burnt,
to that same place,
those monkeys of great prowess became joyful upon obtaining news of her.

Then, having heard those words spoken by the king of vultures regarding the taste of that nectar, those bulls among monkeys rejoiced; and Jāmbavān, the best of monkeys, together with all the forest-dwellers, [was likewise filled with joy].
Suddenly rising from the ground, he spoke to the king of the vultures:
"Where is Sītā? By whom was she seen? Or who is carrying away the princess of Mithilā? Tell me all that; be the refuge for us forest-dwellers."
Who would not contemplate the prowess of the arrows of Daśaratha’s son— arrows that fall with the speed of a thunderbolt and were discharged by Lakṣmaṇa himself? He [Rāvaṇa],
though his mind was fixed on hearing about Sītā, addressed the monkeys who were filled with affection for him.
Comforting him again with joy, he spoke these words:
"Listen now to how I heard of Vaidehī’s abduction, by whom it was told to me, and where that large-eyed lady is."
"I am an old man who has long since fallen upon this inaccessible mountain, which extends for many yojanas; my vital strength and prowess are exhausted.
My son, Supārśva by name, [is here]."

At the proper time, the best of birds sustains himself with food. The Gandharvas have intense desire, the serpents have intense anger, and for deer there is intense fear; therefore, we have intense hunger.
Once, when I was afflicted by hunger and longing for food, my son returned at the end of the day without any meat. Out of old age and anger, I rebuked him.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, that best of those who fall, the prince—
who increases my joy— was afflicted by the lack of food; having paid his respects according to the truth, he spoke these words:
"O father, at the proper time, seeking prey, I leaped into the sky and took my stand blocking the gateway of Mount Mahendra. There,
[I encountered] thousands of creatures that roam within the ocean."

4.058.014c I, alone, stood facing downward, intent on blocking the path. 4.058.015a There, I saw someone approaching, bearing a woman whose radiance was like the rising sun, resembling a mass of crushed collyrium.
4.058.016a Seeking food, I saw them and made up my mind; 4.058.016c by that gentle and humble man, I was asked for the way.
4.058.017a For there is nowhere a striker found against those who approach with gentleness.
"Could even some person among the lowly do this, much less one such as I?
He has gone through the sky with such speed that he seemed to be contracting the firmament itself by his splendor.
Then, I was approached and honored by beings who move through the air.
"By good fortune you live, dear son!"—thus the great seers said to me.
"He has somehow departed with his wife; there is no doubt that it is well with him.
Having been addressed thus by those most auspicious Siddhas, I then [proceeded].
And that King Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
was described to me as one who was carrying off the daughter of Janaka, the wife of Rāma, the son of Daśaratha—
her ornaments and fine silks fallen away, and her overcome by a surge of grief.
Crying out the names of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with her hair disheveled, he—
supreme among those skilled in speech— said, "This is indeed the time for action," and Supārśva explained this entire matter to me.

Even after hearing that, I had no thought at all regarding an effort [to escape], for how could a bird without wings undertake any action? However, that which can be done by me, who exists within the qualities of speech and intellect—
"Listen, I shall declare that which rests upon your manly prowess;
for with both my speech and my mind, I shall do what is pleasing to you all. Whatever is the task of the son of Daśaratha is indeed my own; of this there is no doubt."
You, O sirs, are preeminent in intellect, powerful, and high-minded; united with the king of the monkeys, you are difficult even for the gods to overcome.
And the sharp arrows of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, fletched with heron feathers, [are likewise formidable].

He is sufficient for the restraint and protection of even the three worlds. Granted, O Ten-necked One, you are endowed with splendor and strength; yet for you who are so capable, nothing at all is difficult to achieve.
"Therefore, enough with this delay; let a firm decision be made.
For wise men such as you do not remain stuck in worldly actions.
Then the leaders of the monkey troops [approached] that vulture, who had performed his water-libations and was bathed.
Seated upon that inaccessible mountain, having surrounded him on all sides, Saṃpāti— having gained confidence through joy— spoke again to Aṅgada, who was attended by all those monkeys.
"O monkeys, having become silent and one-pointed in mind, listen to me;
I shall proclaim the truth of how I came to know of Maithilī.
Long ago, I fell here upon the peak of this Vindhya mountain in the forest."
With his limbs enveloped by the heat of the sun and scorched by the solar rays,
he regained consciousness after six nights; yet, helpless and as if overwhelmed,
looking toward all directions, he did not recognize anything at all.
Then, having observed the oceans, mountains, all the rivers, lakes, forests, and wilderness regions, his mind turned toward [the mountain]:
"It is filled with flocks of joyful birds, possessing peaks within its caves."
On the shore of the southern ocean, it was certain that this was the Vindhya range. There stood a holy hermitage, highly honored even by the gods,
where a rishi named Niśākara dwelt, performing rigorous austerities.
"O knowers of dharma, eight thousand years have passed while I have dwelt here without that seer, since the Moon-god ascended to heaven.
And having descended slowly from the peak of the Vindhya with great difficulty, from that rugged height,"
Having returned with great difficulty to this earth covered in sharp darbha grass,
I am deeply distressed and long for the sight of that seer;
indeed, he has been visited many times by both Jaṭāyu and myself.
4.059.012a Fragrant breezes blew in the vicinity of his hermitage; 4.059.012c not a single tree was seen there that was without flowers or without fruit.
4.059.013a Having approached the holy hermitage, he took refuge at the foot of a tree.
"I was waiting, desiring to see the venerable Lord Niśākara.
Then I saw a rishi of blazing splendor standing not far away, who,
having performed his ablutions, was difficult to overcome as he turned back facing north."
4.059.015a Bears, sṛmaras, tigers, lions, elephants, and reptiles,
4.059.015c surrounded him and approached, just as living beings approach a giver;
4.059.016a then, knowing that the sage had arrived, those creatures indeed departed.
When the king had entered with his entire army and ministers,
the seer, having seen me, was pleased and re-entered the hermitage;
after emerging after only a moment, he then asked about my business.
"O gentle one, seeing the mutilation of your feathers, it is not understood by me;
these two wings of yours appear as if burnt by fire, and even your skin is scarred.
I have previously seen two vultures equal to the wind in speed."
The two kings of the vultures, brothers who can assume any form at will—
of whom you, Saṃpāti, are the elder and Jaṭāyu is your younger brother—
having assumed human forms, take hold of my feet.
"What is the cause of your disease, and how did you come to fall from your wings?
Or by whom was this staff held against you? Tell everything to me who asks.
Then [he related] that cruel deed, difficult to perform, which had been done out of rashness.
He related everything concerning the sage’s following of the sun. "O Blessed One, because I am covered in wounds and my senses are overwhelmed with shame,
I am exhausted and unable to speak further."
4.060.003a Both I and Jaṭāyu, deluded by pride through our rivalry, 4.060.003c flew into the sky as heroes, desiring to test our prowess.
4.060.004a On the peak of Kailāsa, we made a wager in the presence of the sages.
The sun was to be followed until it reached the great western mountain; then,
we both arrived simultaneously upon the surface of the earth and saw cities there, each as large as a chariot wheel.
In some places we heard the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas;
we saw many women dressed in red garments singing.
Then, quickly leaping up into the sky, we took our place upon the path of the sun.
The two of us gazed upon that forest covered with lush grass;
the earth appeared strewn with boulders like mountain peaks,
and it was enveloped by rivers as if by threads.
Himavat, Vindhya, and the great mountain Meru appeared upon the surface of the earth like serpents in a body of water;
at that time, intense perspiration, exhaustion, and fear came over us both.
Delusion took possession of him, and from that delusion came a terrible fainting spell.
Neither the southern direction, nor the western, nor the northern could be discerned;
the world appeared as if struck down and consumed by fire at the end of a cosmic age.
With great effort, we looked up once more at the sun;
the maker of light appeared to us as equal in size to the earth itself. Then Jaṭāyu, without taking leave of me, plummeted toward the ground.
Seeing him, I quickly released myself from the sky;
protected by the two birds and by me, Jaṭāyu was not consumed by the fire.
However, due to my negligence, I was scorched there as I fell from the path of the wind.
I suspect that Jaṭāyu has fallen upon Janasthāna,
while I myself have fallen upon the Vindhya mountains, my wings burnt and rendered motionless; deprived of my kingdom, my brother, my wings, and my prowess.
"In every way desiring only to die, I shall throw myself from the mountain peak.
Having spoken thus to the best of sages, I wept, deeply distressed.
Then, after meditating for a moment, the Blessed One said this:
Your two wings and your two secondary wings shall yet come into being;
so too shall your eyes, your vital breaths, your prowess, and your strength.
Indeed, I have heard in the Purāṇas that a very great task awaits you in the future.
"By my ascetic power I have seen it, and having heard it, it is known to me:
there will be a certain king named Daśaratha, the joy of the Ikṣvākus;
his son will be the highly resplendent one named Rāma."
And he, whose valor is truth, being commissioned by his father for that purpose, will go to the forest with his brother Lakṣmaṇa; meanwhile,
a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa will carry off his wife.

The lord of the rākṣasas, who was unslayable by gods or dānavas, [arrived] from Janasthāna. And that illustrious and highly fortunate Maithilī, though tempted with objects of desire and various kinds of food and delicacies, will not eat, for she is submerged in sorrow.
4.061.008a Vāsava will know of Vaidehī’s supreme food and will give it to her—
4.061.008c that food which resembles nectar and is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
4.061.009a Having received that food from Maithilī and recognizing it as being from Indra, [he will understand].
Having set aside the first portion, she will offer it upon the ground for Rāma, saying:
"If my lord, together with Lakṣmaṇa, still lives;
or even if they have attained the state of gods, let this food be for them."
4.061.011a The monkeys, messengers of Rāma, will come searching for her.
4.061.011c O bird, you must tell them that she is the queen of Rāma. 4.061.012a But by no means should you depart; where else could one such as you go?
"Wait for the right place and time; you shall regain your wings.
I am capable of making you winged this very day, but staying here, you will accomplish what is for the welfare of the worlds."
Indeed, you must also perform that task for those two princes,
for the brahmins, the gods, the sages, and for Vāsava. I, too, desire to see my brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"I do not wish to hold onto my life-breaths for long; I shall cast off this body.
With these and many other words, he who was skilled in speech praised me and, having obtained my permission, entered his own hermitage.
Having crept slowly from the mountain cave,
I climbed the Vindhya range and have been waiting for you;
yet, of that time, more than a hundred years have now passed.
4.062.003c Having placed the words of the sage in my heart, I have been waiting for the right time and place.
4.062.004a But now that the Great Departure has been undertaken and the Moon has gone to heaven,
4.062.004c this anguish, filled with many anxieties, consumes me.

I shall turn back the resolve for death that has arisen through the words of the sage; for the wisdom that he has granted me for the preservation of my life removes my sorrow, just as a blazing crest of fire dispels the darkness.
And as I became aware of the prowess of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa,
why was my son not protected by me when he rebuked him with words?
Having heard her lamentation, and seeing those two deprived of Sītā—
"Out of affection for Daśaratha, my son has not brought me any joy.
While Sampāti was speaking thus with the monkeys,
his two wings then sprouted forth before the eyes of the forest-dwellers.
Seeing his own body with its wings emerged and their feathers reddish-brown,
he experienced incomparable joy and spoke thus to the monkeys:
"By the power of the great seer Niśākara, whose self is immeasurable..."
"My wings, scorched by the rays of the sun, have grown back again.
The prowess that I possessed while in my youth— that very same prowess, as well as strength and manliness, I perceive in myself today."
"In every way, let an effort be made so that you shall find Sītā;
this acquisition of my wings will serve as a guarantee of your success.
Having spoken thus to all those monkeys, Saṃpāti, the best of birds, [rested].
Desirous of testing his power of flight, he leapt from the mountain peak;
hearing those words of his, the tigers among monkeys became thrilled with joy in their hearts, intent upon the success of their valorous enterprise.
Then those foremost of monkeys, whose prowess was equal to the wind and who had regained their manly courage,
set out toward the direction facing the constellation Abhijit.
Having been informed by the king of the vultures, the monkeys— intent on searching for the daughter of Janaka— leapt up;
gathering together and filled with joy, they roared with the prowess of lions.
Having heard the words of Sampāti concerning Rāvaṇa’s abode, the monkeys,
thrilled and longing for the sight of Sītā, approached the ocean.
Having reached that region, those of fearsome prowess beheld it.
4.063.003c It stood like a complete reflection of the great world.
4.063.004a Having reached the northern direction from the southern ocean,
4.063.004c those best of monkeys then established their encampment together.
It was filled with various large, transformed beings playing in the water,
with mouths wide open and massive bodies, and it was agitated by waves;
in one place it appeared as if asleep, and in another as if playing.
In some places it was covered by masses of water as vast as mountains;
crowded with lords of the Dānavas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla,
the elephant-like monkeys were despondent upon seeing that hair-raising sight.

Beholding the ocean as difficult to cross as the sky, all the monkeys suddenly despaired, asking, "How shall this task be accomplished? Seeing the army dejected from the sight of the sea, [Hanumān spoke].
The best of monkeys comforted the monkeys who were afflicted by fear:
"We have no business with the Niṣāda; despondency is a far greater evil.
Despondency destroys a man, just as an angry serpent destroys a child."
4.063.011a This despondency overcomes one when the time for valor has arrived; 4.063.011c for one who is devoid of energy, the goal of human endeavor is not accomplished.
4.063.012a When that night had passed, Aṅgada, together with the monkeys, [proceeded].
Having met with the elder monkeys, he again held counsel.
That army of monkeys, surrounding Aṅgada,
shone like the host of Maruts standing around Vāsava.
"Who else besides the son of Vālin and Hanumān would be capable of holding back that monkey army? Then,
[the subduer of enemies] addressed those elder monkeys and that host..."
Having obtained permission, the illustrious Aṅgada spoke these meaningful words:
"Who now, endowed with great energy, shall leap across the ocean? Who shall make Sugrīva true to his promise, that subduer of enemies?"
"O monkeys, what hero could leap across a hundred yojanas?
And who could liberate all these troop-leaders from this great danger?
By whose favor [could one regain] wives, sons, and homes?"
"Returning from here, may we behold them with our goals accomplished and ourselves made happy. By whose grace might we, filled with joy, approach Rāma, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, and the powerful Sugrīva?"
"If any among you, O monkeys, is capable of leaping across the ocean,
let him quickly grant us here the holy gift of safety.
Having heard Angada's words, no one said anything at all.
4.063.021c That entire army of monkeys stood there as if paralyzed.
4.063.022a Again, Aṅgada, the best of monkeys, spoke to those monkeys:
4.063.022c "You are all the foremost among the powerful and possess firm valor."
Born of noble lineage and constantly honored,
you shall indeed never face any obstacle whatsoever in your journey.
O bulls among monkeys, each of you declare what power you possess for the journey.
Then, having heard the words of Aṅgada, all those best of monkeys each declared their own resolve for the journey there in due order:
Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha, and Gandhamādana.
Mainda, Dvivida, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Jāmbavān spoke;
there Gaja said, "I shall leap ten yojanas," and Gavākṣa said,
"I will go twenty yojanas."
There, Gavaya spoke to those monkeys:
"O monkeys, I shall go thirty yojanas.
There, the monkey Śarabha spoke to those monkeys:
"I shall go forty yojanas, of this there is no doubt," said the highly energetic Gandhamādana to the monkeys;
"I shall go fifty yojanas, of this there is no doubt."
Then the monkey Mainda spoke there to those monkeys:
"I am capable of leaping sixty yojanas.
Thereupon, the highly energetic Dvivida replied:
"I shall go without a doubt for seventy yojanas," [said Hanumān]. But Suṣeṇa, the best of monkeys, spoke to those foremost of monkeys: "O bulls among monkeys, I could leap eighty yojanas."
While they were speaking there,
Jāmbavān— the eldest among them— addressed them all after showing respect to everyone:
"In former times, we too possessed a certain degree of mobility and prowess."
4.064.011c We have now reached the end of our lives. 4.064.012a But even though things have come to this, it is not possible to neglect this task,
4.064.012c for which both the King of Monkeys and Rāma have made their firm resolve.
"4.064.013a Now, learn of that destination which occurs through the difference in time. 4.064.013c I shall go ninety yojanas, of this there is no doubt.
4.064.014a And Jāmbavān spoke again to all those best of monkeys:"
Indeed, my prowess in traveling was not limited to this alone;
for in the past, during the sacrifice, I circumambulated the eternal Viṣṇu as he, the Trivikrama, was taking his strides along with those of great strength.
"Now that I am old, my prowess in leaping is diminished;
yet in my youth, my strength was once unrivaled by others.
At present, however, I estimate my power for traveling to be only this much."
"By this much alone, the successful accomplishment of this task will not come to pass.
Then the highly wise Aṅgada, having paid due honor to the great monkey Jāmbavān, spoke these further words of noble meaning.
"I shall go this great hundred yojanas;
however, whether I will have the strength to return or not is not certain.
To him, Jāmbavān, the best of monkeys and skilled in speech, replied:
"O best of monkeys and bears, your power in traveling is well known;
indeed, even a hundred thousand [yojanas] would not be beyond you, for such is not said to be an impossible feat. You are capable of going and returning across these yojanas."
"For the master is by no means to be sent as a messenger;
rather, O best of monkeys, all these people here must be sent by you.
You are our protector, established in the position of our lord."
"O scorcher of enemies, the master is the refuge of the army; this is the way things are.
Therefore, O dear one, you must always protect yourself as you would a wife. Moreover, O subduer of foes, you are the very root of this undertaking."
4.064.025a The root of wealth must be protected; this is the policy of those who know how to act.

4.064.025c For when the root exists, the qualities such as flowers and fruits are accomplished. 4.064.026a Therefore, you, whose valor is true, [should exert yourself] in the accomplishment of this task.
Endowed with intelligence and prowess, you, O scorcher of foes, are the ultimate means in this matter.
For you, O best of monkeys, are both our teacher and the son of our teacher;
indeed, by relying upon you, we are capable of accomplishing our purpose.
When Jāmbavān, the highly wise one, had spoken these words, the great monkey Aṅgada,
son of Vālin, replied with this further speech:
"If I do not go, nor any other bull among monkeys..."
Furthermore, we must indeed undertake this fast unto death;
for without carrying out the command of that wise Lord of Monkeys,
even if I were to go there, I do not see any preservation of my life.
"For Hari is indeed exceedingly prone to both favor and wrath.
If one disregards his command, destruction will follow upon that departure. Therefore, act in such a way that this undertaking does not meet with failure."
"Therefore, you alone, having witnessed the facts, ought to deliberate upon this.
Thus was that heroic leader of the monkeys, Jāmbavān, addressed by Aṅgada; he then spoke these words in reply to Aṅgada.
"O hero, nothing at all shall be lacking for this task of yours.
I shall now urge on him who will accomplish the mission.
Then he spoke to the foremost of leapers, who was full of confidence.
Having retired to a secluded spot and seated himself comfortably,
that hero among monkeys exhorted Hanumān,
the foremost of monkeys.
Beholding the army of monkeys, numbering many hundreds of thousands,
despondent, Jāmbavān then spoke thus to Hanumān:
"O hero, you who have mastered all the scriptures of the monkey world..."
"4.065.002c Remaining silent in a secluded spot, Hanumān, why do you not speak?
4.065.003a Hanumān, for you are indeed equal to Sugrīva, the king of monkeys, And also equal to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in both splendor and strength."
The two sons of Ariṣṭanemi were the mighty Vainateya and Garuḍa,
who is renowned like [the son of Vinatā] and is the foremost of all birds;
for I have many times seen that one of great strength upon the ocean.
That bird of great speed and great fame, while lifting up the serpents,
possessed such strength in his wings as there was in the strength of your arms;
likewise, neither your prowess nor your speed has been diminished by him.
"O best of monkeys, your strength, intelligence, splendor, and courage are superior among all beings; why do you not recognize this about yourself?
You are an Apsaras, the most excellent of Apsarases, renowned as Puñjikasthalā."
She was known as Ajñanā, the wife of the lion-like monkey Keśarin. Due to a curse, my dear, she became a female monkey capable of changing her form at will,
the daughter of the high-souled Kuñjara, the lord of monkeys.
Once, while she was a monkey, she who possessed beautiful limbs and could assume any form at will, assuming a human body and endowed with the highest youth,
wandered upon the mountain peak which resembled a rain-cloud.
Adorned with variegated garlands and ornaments, and dressed in costly silk garments,
the yellow robe of that large-eyed woman— beautiful with its red borders—
was slowly carried away by the wind as she stood upon the mountain peak.
Then he beheld her well-knit thighs,
her full and close-set breasts, and her well-formed, lovely face;
he gazed upon that illustrious woman of broad and long hips and slender waist.
Upon seeing her,
whose every limb was beautiful, Pavana, deluded by desire, embraced that blameless woman with his two stout arms; his entire body possessed by the god of love, his very soul had departed.
But Suvṛttā, bewildered right there, spoke these words:
"Who wishes to destroy this vow of being devoted to a single husband?
Hearing Añjanā's speech, Māruta replied:

"I shall not harm you, O fair-hipped one; let there be no fear for you, O fortunate lady. Since I have approached you with my mind, O illustrious one, you shall give birth to a son who is heroic and endowed with wisdom."
Then, seeing the sun risen in the great forest, you, O child,
desiring to seize it as if it were a fruit, leaped up and rushed toward the sky;
having traveled three hundred yojanas, O great monkey—
Shaken by his splendor, he did not then succumb to despondency.
O great monkey, as he was swiftly approaching through the sky,
the wise Indra, overcome with rage, hurled his thunderbolt at him.
Then, on the peak of the mountain summit, your left jaw was shattered;
for that reason, your name is celebrated as Hanumān.
Then, seeing you struck down, Vāyu himself, the bearer of fragrances, [approached].
4.065.023c In the three worlds, the wind did not blow at all, being violently enraged.
4.065.024a When the three worlds were thus agitated, all the gods became bewildered. 4.065.024c The lords of the world propitiated the furious Wind-god.
When Pavana had been propitiated, Brahmā granted you a boon:
"O dear one of true valor, you shall be incapable of being slain by weapons in battle. And having observed that you were free from pain even by the falling of the thunderbolt, [he granted this].
The thousand-eyed one, his soul delighted, granted you this supreme boon:
"O Lord, may your death occur according to your own will.
Thus, you are the son of Keśarin, born of his wife, possessing terrible prowess.
The son of the Maruts is equal to him in splendor;
for you, O child, are the son of Vāyu and are likewise equal to him in leaping.
We are now as if our life-breath has departed, and you alone remain among us at this moment.
Endowed with skill and prowess, like another king of birds, O dear one, during the three strides, I circumambulated the earth— along with its mountains, forests, and groves—
twenty-one times from left to right.
"Then, by the command of the gods, we gathered medicinal herbs;
through them, the nectar was produced, and at that time we possessed great strength.
But now I am old and my prowess has declined."
"Now is the time for us; you are endowed with every virtue.
Therefore, O valiant one, display your prowess, for you are indeed the best among leapers. This entire army of monkeys desires to behold your heroism."
"Arise, O tiger among monkeys! Leap across the great ocean.
For your speed, Hanumān, surpasses that of all living beings.
All the monkeys are despondent; why, Hanumān, do you remain indifferent?"
"Display your prowess with great speed, like Viṣṇu taking his three strides!
Then, urged by Jāmbavān,
the monkey, the son of the Wind, exerted his full force.
Gladdening that army of monkey heroes,
he then assumed a massive form for himself;
being thus praised, the mighty Hanumān grew in stature.
Whirling his tail and filled with joy, he attained great strength;
as he was being praised by all the foremost of monkeys and was being suffused with splendor, his form became unsurpassed.
Just as a full-grown lion yawns within a mountain cave,
so now does the legitimate son of the Wind-god yawn.
As that wise one yawned, his face shone with splendor.
Resplendent like a glowing frying pan and like a smokeless fire,
Hanumān rose up from the midst of the monkeys with his hair standing on end;
having saluted the elder monkeys, he spoke these words.
The wind, the friend of fire, shattered the mountain peaks;
it was powerful, immeasurable, and its domain is the sky.
Of that great-souled one, who moves with such swift speed and rapid gait, I am the vehicle.
The son born from the breast of Maruta, there is no one equal to me in leaping. Indeed, I am able to circle Mount Meru a thousand times without attachment, as if scraping the vast sky.
4.066.009a Driven by the force of my arms, I am able to inundate the world, including its mountains, rivers, and lakes, with the ocean.
4.066.010a By the force of my thighs and shanks, [the ocean] shall be stirred up.

I am capable of overtaking from all sides, even a thousand times over, the son of Vinatā, who is frequented by birds as he flies through the sky devouring serpents, while the ocean— the abode of Varuṇa— is filled with great sea-monsters in a state of stupor.
I am prepared to approach the sun as it rises, blazing and garlanded with rays, before it has set; thereafter,
I am prepared to return without having touched the earth.
"O bulls among monkeys, with this very great and terrible speed,
I am able to surpass all those who range through the sky;
I shall agitate the ocean and I shall rend the earth."
"O monkeys, leaping through the air, I shall cause the mountains to tremble;
and leaping with the speed of my thighs, I shall carry away the great ocean.
I shall take all the flowers of the creepers, the shrubs, and the trees from every side."
Today he shall follow me as I soar through the sky;
for my path in the air will be like the path of the constellation Svāti. He shall follow me as I move through the terrible firmament and even as I spring upward.
All beings and the monkeys shall behold me as I fall; O monkeys, you shall see me, who resemble the great Mount Meru, moving through the sky,
covering the heavens as if devouring the firmament.
"I shall scatter the clouds and shake the mountains;
leaping with concentrated mind, I shall agitate the ocean.
Whether it be the power of Vainateya, or mine, or that of Māruta," so he spoke.
4.066.020c Except for the king of birds or the mighty Maruts,
4.066.020e I do not see any being who could follow me as I leap through the air. 4.066.021a In the mere twinkling of an eye, I am in the supportless sky.
I shall descend suddenly like lightning flashing from a cloud;
for my form as I leap across the ocean will be like that of Viṣṇu taking his three strides.
"By my intellect, as well as by my mind and my intuition, I clearly perceive this:
I shall see Vaidehī; rejoice, O monkeys!
I am equal to the Wind-god in speed and equal to Garuḍa in swiftness."
"It is my resolve that I shall go ten thousand yojanas;
by exerting my prowess, I shall suddenly bring that nectar here from the hand of Vāsava armed with the thunderbolt, or even from that of the self-existent Brahmā."
"It is my thought that I could even lift up Laṅkā and depart.
To that best of monkeys, who was thus roaring with immeasurable energy,
Jāmbavān, the foremost of the monkeys, spoke with great joy.
O hero, son of Kesarin, O impetuous one, son of the Wind-god!
Dear child, you have destroyed the immense sorrow of your kinsmen.
These foremost of monkeys, radiant with auspiciousness, have gathered around you.
With concentrated minds, they will perform auspicious rites for the sake of accomplishing your mission.
By the grace of the sages, by the counsel of the elder monkeys,
and by the favor of your gurus, cross over the great ocean.
"We shall stand on one foot until your return;
for the lives of all these forest-dwellers depend entirely upon you.
Then that tiger among monkeys spoke to those forest-dwellers.
"This earth will not be able to sustain my momentum as I leap;
for these peaks of Mount Mahendra, abounding with dense clusters of rocks, are both firm and vast."

"O best of monkeys, these shall support me as I leap a hundred *yojanas* from here, even as I press down upon them with my feet. Then that monkey, the son of the Wind-god, who resembled the Wind-god himself—
The crusher of enemies ascended Mahendra, the best of mountains,
which was covered with various kinds of trees, possessed grassy meadows frequented by deer,
was thick with flowering creepers, and had trees that bore fruit and flowers perpetually.
That one of great strength beheld Mount Mahendra, which was frequented by lions and tigers and inhabited by rutting elephants;
it resounded with the cries of flocks of intoxicated birds and was filled with the surging of its waters;
and it was raised high with massive peaks.
The best of monkeys, whose prowess was equal to that of Mahendra, strode about.
That great mountain, pressed down by the feet of that high-souled one,
roared like a mighty elephant in rut struck by a lion.
With its masses of rocks scattered, it released torrents of water;
its deer and elephants were terrified, and its great trees shook violently.
It was filled with various pairs of gandharvas, harsh from their indulgence in drinking.
With birds flying upward and throngs of *vidyādharas* as well,
that great mountain then had its vast ridges abandoned and its great serpents hidden; it became a place where the peaks and rocks were shattered.
With those serpents hissing as they emerged halfway out,
that mountain then appeared as if adorned with banners;
the mountain peak was being abandoned by the sages, who were agitated with fear.
Sinking as if a traveler separated from his caravan in a vast wilderness,
that heroic monkey, a slayer of enemy heroes, possessed great speed and concentrated his mind upon that velocity.
Having composed his mind, the high-souled and wise one went to Laṅkā by means of his mind.
